In contrast, subjective norms have a much stronger effect in modelling customers' intention. The most effective strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms simultaneously.

AI.tldr: A six-step Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) framework using ensembles of AI agents to estimate probabilities and applying a trimmed-mean rule to reduce noise, applied to model customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system. Findings indicate self-efficacy has a small causal impact, while subjective norms exert a stronger influence; the recommended strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between expert judgement and data-driven learning in BBN construction by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) as a panel of AI agents, enabling context-aware probability estimation without requiring large domain datasets.
AI.method: A panel of AI agents, each with specific personas and context, estimates conditional probabilities for the BBN. Responses are aggregated using a trimmed-mean rule to reduce noise. A six-step BBN framework is developed and applied to a case study modeling customers' intention to consult a doctor within an alternative healthcare system.
AI.result: The model finds that self-efficacy appears to be a major factor, but its actual causal impact is small; subjective norms have a much stronger effect on intention. The most effective strategy is to improve both confidence and community norms simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: LLM-enabled, ensemble-based probability estimation can effectively bridge expert opinion and data-driven learning in BBNs when structured within a clear framework. The approach yields practical insights for intervention design, though validation and calibration against real data are essential to ensure robustness.

title: How Much of a 10-K Matters? Aggregation-Dependent Value of Full-Text versus Risk-Factor Sentiment
summary: Financial sentiment extraction has largely relied on news text and supervised extraction against return labels alone, leaving 10-K filings -- and volatility, the target risk disclosure is arguably best suited to informing -- comparatively unexplored. We extend a supervised lexicon-learning approach to 10-K filings and their Item 1A risk-factor sections, training sentiment scores against both return and volatility labels at three levels of aggregation: sector, portfolio, and individual firm. Across 1,383 filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 technology constituents (2006--2023), we evaluate the resulting twelve sentiment metrics on classification accuracy, correlation with realised market outcomes, and qualitative lexical content. Full-filing text produces more accurate sentiment at the sector and portfolio level for both targets, but this reverses at the individual-firm level, where the narrower Item 1A section performs better -- an effect we attribute to the interaction between document volume and the amount of independent training signal available at each level of aggregation. A Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline is consistently, strongly negatively correlated with price at every level tested, underscoring the value of a supervised approach for regulatory disclosure text. These findings, and the design choices they motivate, establish the sentiment-generation methodology underlying a subsequent, larger-scale, multi-source system.

AI.tldr: Supervised lexicon-learning on 10-K risk factors yields informative sentiment signals across sector/portfolio; for individuals, full-text underperforms and Item 1A is more informative; Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline correlates negatively with price; supports building a larger multi-source sentiment system.
AI.motivation: Regulatory disclosures (10-K) are underexplored for sentiment and predictive signals compared to news; understanding how sentiment signals from different parts of filings and aggregation levels relate to returns/volatility can inform design of market-aware NLP tools.
AI.method: Train sentiment scores using a supervised lexicon-learning approach on 10-K filings and Item 1A risk-factor sections, with targets of return and volatility. Evaluate twelve sentiment metrics at three aggregation levels (sector, portfolio, firm) using 1,383 filings from 94 Nasdaq-100 tech constituents (2006–2023). Assess classification accuracy, correlation with realized market outcomes, and qualitative lexical content. Compare full-filing text vs Item 1A, and against a Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline.
AI.result: Full-filing text yields more accurate sentiment at the sector and portfolio levels for both return and volatility targets; at the individual-firm level, the narrower Item 1A section performs better due to data-volume constraints and signal availability. The Loughran-McDonald dictionary baseline shows strong negative correlation with price at all levels. Overall, results support a supervised approach and provide design guidance for a larger, multi-source sentiment system.
AI.conclusion: These findings establish the sentiment-generation methodology and justify design choices, forming the foundation for a broader, multi-source sentiment system applied to regulatory disclosure text.

title: XCT-SAM: Sequential Parameter-Efficient Domain Adaptation of SAM for Industrial XCT Defect Segmentation
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the IAPR Workshop on Machine Vision for Industrial Inspection (MVI2), in conjunction with ICPR 2026. Code: https://github.com/Mahedi-61/XCT-SAM
summary: Defect segmentation in additive manufacturing (AM) X-ray computed tomography (XCT) images remains challenging due to severe class imbalance and large distribution shifts across scan conditions. Although recent foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) provide strong general-purpose segmentation priors, their natural-image pre-training transfers poorly to the AM XCT domain, where defects appear as subtle non-semantic microstructural anomalies. Moreover, adapting SAM to the AM domain is further limited by the large domain gap and scarcity of labeled real XCT data. We present XCT-SAM, a sequential parameter-efficient adaptation framework for AM XCT defect segmentation. Instead of adapting SAM directly from natural images to XCT data, we first fine-tune Conv-LoRA adapters on an alloy-microstructure dataset and subsequently transfer the adapted model to XCT images, progressively bridging the domain gap. Using Conv-LoRA adapters with rank r=2, the framework injects convolutional spatial inductive bias into SAM's backbone while training approximately 4.15M parameters and keeping over 99% of the model frozen. We evaluate XCT-SAM on out-of-distribution CycleGAN-XCT benchmarks and real-world NIST XCT scans. Across both settings, XCT-SAM consistently outperforms zero-shot SAM and other domain-adapted SAM baselines, achieving the best overall IoU and Dice scores. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of intermediate domain adaptation with parameter-efficient adapters for industrial XCT defect segmentation. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Mahedi-61/XCT-SAM.git

AI.tldr: Sequential domain adaptation with Conv-LoRA adapters enables SAM to perform AM XCT defect segmentation with strong OOD performance using ~4.15M trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: XCT defect segmentation faces severe class imbalance and distribution shifts; SAM pretraining on natural images underperforms in XCT; scarcity of labeled XCT data; need an efficient bridging strategy.
AI.method: Fine-tune Conv-LoRA adapters on alloy microstructure data (rank r=2) to inject spatial inductive bias, then transfer the adapted model to XCT images; train ~4.15M parameters while keeping >99% of SAM frozen; evaluate on CycleGAN-XCT and real NIST XCT scans; code available.
AI.result: XCT-SAM consistently outperforms zero-shot SAM and other domain-adapted baselines on IoU and Dice across both OOD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate, parameter-efficient domain adaptation bridges the SAM-XCT gap for industrial defect segmentation; demonstrates practical potential and provides accessible code.

title: Beyond Visual Grasping: Benchmarking Complex Grasping from Detection to Execution
summary: Robust robotic grasping remains a fundamental challenge for complex real-world applications. Recent advances in large-scale models demonstrate promising capabilities for reasoning in robotic tasks. However, existing benchmarks for grasping primarily focus on isolated, visual-based grasp pose detection, failing to capture the complexity of grasping tasks that require multi-step reasoning and semantic understanding during execution. To address this gap, we propose GCA-Bench, a benchmark featuring challenging \textit{grasping with complex action} scenarios that involve both scene-level reasoning and semantic constraints. GCA-Bench enables the evaluation of recent large foundation models under the same settings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our new benchmark, we implement a diverse set of baselines, ranging from traditional grasp detection pipelines to end-to-end learning methods. Empirical studies achieve success rates below 70\% on complex grasping scenarios, underscoring critical limitations. In addition, we propose new evaluation metrics, analyze critical failure models, and provide insights to guide the development of more robust and generalizable grasping strategies.

AI.tldr: Introduces GCA-Bench, a benchmark for grasping with complex actions requiring scene-level reasoning and semantic constraints; shows current models underperform (<70% success); provides new metrics and analyses to guide robust grasping strategies.
AI.motivation: Current grasping benchmarks are limited to isolated, visual pose detection and do not capture multi-step reasoning or semantic constraints critical for real-world grasping tasks.
AI.method: Proposes GCA-Bench as a common evaluation platform; implements diverse baselines from traditional grasp detection to end-to-end learning; defines new evaluation metrics; analyzes failure modes.
AI.result: Empirical studies show success rates remain below 70% in complex scenarios, highlighting gaps in current models; the benchmark reveals critical failure modes and areas for improvement.
AI.conclusion: GCA-Bench can drive development of robust, generalizable grasping strategies and enable fair comparison of large foundation models on complex grasping tasks.

title: Capability from Access Structure, Not Scale: Lower Bounds and Pre-Registered Tests for Hybrid Sequence Models
comment: 41 pages, 16 figures. Pre-registered small-scale experiments (scorecard: 11 supported, 7 partial, 1 failed). Information-theoretic lower bounds plus controlled trained witnesses. Jianlin Chen and Ziyao Lin contributed equally. Corresponding author: Chi Man Vong (cmvong@um.edu.mo)
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that as models scale, representations of heterogeneous networks converge toward a shared model of reality. We propose its sequel and boundary, the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH): under a fixed per-token inference budget, representational convergence does not entail capability convergence. Capability instead converges toward a class, the access-complete hybrid: any architecture holding both a compressive O(1)-state channel and a scalable verbatim-index channel. We anchor it on a witness task, the Newton's-apple problem in an infinite stream, and name three resource walls: a Shannon wall barring any o(Nb)-state architecture, a horizon wall barring any fixed window, and a circuit wall barring fixed-depth attention-only composition (conditional on TC0 != NC1). Under an explicit separability assumption a hybrid crosses all three by paying each wall's price, so capability is strictly super-additive under composition. We separate what we prove from what we conjecture: the access-completeness principle rests on information-theoretic lower bounds and pre-registered experiments, while the field-level convergence trend is an economics-motivated conjecture. We report the first pre-registered small-scale tests under criteria frozen before the data: the predicted scissors gap is measured (exact-retrieval error 0.994 vs. 0.000 once a 64-scalar state gains one global-attention layer), the state-tracking bifurcation lands at the registered boundary, and a conjunction witness shows an irreducibly two-channel solution; one prediction failed with its direction reversed and is reported as such. Representational convergence is given freely by scale; capability convergence must be purchased by access structure.

AI.tldr: The paper posits two phased effects of scaling: representations in heterogeneous networks converge toward a single model of reality (Platonic Representation Hypothesis), while capabilities may not converge purely with scale. It formalizes a Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH) stating that, under a fixed per-token budget, representational convergence does not imply capability convergence; capabilities converge only when an access-complete hybrid architecture—combining a compressive O(1)-state channel with a scalable verbatim-index channel—is present. Anchored by a witness task (Newton’s-apple problem in an infinite stream) and bounded by three walls (Shannon: no o(Nb)-state; horizon: no fixed window; circuit: fixed-depth attention-only; conditional on TC0 ≠ NC1). Under a separability assumption, a hybrid can cross all walls by paying each price, making capability strictly super-additive under composition. The authors separate proven results (information-theoretic lower bounds, pre-registered experiments) from conjectured field-level convergence (economics-motivated). They report initial pre-registered small-scale tests: a predicted scissors gap (exact retrieval error 0.994 vs 0.000 after a 64-scalar state gains a global-attention layer), a state-tracking bifurcation at the registered boundary, and a two-channel irreducible conjunction witness; one prediction failed with reversed direction and is disclosed. Overall, representational convergence scales freely; capability convergence must be purchased via access structure.
AI.motivation: To disentangle whether scaling of heterogeneous-model representations also yields convergent capabilities, and to formalize the distinction with information-theoretic and resource-based bounds. The work aims to separate robust, scalable representation convergence from the potentially harder, costlier convergence of capabilities, guided by explicit walls and a witness task, and to pre-register small-scale tests to probe the boundaries.
AI.method: Theoretical framework introducing the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) and Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH). Use of information-theoretic lower bounds, a witness task (Newton’s-apple problem in an infinite stream), and three architectural/resource constraints (Shannon wall, horizon wall, circuit wall). A separability assumption enabling a crossover hybrid that incurs costs per wall and yields super-additivity under composition. Empirical validation via pre-registered, small-scale experiments with clearly defined metrics (exact-retrieval error, state-tracking bifurcation, conjunction witness).
AI.result: A boundary is drawn: scale yields representational convergence; capability convergence requires specific access structures and is not guaranteed by scale alone. The first pre-registered tests partially validate predictions: a large predicted scissors gap turns into near-perfect retrieval once a global-attention layer is added (64-scalar state), the state-tracking bifurcation aligns with the boundary, and a two-channel irreducible conjunction witness is observed. One prediction’s direction was reversed. The results support a separation between representational convergence and capability convergence, with the latter being purchasable via access structure; some predictions remain contested or require refinement.
AI.conclusion: Scale suffices for representational convergence in heterogeneous networks, but capability convergence is contingent on the availability of an access-complete hybrid and is not automatically achieved by scaling alone. The framework cleanly separates what is proven from what is conjectured and highlights economically-driven considerations for field-wide convergence. Further replication and broader-scale tests are needed to confirm the generality of the CCH and to refine the wall-based bounds.

title: Low-Latency Relay Selection in NR-V2X Vehicular Communications via Graph Isomorphism Networks with Edge Features
summary: Reliable, low-latency uplink connectivity is a key requirement for C-V2X networks in dense urban environments, where fast channel variations and blockages often degrade direct vehicle-to-infrastructure links. Multi-hop relaying can restore coverage, but relay-link activation under radio, capacity, and routing constraints results in an NP-hard optimisation problem, typically solved via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), whose runtime scales poorly with graph size. This paper introduces an edge-aware Learning-to-Optimise framework for real-time relay selection. Each V2X snapshot is modelled as a directed graph: node features encode vehicle state and traffic demand, while edge features capture radio-link capacity. An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay configurations that supervise a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE), enabling edge-level relay activation through a single forward pass, with tightly bounded inference latency. To bridge learning and exact optimisation, we also propose a hybrid GINE-Pruned MILP (GP-MILP) strategy in which GINE predictions prune the MILP search space. Experiments on a large-scale dataset generated via an OSM-SUMO-GEMV$^2$ pipeline show that GINE closely matches MILP decisions at the link level (accuracy 0.9589), F1-score (0.9544) on validation) and yields consistent end-to-end connectivity gains over a 1-hop MILP baseline (up to 9.2% with four RSUs and 12% with two RSUs). Inference latency remains tightly bounded, with all evaluated instances completing within 5~ms. Moreover, GP-MILP preserves MILP-equivalent solutions (same objective value) while achieving solver runtimes below 30~ms for more than 98%) of the graph instances, making MILP-grade optimisation compatible with stringent NR-V2X latency budgets.

AI.tldr: An edge-aware learning-to-optimize framework using GINE to predict relay activation for multi-hop C-V2X; achieves near-MILP-optimal decisions with low latency and GP-MILP pruning for MILP-grade solutions within tight NR-V2X budgets.
AI.motivation: In dense urban NR-V2X, reliable low-latency uplink faces fast channel variation and blockages; relay selection is NP-hard and MILP scales poorly; need real-time, latency-bounded decisions.
AI.method: Model V2X snapshots as directed graph; node features: vehicle state, traffic demand; edge features: radio-link capacity. Use offline MILP to generate optimal relay configs as supervision for a Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge Features (GINE). Train to enable edge-level activation in one forward pass. Propose GP-MILP where GINE predictions prune MILP search. Dataset from an OSM-SUMO-GEMV2 pipeline. Evaluate on a large-scale dataset; compare to 1-hop MILP baseline.
AI.result: GINE accuracy 0.9589; F1-score 0.9544 on validation; end-to-end connectivity gains: up to 9.2% with four RSUs, 12% with two RSUs; latency <=5 ms across instances; GP-MILP maintains MILP-equivalent objective values while runtime <30 ms for >98% of instances, enabling MILP-grade optimisation under strict budgets.
AI.conclusion: Edge-aware L2O via GINE provides real-time, near-optimal relay decisions for C-V2X with bounded latency; GP-MILP offers a practical compromise between speed and optimality, demonstrating feasibility for NR-V2X in dense networks.

title: DCVC-MB: Neural B-Frame Video Compression using State Space Models
summary: In this paper we propose DCVC-Mamba (DCVC-MB), a neural video codec framework for B-frame coding. Our approach incorporates an IBP frame strategy for low-delay B-frame coding, a spatio-temporal fusion model based on state-space models for bidirectional temporal prediction, and an entropy-aware skipping mechanism that selectively omits coding certain latents to reduce entropy coding times. In addition to our model contributions we also implement two inference-time strategies that enhance compression performance. Experimental evaluation shows that DCVC-MB compares favorably to existing NVCs and traditional codecs. The method demonstrates BD-rate reductions of up to $8.98\%$ on average compared to prior neural video codecs, and improvements of up to $30.45\%$ and $1.81\%$ over the VTM-19.0-LDP and VTM-19.0-RA(Inter-GoP=16) benchmarks, respectively, contributing to advances in neural video compression.

AI.tldr: A neural video codec (DCVC-Mamba) tailored for B-frame coding, introducing an IBP frame strategy, a spatio-temporal fusion model with state-space bidirectional prediction, and an entropy-aware latent skipping mechanism, plus inference-time strategies. It achieves BD-rate reductions up to 8.98% vs prior neural codecs and gains over VTM benchmarks, indicating meaningful improvements in neural video compression for low-delay B-frames.
AI.motivation: Improve efficiency and practicality of neural video codecs for B-frame coding by (i) enabling low-delay B-frame coding (IBP frame strategy), (ii) enhancing bidirectional temporal prediction with a state-space fusion model, (iii) reducing entropy coding time via selective latent skipping, and (iv) demonstrating performance gains with inference-time strategies and comparisons to traditional codecs.
AI.method: Propose DCVC-Mamba (DCVC-MB) featuring: (1) IBP-based low-delay B-frame coding strategy, (2) a spatio-temporal fusion module based on state-space models for bidirectional temporal prediction, (3) an entropy-aware mechanism to skip certain latents during encoding/decoding to reduce entropy coding workload, (4) two inference-time strategies to boost compression performance.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation shows DCVC-MB outperforms existing neural video codecs and traditional codecs, with BD-rate reductions up to 8.98% on average against prior neural codecs, and improvements up to 30.45% and 1.81% over VTM-19.0-LDP and VTM-19.0-RA(Inter-GoP=16), respectively.
AI.conclusion: DCVC-MB advances neural video compression for B-frame coding, delivering notable bitrate savings and demonstrating the effectiveness of combining IBP low-delay frame strategy, state-space bidirectional fusion for temporal prediction, and entropy-aware latent skipping, reinforced by inference-time strategies.

title: An offline approach to fNIRS-guided reinforcement learning for robot behavior
summary: Human-in-the-loop Reinforcement Learning has become a popular approach to training, finetuning, and aligning robot behavior with user preferences. Our paper explores the feasibility of using brain signals via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to modulate robot learning in simulation. We compare agents trained on passive (observational) versus active (demonstrative) interaction tasks, and test multiple methods for enhancing the RL algorithm with the neural signal, focusing on parameter augmentation rather than replacement. We further examine how model granularity and noise affect agent learning. Our results show that this framework is effective: the neural signal improves learning when augmenting trajectory priorities and state-action q-values. Additionally, the framework learns successfully from offline data, offering a practical alternative for settings where real-time BCI setups are impractical or only limited data is available.

AI.tldr: Using fNIRS brain signals to augment RL learning in simulation via parameter augmentation improves learning, with benefits to trajectory prioritization and Q-value updates; effective for both passive and active tasks and usable with offline data, offering a practical alternative to real-time BCI.
AI.motivation: To enhance human-in-the-loop RL by leveraging non-invasive brain signals, enabling more efficient robot learning and alignment with user preferences, and to address scenarios where real-time BCI is impractical by exploiting offline data.
AI.method: Evaluate fNIRS-based signals as parameter augmentation rather than replacement in RL. Compare passive (observational) versus active (demonstrative) interactions. Analyze effects of model granularity and noise. Apply augmentations to trajectory priorities and state-action Q-values. Test learning from offline data in simulation.
AI.result: Neural signals augmented into RL improve learning when used to adjust trajectory priorities and Q-values. The framework can also learn from offline data, increasing practicality when real-time BCI is not feasible. Effects are studied across granularity/noise settings and interaction types.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-augmentation of RL with fNIRS brain signals is feasible and beneficial, enabling improved learning and offline applicability, and suggesting a viable path for neural-guided RL without relying on direct signal replacement.

title: ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability
summary: Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: ToolAnchor mitigates behavioral inertia in tool-augmented LLM agents by injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at decision points, enabling the use of new tools without full retraining; it uses teacher models to hypothesize contexts, verifies via rollouts, and internalizes interventions through post-training, achieving competitive performance across GAIA, BrowseComp, and VDR-Bench.
AI.motivation: To overcome the core obstacle of expanding toolsets for long-horizon agents: behavioral inertia that causes agents to revert to known tools and reasoning patterns even when new tools are available.
AI.method: ToolAnchor framework: teacher models hypothesize counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points; student rollouts verify these contexts; successful interventions are internalized through agentic post-training to update the agent.
AI.result: Across GAIA (general AI assistant), BrowseComp (textual search), and VDR-Bench (visual search) tasks, ToolAnchor consistently achieves competitive performance under expanded toolsets.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a bridge between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, proposing a scalable path for agentic RL by learning to override inertia with counterfactual interventions.

title: RENEW: Towards Learning World Models and Repairing Model Exploitation from Preferences
summary: World models are widely used in offline reinforcement learning (RL) to improve sample efficiency and generate experience beyond a fixed dataset. However, they are vulnerable to model exploitation where data coverage is thin. Prior work addresses this either by collecting more expert demonstrations, which is often expensive, unsafe, or unavailable, or by conservative algorithms that avoid uncertain regions, which limits generalization. We propose instead to repair exploitation directly using human preferences over imagined rollouts, leveraging the strong intuitive physics that allows humans to easily spot egregious dynamics hallucinations. We formalize this as Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF), a Bradley-Terry preference loss over trajectory log-likelihoods under a learned dynamics model. Unfortunately, naive DLHF is sample inefficient, so we introduce RENEW, which uses epistemic uncertainty to focus finetuning where the model is most exploitable. We evaluate on several Jumanji and classic control environments and find that while naive DLHF requires an outsize preference budget, RENEW makes the framework practical by improving sample efficiency, limiting catastrophic forgetting, and reducing exploitation in pretrained world models. Taken together, our results provide initial evidence that preferences can supervise world model dynamics directly, offering a new approach to addressing exploitation in offline model-based RL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF) to repair exploited dynamics in offline world models, and its data-efficient variant RENEW that uses epistemic uncertainty to focus fine-tuning on exploitable regions.
AI.motivation: Offline model-based RL suffers from exploitation when data coverage is thin; existing remedies (more demonstrations or conservatism) have drawbacks. Human preferences over imagined rollouts offer a scalable, intuitive signal to align dynamics.
AI.method: Formalize DLHF as a Bradley-Terry preference loss over trajectory log-likelihoods under a learned dynamics model; identify naive DLHF as sample-inefficient. Develop RENEW, which uses epistemic uncertainty to steer fine-tuning toward regions where the model is most exploitable.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Jumanji and classic control shows naive DLHF requires a large preference budget, while RENEW improves sample efficiency, curbs catastrophic forgetting, and reduces exploitation in pretrained world models.
AI.conclusion: Preferences can supervise world-model dynamics directly, providing a practical approach to mitigate exploitation in offline model-based RL through targeted, uncertainty-guided learning.

title: SD-MAR: Multi-image Analytical Reasoning via Synthetic Data and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate strong perceptual abilities but remain limited in tasks requiring analytical reasoning across multiple visual states, such as multi-image comparison, change detection, and multi-step visual inference. These capabilities are critical for real-world multimodal applications where reasoning must be grounded in systematic differences between visual contexts. However, existing benchmarks rarely require both explicit visual comparison and analytical reasoning, leaving this capability underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce SD-MAR (Synthetic Data for Multi-image Analytical Reasoning), a framework for training and evaluating VLMs on multi-image analytical reasoning. SD-MAR constructs paired visual scenarios through controlled perturbations and generates reasoning tasks spanning semantic change attribution and quantitative comparison. We further train VLMs using GRPO-lite with Backward Discounted Allocation (BDA), a reinforcement learning approach that removes KL regularization to encourage stronger policy optimization while allocating greater credit to the later reasoning steps where analytical conclusions are formed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B show that GRPO-lite fine-tuning on SD-MAR improves in-domain accuracy by up to 36.95%, with Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforming GPT-4.1 on the SD-MAR benchmark. Importantly, out-of-domain generalization is preserved or improved: performance remains within 1% on MME, MMMU-Pro, and MathVista, while improving by up to 4% on MMBench. LLM-as-judge evaluation further demonstrates consistent improvements in logical coherence and explanation quality across both models.

AI.tldr: SD-MAR provides synthetic data for multi-image analytical reasoning and trains VLMs with GRPO-lite + Backward Discounted Allocation (BDA); yields substantial in-domain gains (up to ~37%) and robust out-of-domain generalization, with improved reasoning quality.
AI.motivation: VLMs struggle with tasks requiring explicit visual comparison and multi-step reasoning across multiple visual states. Existing benchmarks rarely combine explicit comparison with analytical inference, limiting evaluation and training for this capability. SD-MAR aims to fill this gap with synthetic paired scenarios and a specialized RL fine-tuning approach.
AI.method: SD-MAR constructs paired visual scenarios via controlled perturbations to enable semantic change attribution and quantitative comparison tasks. Fine-tuning uses GRPO-lite with Backward Discounted Allocation (BDA), a reinforcement learning regime that removes KL regularization to encourage stronger policy optimization and credits later reasoning steps where conclusions form.
AI.result: In-domain accuracy improves up to 36.95% on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B; Qwen2.5-VL-7B surpasses GPT-4.1 on the SD-MAR benchmark. Out-of-domain generalization remains or improves: accuracy within 1% on MME, MMMU-Pro, and MathVista; up to +4% on MMBench. LLM-as-judge evaluation shows consistent gains in logical coherence and explanation quality across both models.
AI.conclusion: SD-MAR paired data plus GRPO-lite with BDA enables effective multi-image analytical reasoning in VLMs and generalizes well to unseen domains; the RL approach enhances credit assignment to later reasoning steps, yielding stronger reasoning capabilities and explanation quality.

title: ConFlow: Constraints-Guided Learning with Flow Matching for Motion Generation
comment: RSS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion for Robot Learning
summary: In recent years Flow Matching has become a prominent method for generative modeling robot motion generation. In its generic form Flow Matching is an ODE-based neural sampler that is trained by regressing empirical flow fields associated with motion samples as data. However, in robot motion generation we often have additional constraints that might not be present in the collected data. The majority of current approaches train the flow on the available data and use inference-time guidance to enforce task-specific constraints. To address this mismatch, we propose \textbf{ConFlow}, a constraint-guided flow matching framework that incorporates constraint information directly into the training objective via differentiable barrier or cost functions. To address design specifications such as smoothness and boundary conditions, we propose replacing the standard Gaussian source distribution used in flow matching training with a conditional Gaussian Process. Our approach also uses infeasible demonstrations as negative supervision, improving constraint satisfaction without requiring additional expert data. Experiments on a two-robot navigation task demonstrate that ConFlow achieves lower collision rates and higher trajectory quality than standard flow matching baselines, with or without inference-time guidance. These results validate training-time constraint integration as an effective approach to closing the training--inference gap in generative motion models.

AI.tldr: ConFlow tightly integrates motion constraints into flow-matching training, using a constraint-aware objective with differentiable barriers, a conditional Gaussian Process source, and negative demonstrations, achieving better constrained robot motion than standard flow matching baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between constrained robot motion generation data and unconstrained training objectives in Flow Matching by bringing constraint information into training to improve constraint satisfaction and compliance.
AI.method: Introduce ConFlow: a constraint-guided flow-matching framework that adds differentiable barrier/cost terms to the training objective, replaces Gaussian sources with a conditional Gaussian Process to enforce smoothness and boundary conditions, and uses infeasible demonstrations as negative supervision to improve constraint satisfaction without extra expert data.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a two-robot navigation task showing lower collision rates and higher trajectory quality compared to standard flow-matching baselines, with or without inference-time guidance.
AI.conclusion: Training-time integration of constraints via barriers, constrained sources, and negative demonstrations effectively closes the training–inference gap and enhances constrained generative motion models.

title: Enhancing Small Language Models Reasoning through Knowledge Graph Grounding
comment: Presented at the 2nd Causal Neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence (Causal NeSy): Toward Agentic LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic and Graph Based Reasoning Workshop @ ESWC2026
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. Our approach transforms the SLM into a minimalist agent utilizing two specialized tool calls: extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction and get_hint for expert reasoning via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). We evaluate these models across two configurations, both in an Oracle scenario with ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge. Our results reveal that while RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5 - 2x performance gain over story-only baselines, the system is constrained by the extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early extraction errors compound over multi-hop chains. Furthermore, we identify a "distraction effect" in specific architectures where noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite the presence of expert hints. This work characterizes the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and provides a roadmap for iterative verification in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic agentic framework enhances small language models with symbolic extraction and RGCN-based hints for multi-hop reasoning on CLUTRR, achieving 1.5–2x gains but limited by extraction bottlenecks, error propagation, and distraction from self-generated facts.
AI.motivation: Large language models are powerful but costly; scalable, low-resource agents struggle with multi-hop reasoning. Introducing symbolic grounding via an RGCN and explicit fact extraction aims to improve SLM reasoning while maintaining efficiency.
AI.method: Treat SLMs as minimalist agents equipped with two tools: extract_facts to extract symbolic triplets from narratives and get_hint to obtain reasoning hints via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network. Evaluate Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B) on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark in two configurations: Oracle (ground-truth triplets) and Realistic (self-extracted knowledge). Compare against story-only baselines.
AI.result: RGCN-provided hints yield ~1.5–2x improvements over story-only baselines. Gains are tempered by an extraction bottleneck and the fragility of sequential deduction, where early extraction errors cascade through multi-hop reasoning. A “distraction effect” is observed when noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite having expert hints.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic grounding in low-resource, agentic NLP systems is challenging; the work maps the key bottlenecks and points toward iterative verification and robust grounding strategies in neuro-symbolic pipelines.

title: Closed-Loop Knowledge Dynamics: An Operational Framework for Saturation and Escape
summary: Feedback-driven loops support iterative improvement in large language models, reinforcement learning, and autonomous discovery, yet their gains often diminish under repeated internal feedback. We study why closed-loop knowledge systems saturate and what external information can move them beyond their current attractors. We introduce a three-level operational framework in which knowledge states $x_t$ evolve through transition kernels $K_θ$ indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. The governing structure is defined as the observational equivalence class of $θ$ induced by these kernels, while attractors and basins are properties of the fixed-$θ$ dynamics. A structural intervention changes $θ$ and produces a detectable kernel discrepancy on pre-specified probe states, making structural change falsifiable. Using a Lyapunov drift condition, we show that stable internal dynamics approach bounded stability regions with exponentially attenuated transients and a noise-controlled residual floor. We characterize escape through a metric condition on intervention-induced attractor displacement and a baseline-relative KL lower bound for increasing escape probability. This analysis also explains why conditional mutual information alone cannot certify escape: it measures variation among intervention-conditioned updates rather than departure from the no-intervention law. Case studies in LLM code repair, sparse-reward reinforcement learning, and Bayesian optimization use matched continuation controls to illustrate how feedback strength and alignment affect quality-improving escape. Our contribution is an operational connection among stability tools, measurable intervention effects, and cross-domain diagnostics.

AI.tldr: Three-level framework for closed-loop knowledge systems; external structural interventions can shift attractors via kernel discrepancies, enabling escape from saturation; links Lyapunov stability to intervention metrics and KL-based escape criteria; demonstrated in LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, and Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Explain why feedback-driven loops saturate and how external information can move systems beyond current attractors; connect stability analysis with measurable intervention effects and cross-domain diagnostics.
AI.method: Model knowledge states x_t evolving through transition kernels K_θ indexed by θ; define governing structure as the observational equivalence class of θ; treat attractors/basins as fixed-θ properties; apply structural interventions that change θ and yield detectable kernel discrepancies on probe states; use Lyapunov drift to show stability implies bounded regions with exponentially damped transients and a noise floor; characterize escape via a metric on intervention-induced attractor displacement and a baseline-relative KL lower bound for increasing escape probability; explain why conditional mutual information alone cannot certify escape; illustrate with case studies (LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, Bayesian optimization) using matched continuation controls.
AI.result: Establishes conditions for stable dynamics within bounded regions, with exponentially decaying transients and a noise-controlled residual; provides quantitative metrics (intervention-induced attractor displacement and KL-based bounds) to gauge escape probability; clarifies limitations of conditional mutual information for escape certification; case studies demonstrate how feedback strength and alignment influence quality-improving escape across domains.
AI.conclusion: Provides an operational link among stability tools, measurable intervention effects, and cross-domain diagnostics; informs design of structural interventions to overcome saturation in feedback-driven knowledge systems.

title: MixCompress: Mixture of Experts for Variable Rate Learned Image Compression
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) is bottlenecked by the need to store independent models for each rate-distortion operating point. Existing variable bit-rate (VBR) methods aim to reduce this overhead via dense parameter modulation, but forcing a shared backbone to approximate divergent mappings causes severe feature entanglement. Specifically, low-rate smoothing gradients inherently conflict with the preservation of high-frequency textural details, leading to sub-optimal performance. To resolve this, we propose MixCompress, a unified VBR framework based on sparse structural specialization. While sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing successfully mitigates gradient conflict, it operates on a fixed computational budget. To address the increased representational demands of higher bit-rates we introduce a Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) extension to dynamically scale model capacity. Combined with Conditional Auxiliary Transforms (CAT) for dynamic sub-band energy modulation, our hierarchical framework effectively dynamically scales capacity. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MixCompress not only matches individually optimized single-rate baselines but can even surpass them, establishing a new Pareto frontier for computationally efficient image coding.

AI.tldr: MixCompress introduces a unified variable-rate image compression framework using sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing with a Mixture-of-Depths extension to dynamically scale capacity, plus Conditional Auxiliary Transforms for sub-band modulation, achieving competitive performance across rates with a single model.
AI.motivation: Address the storage and gradient-conflict inefficiencies of traditional VBR LIC systems that require separate models per rate-point, and reduce feature entanglement and high-frequency loss at low rates.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework: (1) sparse gating Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing to allocate capacity without fixed budgets, (2) Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) to scale model capacity with bit-rate demands, (3) Conditional Auxiliary Transforms (CAT) to dynamically modulate sub-band energies, enabling flexible rate adaptation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show MixCompress matches or surpasses individually optimized single-rate baselines and sets a new Pareto frontier for computation-efficient image coding.
AI.conclusion: A unified, dynamically scalable VBR framework that alleviates gradient conflict and entanglement while delivering high-quality compression across rates without retraining multiple models.

title: Motion Planning with Model-Based Diffusion via Constraint Optimization and Adaptive Scheduling
summary: Single-Robot Motion Planning (SRMP) in highly non-convex constrained environments, where robots must satisfy collision-free guarantees, dynamic feasibility, and task-related constraints, is challenging under complex constraints and computational limits. Recent Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) approaches recast the SRMP as trajectory optimization that samples from a posterior over trajectories, using known dynamics, and analytically estimates the score function from rollout samples to guide diffusion denoising toward a low-cost, clean trajectory without demonstration learning. While existing works further adapt MBD to constrained environments and showcase promising performance, they are still limited by (1) enforcing safety either via soft feasibility diffusion priors or hard projection operators, but lack a unified framework to integrate both, and (2) fixing safety enforcement to neglect the changing of diffusion scheduling. Therefore, we introduce Model-Based Diffusion via Constraint Optimization and Adaptive Scheduling (MD-COAS) for SRMP that unifies the inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method (iALM) soft diffusion prior with a Convex Feasible Set (CFS)-based hard projection operator, and adaptively schedules and co-optimizes safety enforcement, along with diffusion scheduling. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher safety \& success rates, faster convergence, and lower final costs than baseline planners on randomly generated highly non-convex 2D benchmarks and a 7-DoF robot arm avoidance task.

AI.tldr: MD-COAS unifies inexact iALM soft diffusion priors with a Convex Feasible Set hard projection and adaptive scheduling to improve single-robot motion planning under non-convex constraints, outperforming baselines on 2D benchmarks and a 7-DoF arm task.
AI.motivation: SRMP under highly non-convex constraints requires reliable safety and feasibility guarantees within computational limits. Existing MBD methods either rely on soft priors or hard projections but lack a unified framework and do not adapt safety enforcement to diffusion scheduling, limiting performance.
AI.method: Introduce MD-COAS: Model-Based Diffusion via Constraint Optimization and Adaptive Scheduling that combines an inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method soft diffusion prior with a Convex Feasible Set hard projection operator, and jointly and adaptively schedules safety enforcement and diffusion steps.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show higher safety and success rates, faster convergence, and lower final costs compared to baseline planners on randomly generated highly non-convex 2D benchmarks and a 7-DoF robotic arm avoidance task.
AI.conclusion: MD-COAS provides a unified framework for integrating soft and hard safety mechanisms with adaptive diffusion scheduling in MBD-based SRMP, yielding improved performance and robustness in non-convex constrained environments.

title: Orchestrating Power Grid Studies with Multi-Agent AI and MCP Servers
summary: This position paper explores how Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) can support power-grid studies in a Transmission System Operator (TSO) context. We focus on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision. We identify key industrial requirements for agent assisted grid studies and introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface exposing selected capabilities of our simulation tool, pypowsybl to AI agents. This first step provides a testbed to study how agents can setup simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls. We also discuss principles for human-in-the-loop, multi-agent workflows and outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback. The paper positions MCP-based tool integration as a step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments.

AI.tldr: Agentic AI with Model Context Protocol (MCP) is proposed to enable agent-assisted power-grid studies in a TSO setting by exposing selected pypowsybl capabilities to AI agents through an MCP-based interface, enabling automated setup, execution, and retrieval of simulations, with human-in-the-loop and multi-agent workflows evaluated via technical metrics and practitioner feedback.
AI.motivation: The need for interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments that integrate AI agents with numerical power-system simulators, addressing industrial requirements for agent-assisted studies and governance.
AI.method: Introduce Agentic AI and MCP to expose a subset of pypowsybl capabilities through a dedicated MCP-based interface (pypowsybl-mcp). Develop a testbed enabling AI agents to set up simulations, run analyses, fetch results, and interact with power-system simulators via standardized tool calls. Discuss human-in-the-loop principles, multi-agent workflows, and an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback.
AI.result: First-step testbed demonstrating the feasibility of agent-driven grid studies within an MCP-enabled interface; outlines principles for human-in-the-loop and multi-agent workflows and proposes an evaluation strategy.
AI.conclusion: MCP-based tool integration advances interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments, forming a foundation for more capable agent-assisted grid studies in TSO contexts.

title: A Temporal Machine Learning-Based Time-to-Event Model for Predicting ALS Progression and Healthcare Utilization
summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease in which predicting clinically meaningful milestones, such as assistive device use, remains challenging. We developed a time-to-event, digital-twin-inspired framework that integrates longitudinal ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) trajectories with survival modeling to support individualized prediction of functional decline and assistive device utilization. We constructed a harmonized longitudinal dataset by integrating diagnosis records, ALSFRS-R assessments, activities of daily living, and demographic information, followed by preprocessing to ensure data quality, temporal alignment, and cohort consistency. Correlation-based clustering identified coherent functional domains spanning bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, and respiratory systems. Generalized additive mixed models characterized nonlinear, domain-specific functional decline across all domains. In addition, a temporal machine learning model was developed to predict longitudinal functional decline and capture stage-dependent disease progression. Cox proportional hazards modeling further identified lower limb function, particularly walking and stair climbing, as the strongest predictors of earlier wheelchair access. Building on these results, we implemented a digital twin-inspired temporal machine learning-based time-to-event (TTE) model that generates individualized survival curves and dynamically predicts wheelchair-free survival. This framework provides a scalable, interpretable, and clinically actionable approach for linking ALS progression with personalized decision support, with applications in proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine.

AI.tldr: A digital-twin-inspired, time-to-event framework links longitudinal ALSFRS-R trajectories with survival modeling to predict functional decline and wheelchair-free survival, integrating harmonized data and domain-specific clustering.
AI.motivation: To enable individualized prediction of functional milestones and assistive device use in ALS, addressing heterogeneity and timing for proactive care and trial design.
AI.method: Harmonized dataset of diagnosis, ALSFRS-R, activities of daily living, and demographics; correlation-based clustering to identify functional domains; generalized additive mixed models for nonlinear, domain-specific decline; a temporal machine learning model to predict longitudinal decline; Cox proportional hazards modeling to identify predictors; a digital-twin-inspired time-to-event model to generate individualized survival curves and wheelchair-free predictions.
AI.result: Identified functional domains (bulbar, upper limb, axial, lower limb, respiratory); walking and stair climbing are the strongest predictors of earlier wheelchair access; the TTE model provides personalized survival curves and dynamic wheelchair-free predictions; framework is scalable, interpretable, and clinically actionable.
AI.conclusion: Framework supports clinically actionable decision support for proactive care planning, clinical trial stratification, and precision medicine in ALS.

title: Beyond scalar losses: calibrating segmentation models via gradient vector field surgery
summary: Region-based loss functions, such as the Dice loss, have established themselves as the de facto standard for highly class- and region-imbalanced segmentation tasks. However, models trained using region-based loss functions are notoriously miscalibrated and typically yield over-confident predictions. In medical imaging applications, such as defining tumor resection margins, this miscalibration is hindering clinical adoption. In this work, we outline a novel gradient perspective on this overconfidence and show how it affects region-based loss functions. We propose a "surgery" on the gradient vector field as a simple, yet effective intervention to mitigate calibration issues. This surgery adds a factor to the loss's partial derivative, scaling the gradient's magnitude linearly with the prediction error. In empirical evaluations across 2D and 3D medical segmentation tasks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this intervention while maintaining high prediction accuracy when used in conjunction with any region-based loss function.

AI.tldr: Gradient-based calibration improvement for region-based segmentation losses via a gradient surgery that scales gradients with prediction error; improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy across 2D/3D medical tasks.
AI.motivation: Region-based losses (e.g., Dice) often produce overconfident predictions in imbalanced segmentation, hindering clinical adoption. A calibration-aware training objective is needed in medical imaging.
AI.method: Analyze gradient dynamics of region-based losses and introduce a simple gradient modification—the 'gradient surgery'—that multiplies the loss gradient by a factor proportional to the prediction error. This factor can be applied on top of any region-based loss such as Dice or IoU.
AI.result: Calibration improves (reduced overconfidence) while maintaining or improving segmentation accuracy across 2D and 3D medical imaging tasks when combined with existing region-based losses.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight, generalizable gradient-based intervention can mitigate miscalibration in region-based segmentation without sacrificing performance, potentially accelerating clinical adoption.

title: Mixed-Agent Museum Tour Guide Design Improves Gendered Learning Outcomes and Visitor Preferences
summary: Robots are increasingly integrated into everyday contexts, including museums, where they can both entertain and educate visitors. To enhance visitor experience and engagement, we present a novel mixed-agent tour guide system that combines a physical robot with a projected virtual agent that actively participates in the tour through conversation and interaction, achieving the interaction richness of two mobile agents from a single platform. We validate the system through a within-subjects study with 30 participants to assess engagement, quality of experience, and learning performance. Participants experienced different conversational styles and agent configurations, and data were collected via surveys, behavioral sensors, and interviews. Results showed that engagement and quality of experience remained consistent across conditions. Learning performance revealed a significant gender-moderated difference: the mixed-agent conditions improved learning performance for female participants. This suggests that the proposed dyadic conversational style in this paper influenced learning performance differently by gender. Nonetheless, in interviews, participants reported a greater preference for mixed-agent teams regardless of gender, citing interaction as a key factor in their experience.

AI.tldr: A mixed-agent tour guide combining a physical robot with a projected virtual agent enhances interaction richness; within-subjects study (n=30) shows stable engagement/QoE with mixed-agent setups and gender-modulated improvements in learning for female participants; overall preference for mixed-agent teams.
AI.motivation: To enhance museum visitor experience by delivering richer, dyadic conversation through a single platform, leveraging both physical and projected agents.
AI.method: Within-subjects experiment with 30 participants testing different conversational styles and agent configurations; measures include engagement, quality of experience, and learning performance; data collected via surveys, behavioral sensors, and interviews.
AI.result: Engagement and QoE remained consistent across conditions; learning performance showed a significant gender-moderated improvement for female participants under mixed-agent conditions; participants preferred mixed-agent teams in interviews.
AI.conclusion: The dyadic conversational style in the mixed-agent system can sustain engagement while potentially enhancing learning for certain groups; interaction with both agents is a key driver of preference; results motivate further exploration of gender effects and design of co-active agent interactions.

title: MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience
summary: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

AI.tldr: MemoHarness is an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions to customize per-case control settings of an agent harness via a dual-layer experience bank, enabling retrieval-based, test-time adaptation without labels or extra search.
AI.motivation: Harness design strongly shapes agent behavior, yet most improvements target narrow artifacts and static, global harnesses; adaptive, experience-driven harness customization promises better task-specific performance and efficiency.
AI.method: Decompose the harness into six editable control dimensions (context management, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, output handling); maintain per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank; adapt the harness for a test case by retrieving past executions without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search; evaluate on shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks; compare against fixed harness baselines and assess transfer to unseen suites/models and cacheability of retrieved context.
AI.result: MemoHarness outperforms fixed harness baselines across multiple domains; shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models; added context can be cost-competitive when retrieved experience is largely cacheable; supports the claim that execution experience is a practical substrate for adaptive harnesses.
AI.conclusion: Execution experience can underpin more adaptive agent harnesses than a single static configuration; broader claims about robustness and component attribution require future work.

title: TEDDY: A Pediatric Foundation Model for Risk Forewarning from ICD-Coded Diagnostic Histories
summary: Pediatric electronic health records capture developmentally structured clinical trajectories, yet their potential for generative healthcare foundation models remains largely unexplored. Here we present TEDDY (Temporal Event Decoder for Disease in Youth), a 1.84-million-parameter decoder transformer trained on approximately 73 million ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6 million children at a single pediatric institution. TEDDY models longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing. Predictions were made before visit codes were revealed, limited to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls. Across 797 disease-onset prediction tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters, TEDDY achieved a median AUC of 72.0%, outperforming same-data DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), and LSTM (62.7%) baselines on 96-99% of tasks. Performance held across sex and age and was strongest among lower-prevalence diagnoses; 202 of the 225 rarest conditions (90%) had 95% confidence intervals above chance. Predictive signal remained detectable more than two years before first recorded diagnosis, with median AUCs of 59.7% in the unrestricted analysis and 64.4% in a fixed-cohort sensitivity analysis. In asthma and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder benchmarks, AUCs were 79.3% and 84.7%, compared with 62.7% and 71.7% for the strongest comparators, including a general-purpose language model three orders of magnitude larger. Visit-timing predictions had a 3.0-day mean absolute restricted mean survival-time error over 365 days, although median and long-tail return intervals remained miscalibrated. Together, these results establish pediatric diagnostic histories as a substrate for compact generative models supporting broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: TEDDY: a 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer trained on ~73M pediatric ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6M children, achieving strong long-horizon disease-onset predictions (median AUC 72.0%) across 797 tasks, outperforming larger baselines, with signals present >2 years before first diagnosis; suggests compact generative models can leverage pediatric EHR trajectories for broad, rare-disease risk forecasting without large-scale data or billion-parameter models.
AI.motivation: Pediatric EHRs hold rich, developmentally structured trajectories that could enable compact generative models for long-horizon disease risk forecasting, particularly for rare conditions, while avoiding reliance on extremely large models or population-scale data.
AI.method: Train a 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer (TEDDY) on ~73 million ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6 million children at a single pediatric institution. The model predicts longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing, using only first-occurrence events, with predictions made before visit codes are revealed. Evaluate across 797 disease-onset tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters, comparing to DenseNet, CNN, RNN, and LSTM baselines, and assess performance for asthma/ADHD benchmarks and fixed-cohort sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: Median AUC of 72.0% across tasks; surpasses baselines (DenseNet 50.0%, CNN 57.2%, RNN 60.1%, LSTM 62.7%). Performance robust across sex and age; strongest for lower-prevalence diagnoses (90% of rarest conditions with CIs above chance). Predictive signal detectable >2 years before first diagnosis (unrestricted AUC 59.7%, fixed-cohort 64.4%). Asthma AUC 79.3%, ADHD AUC 84.7% versus stronger baselines. Visit timing predictions: mean absolute restricted RMSE 3.0 days over 365 days; long-tail calibration remains imperfect.
AI.conclusion: Pediatric diagnostic histories can serve as a substrate for compact generative models that support broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without resorting to population-scale data or extremely large models.

title: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for HAR: Beyond Pairwise Relations: Dynamic Manipulation Hypergraphs for Vision-Based Human Activity Recognition
summary: Fine-grained manipulation recognition requires modeling evolving relations among hands, objects, tools, and supporting surfaces. Conventional graph-based methods use pairwise edges that can fragment a coordinated event into disconnected binary relations. We propose a dynamic manipulation hypergraph framework that represents multi-entity configurations as higher-order relational units. At each temporal step, relevant entities are encoded using appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features. Hyperedge candidates are instantiated and ranked using proximity, contact, and motion-coupling predicates. A hypergraph reasoning network performs node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing, followed by temporal attention over the evolving interaction structure. The framework provides class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores that identify entity configurations and temporal intervals emphasized by the model without treating them as causal explanations. Quantitative evaluation is conducted on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and Assembly101 under an annotation-assisted entity-localization protocol. Video-only and entity-based methods provide contextual comparisons, while a matched pairwise graph and a static hypergraph serve as the principal controlled baselines because they use identical entity inputs and comparable relational settings. The proposed method improves HO-F1 over the matched pairwise graph by 6.9 percentage points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and 9.5 points on Assembly101, and exceeds the static hypergraph by 4.4 and 5.8 points, respectively. Qualitative analysis on ARCTIC further shows correspondence between highly ranked hyperedges and contact-rich manipulation intervals. These results demonstrate the value of time-varying higher-order relational modeling for fine-grained manipulation activity recognition.

AI.tldr: Dynamic manipulation hypergraph framework models evolving, higher-order interactions among hands, tools, objects, and surfaces for fine-grained manipulation recognition; it outperforms pairwise graphs and static hypergraphs on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional pairwise graphs fragment coordinated events into disconnected relations; need to capture higher-order, time-varying interactions to improve recognition of fine-grained manipulation actions.
AI.method: Construct a dynamic hypergraph where nodes represent entities at each time step with appearance, spatial, motion, and semantic-role features. Instantiate and rank hyperedges using proximity, contact, and motion-coupling predicates. Use a hypergraph reasoning network with node-to-hyperedge and hyperedge-to-node message passing, followed by temporal attention. Provide class-agnostic hyperedge-importance scores for entity configurations and time intervals without claiming causal explanations.
AI.result: HO-F1 improvements over baselines: +6.9 points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100/VISOR and +9.5 points on Assembly101 vs a matched pairwise graph; +4.4 and +5.8 points vs a static hypergraph for the two datasets. Qualitative ARCTIC analysis shows correspondence between high-ranked hyperedges and contact-rich intervals.
AI.conclusion: Time-varying, higher-order relational modeling enhances fine-grained manipulation activity recognition and outperforms strong graph-based baselines on multiple benchmarks.

title: MIDAS Hand: Modular low-Impedance Direct-drive Anthropomorphic Sensing Hand
summary: Dexterous manipulation is limited not only by algorithms but by a shortage of accessible hand hardware that combines human-scale morphology, ease of manufacturing or maintenance, tactile sensing, and practical cost. Existing dexterous hands tend to optimize some of these properties at the expense of others. We present MIDAS Hand, a low-cost, open-source, human-scale dexterous hand with integrated tactile sensing for manipulation research. MIDAS Hand provides 16 total degrees of freedom (DoF) with 13 active DoF, directly driven actuation with measurably low backdrive torque, and 283 three-axis tactile taxels in a compact 700 g package with a bill of materials under 3,000 USD. Built from 3D-printed components, it assembles in under three hours while providing the strength, repeatability, and maintainability needed for repeated real-world experiments. Alongside the hardware, we release a full stack: design files, build documentation, control and tactile Python APIs, simulation models, and retargeting and teleoperation pipelines. We characterize MIDAS Hand through workspace and grasp-taxonomy analysis, payload and reliability tests, backdrivability measurements, and teleoperation demonstrations with tactile sensing, showing that it offers a balanced, reproducible platform for tactile dexterous manipulation and human-to-robot data collection. Project page: https://midas-hand.com

AI.tldr: A compact, low-cost, open-source, human-scale dexterous hand (MIDAS Hand) with 16 DoF (13 active), integrated tactile sensing (283 three-axis taxels), 700 g, BOM <$3k, and a full software/hardware stack for reproducible tactile manipulation research.
AI.motivation: There is a trade-off in existing dexterous hands between human-scale morphology, manufacturability, tactile sensing, and cost. A readily available, open-source platform is needed for tactile dexterous manipulation research and data collection.
AI.method: Design and fabricate MIDAS Hand using 3D-printed parts, 16 DoF (13 active) with direct actuation, low backdrivability torque, and 283 three-axis tactile taxels in a ~700 g package. BOM under $3k. Release complete stack: design files, build docs, control/tactile Python APIs, simulation models, retargeting/teleoperation pipelines. Characterize via workspace and grasp-taxonomy analysis, payload and reliability tests, backdrivability measurements, and teleoperation demonstrations with tactile sensing.
AI.result: A ready-to-use, balanced platform for tactile dexterous manipulation and data collection. Demonstrations include teleoperation with tactile sensing, strong maintainability and reproducibility, easy assembly (under three hours), and open-source materials and APIs.
AI.conclusion: MIDAS Hand offers an accessible, human-scale, tactile dexterous hand that balances morphology, sensing, cost, and manufacturability, enabling broader research adoption and reproducible, data-driven manipulation studies.

title: When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. Code and reproduction log: https://github.com/JaviMaligno/code-world-models
summary:
Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

AI.tldr: LLM-synthesized Code World Models can appear perfect by transition/state accuracy yet fail in play due to rare pivotal rules; adequacy for planning should be measured by search distribution or direct play, not sampled transitions; introduces a quantitative danger law and a coverage bound to explain failures.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of world-model adequacy relies on transition accuracy. The authors argue this is insufficient for planning, as rare but pivotal dynamics can cause systematic play failures despite high accuracy metrics.
AI.method: Synthesize executable game rules as a Code World Model (CWM) via an LLM, then use a classical planner to search. Evaluate on (1) sampling gate transition accuracy and (2) planner’s search distribution state accuracy. quantify play outcomes, derive a danger law, test across GPT-5.x, DAgger/targeted data, and construct a belief-inference function Beacon to illustrate the gap.
AI.result: Demonstrates a verified-vs-correct gap: 100% transition accuracy and ≥98% state accuracy on the planner's search distribution can still yield suboptimal play. The harm follows danger = play_cost × (1 − rarity)^N with a proven gate-miss factor and empirically bounded play cost. Data alone does not fix the gap; rule translation dominates. A coverage bound explains when belief-inference gates identify states, and Beacon shows a verified-but-wrong inference function that plays poorly. Kuhn poker shows no gap, illustrating dependence on game structure.
AI.conclusion: Adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be evaluated on the planner's search distribution or actual play, not solely on sampled-transition accuracy; dedicated metrics and analysis are required to assess planning performance and robustness of CWMs.

title: Long-term User Engagement Optimization through Model-agnostic Downstream Rewards Learning
summary: As recommender systems mature in the past few years, their optimization objectives have evolved from a primary focusing on short-term behavioral signals to a broader emphasis on long-term user engagement and retention. However, directly optimizing retention is difficult because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Prior work has addressed this challenge with sequential modeling and reinforcement learning, but these approaches typically require task specific reward engineering, substantial computational overhead, and surface specific implementations that are difficult to generalize. In this paper, we present a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems. First, we formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. We then propose several model-agnostic downstream rewards signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. We further discuss the engineering effort to productionize the proposed rewards derivations and challenges we faced when adding them to our ranking models. Online A/B experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics, and the framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.
