AI.tldr: A unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework to optimize long-term user value in large-scale recommenders, using offline screening to identify early, predictive session signals and multiple data-driven reward signals; online deployment shows engagement/retention gains across Pinterest surfaces.
AI.motivation: Directly optimizing retention is hard due to sparse, delayed signals and attribution uncertainty. Prior RL/sequential methods require task-specific rewards and heavy engineering; a generalizable, scalable reward framework is desirable.
AI.method: Develop an offline screening framework to identify session-level behaviors observable early and predictive of future retention; derive several model-agnostic downstream reward signals from observed user actions across multiple sources; discuss productionization and integration with ranking models; apply framework across multiple surfaces.
AI.result: Online A/B experiments show consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics; framework deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical, scalable, and generalizable approach to optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommender systems, reducing the need for task-specific reward engineering while delivering measurable gains; deployment across multiple surfaces demonstrates robustness.

title: $K$-NeAS: Scalable Multi-Material CT Reconstruction Using Neural SDFs
summary: Computed Tomography (CT) carries significant ionizing radiation risks, driving the need for sparse-view reconstruction. Implicit scene representations (ISRs) address this by recovering continuous volumetric attenuation fields directly from sparse projections, and recent geometry-aware extensions jointly model surface geometry alongside attenuation to improve fidelity and enable clean tissue segmentation without manual thresholding. However, these methods remain limited by manually tuned attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints. This paper proposes $K$-NeAS, a unified and scalable architecture for automated, multi-material surface reconstruction. We replace independent material networks with a shared latent backbone and introduce a fully differentiable $K$-material sequential soft selector to model an arbitrary number of overlapping tissues. To eliminate manual tuning, we automate attenuation bounding using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and implement a scheduled auxiliary floater loss to mitigate geometric hallucinations common under extreme sparsity. Evaluated across four clinical Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) datasets, $K$-NeAS successfully scales to arbitrary material counts, achieving superior 3D volumetric fidelity at $K=3$ materials on complex multi-tissue regions such as the Abdomen ($33.28\text{ dB}$ 3D PSNR vs. $31.40\text{ dB}$ single-material NeAS baseline, a $+1.88\text{ dB}$ improvement). Furthermore, our model exhibits enhanced robustness under sparse-sampling conditions, outperforming baseline 3D PSNR by up to $1.17\text{ dB}$ under 5- and 10-view constraints.

AI.tldr: K-NeAS is a scalable, automated, multi-material surface reconstruction method for sparse-view CT using a shared backbone, a differentiable K-material sequential soft selector, GMM-based attenuation bounds, and a floater loss, achieving higher 3D fidelity and robustness across CBCT datasets.
AI.motivation: Mitigate ionizing radiation risks in CT by enabling accurate reconstruction from sparse projections. Limitations of existing implicit scene representations (ISRs) include manual attenuation bounds and rigid two-material constraints, hindering multi-tissue segmentation without thresholding.
AI.method: A unified architecture (K-NeAS) with a shared latent backbone and a differentiable K-material sequential soft selector to model arbitrary overlapping tissues. Attenuation bounding is automated with a Gaussian Mixture Model; a scheduled auxiliary floater loss mitigates geometric hallucinations under extreme sparsity. Evaluation on four clinical CBCT datasets with varying material counts (K).
AI.result: K-NeAS scales to multiple materials (K=3) and delivers superior 3D volumetric fidelity, e.g., Abdomen region achieving 33.28 dB 3D PSNR vs. 31.40 dB for single-material NeAS (+1.88 dB). Under sparse sampling (5–10 views), robustness improves 1.17 dB in 3D PSNR over baselines.
AI.conclusion: The architecture enables automated, multi-material surface reconstruction in CT, eliminating manual attenuation bounds and enabling higher fidelity segmentation across complex multi-tissue regions, while maintaining robustness under sparse-view constraints.

title: Safe Execution of RL Policies Via Acceleration-Based CBF-QP Constraint Enforcement for Real-World Robotic Deployments
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication at IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities for solving complex robotic control problems, but its lack of safety guarantees severely limits deployment on hardware. In particular, as legged robots and manipulators often operate near safety-critical boundaries, out-of-distribution states can lead to failure upon deployment. To address this, we introduce Acc-CBF-QP, an acceleration-based Quadratic Program (QP) safety filter using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that constrains any RL policy onto a safe set at runtime without modifying training. The method applies to unconstrained and Safe-RL policies, and enforces joint position, velocity, torque, and collision constraints within a unified optimization framework. A key contribution is the formulation of RL+QP tasks that regulate deviation from the RL command when constraints would otherwise be violated. We introduce a TorqueTask, minimizing torque deviation, and a Forward Dynamics Task, minimizing induced acceleration deviation, thus providing principled control over safety-performance trade-offs. Experiments on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 manipulator and a 19-DoF Unitree H1 humanoid, both in simulation and on hardware, highlight substantial reductions in constraint violations. On the real H1 hardware, a Safe-RL policy alone yielded 10.04 violations/s, which were reduced by 92% to 0.80 violations/s when augmented with Acc-CBF-QP. On the Kinova Gen3, Acc-CBF-QP fully eliminated violations. Nominal task performance of the RL objective is preserved in violation-free regimes. Under aggressive velocity commands on H1, Acc-CBF-QP improves execution by preventing constraint-induced shutdowns, yielding longer survival times. The full pipeline is open-source.

AI.tldr: An acceleration-based CBF-QP safety filter (Acc-CBF-QP) constrains RL policies at runtime to a safe set via Control Barrier Functions, preserving nominal RL performance while dramatically reducing constraint violations on robotic hardware (7-DoF Kinova Gen3, 19-DoF Unitree H1). The approach is training-agnostic and open-source.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement Learning for robotics often lacks safety guarantees; out-of-distribution states near safety-critical boundaries can cause violations or failures upon deployment. A runtime safety layer is needed to enforce constraints (joint positions/velocities/torques, collisions) without altering training, enabling Safe-RL and unconstrained RL policies to operate safely.
AI.method: Formulates Acc-CBF-QP as an acceleration-based Quadratic Program using Control Barrier Functions to enforce safety constraints within a unified optimization framework. Applies to both unconstrained and Safe-RL policies and maintains nominal RL performance within the safe set. Introduces RL+QP tasks to regulate deviation from the RL command when constraints would be violated: TorqueTask (minimize torque deviation) and Forward-Dynamics Task (minimize induced acceleration deviation). Enforces joint position, velocity, torque, and collision constraints for 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 and 19-DoF Unitree H1, evaluated in simulation and on hardware; the full pipeline is open-source.
AI.result: The safety filter yields substantial reductions in constraint violations: on the real H1, violations drop from 10.04/s (Safe-RL policy alone) to 0.80/s with Acc-CBF-QP (92% reduction). On the Kinova Gen3, violations are fully eliminated. Nominal RL performance is preserved in violation-free regimes; under aggressive velocity commands, Acc-CBF-QP prevents constraint-induced shutdowns, extending survival time. The approach is validated in both simulation and hardware, and the pipeline is open-source.
AI.conclusion: Acc-CBF-QP provides a runtime safety layer that enforces safety constraints for RL in robotics without modifying training. It accommodates both unconstrained and Safe-RL policies, supports multiple constraint types (joint limits, torques, collisions), and offers principled safety-performance trade-offs via TorqueTask and Forward-Dynamics Task. The method improves safety, maintains performance within safe regimes, and is openly available.

title: ReasFlow: Assisting Reasoning-Centric Scientific Discovery in Applied Mathematics via a Knowledge-Based Multi-Agent System
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models have fueled autonomous AI agents capable of tackling complex scientific tasks, yet existing automated research systems remain predominantly focused on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery, particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge, largely underexplored. Key challenges include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for autonomous frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature. We introduce ReasFlow, an end-to-end autonomous agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that operationalizes a collaborative paradigm where the human expert acts as Principal Investigator while the agent executes rigorous derivations as a capable graduate student. ReasFlow incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors prior to human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that proactively surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics, substantially reducing expert intervention. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single system. Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform, providing a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research. Github repo: https://github.com/ReasLab/ReasFlow.git.

AI.tldr: ReasFlow is an end-to-end autonomous agent system designed for reasoning-centric, theory-driven scientific discovery, combining a human Principal Investigator role with an autonomous agent that performs rigorous derivations and proofs, supported by internal verification and automated knowledge retrieval; it reportedly generated five complete papers with strong content and scored highest among baselines on a paper-review rubric, and is available on ReasLab/GitHub.
AI.motivation: There is a gap in AI-enabled scientific systems for theory-driven disciplines requiring proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge. Existing systems struggle with verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, autonomous frontier exploration, and sparse procedural heuristics. A system that can audit reasoning, surface missing procedural knowledge, and integrate literature, theorem proving, experiments, and manuscript generation could accelerate theoretical discovery with reduced expert intervention.
AI.method: An end-to-end autonomous agent framework (ReasFlow) that lets a human expert act as PI while the agent acts as a capable graduate student. It features (i) an internal verification loop auditing logical coherence and correcting fundamental errors before human inspection, and (ii) automated knowledge retrieval/self-improvement that surfaces declarative facts and procedural heuristics. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single platform, and operates with minimal prompts to autonomously generate multiple papers.
AI.result: Autonomously generated five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content. In evaluations against state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric, ReasFlow achieved the highest scores.
AI.conclusion: ReasFlow demonstrates that a reasoning-centric, tightly integrated autonomous research assistant—coupled with a collaborative PI-agent paradigm and internal verification—can produce high-quality theoretical research with reduced human intervention, and is publicly accessible for collaborative AI-assisted theoretical research.

title: Augmentations for Robust and Efficient Imitation Learning in Streamed Video Games
comment: To be published in proceedings of IEEE Conference on Games (CoG), 2026
summary: Imitation learning is an appealing way to scale game-playing agents to complex 3D environments by training policies to map visual observations to actions from human demonstrations. However, these demonstrations are expensive to collect and modern game-playing is often done through streaming in which network delay and compression introduce spatiotemporally correlated visual artifacts that can cause a covariance shift at test time. To address these challenges, we propose streaming augmentations that mimic four types of artifacts commonly encountered during streaming with low-bandwidth network connection: pixelated blocks and scrubs, global blur, and ghosting. We instantiate our approach on top of predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDM), which combine future-state conditioning with an inverse dynamics policy in a learned latent space, and evaluate the impact of our augmentations across three tasks in modern 3D video games. Under stable streaming conditions, agents trained with spatiotemporal augmentations achieve up to 41% higher evaluation performance compared to agents trained without augmentations under an identical data budget. When network lag is introduced, agents trained with augmentations degrade by only 7.45% vs 49.82% of the original performance for agents trained only with the original data. These results clearly indicate that spatiotemporal augmentations tailored for the streaming setting are a simple yet powerful tool to train robust and efficient game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: Streaming-specific spatiotemporal augmentations improve imitation-learning agents' robustness to artifacts from low-bandwidth streaming, with substantial performance gains and reduced sensitivity to network lag.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning in 3D environments suffers from expensive demonstrations and covariance shift caused by streaming-induced artifacts (delay, compression). There is a need for training-time strategies that make policies robust to such artifacts without requiring more data.
AI.method: Introduce streaming augmentations that mimic artifacts (pixel blocks/scrubs, global blur, ghosting) and integrate them with predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDM). Evaluate on three modern 3D game tasks, comparing performance under stable streaming and with introduced network lag.
AI.result: Under stable streaming, augmented agents achieve up to 41% higher evaluation performance at the same data budget. With network lag, augmented agents degrade by 7.45% versus 49.82% for agents trained on original data alone, indicating improved robustness to streaming artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal streaming augmentations are a simple, effective approach to train robust and efficient game-playing agents, mitigating covariance shift and preserving performance under realistic streaming conditions.

title: Emergent Region-Level Facial Correspondence in Frozen Vision Foundation Models
summary: Frozen self-supervised vision models can align parts of generic objects, but it remains unclear whether this correspondence extends to human faces, where global layout is shared while identity-specific appearance varies sharply. We test whether frozen DINOv3 features define a region-level facial coordinate system: a feature space in which eyes, brows, nose, mouth, skin, and hair remain distinguishable across people and across time without face-specific training. Using DINOv3 ViT-L/16 patch embeddings and FaRL only as a face-part labeling interface, we evaluate cross-identity nearest-neighbor matching and temporal label propagation on 200 CelebDF-v2 real videos. DINOv3 achieves 83.0% region-level semantic accuracy under unconstrained cross-identity matching, compared with a 23.0% area-weighted random baseline, and 95.5% temporal tracking accuracy without a learned temporal module. A no-FaRL control collapses to 0.9%, showing that FaRL supplies semantic initialization while DINOv3 supplies dense spatial correspondence. The strongest correspondence appears at an intermediate layer: block 18 gives a 4.93x same-region versus cross-region discrimination ratio, compared with 1.48x at the final block. Against CLIP ViT-L/14, DINOv3 shows only a small aggregate advantage but a +16.8 pp gain on anatomical regions, indicating that image-level contrastive supervision captures coarse facial layout but not fine-grained anatomical identity. These results establish frozen DINOv3 as a strong zero-shot representation for region-level facial correspondence and identify intermediate self-supervised features as the most useful layer for dense face analysis.

AI.tldr: Frozen DINOv3 features form a region-level facial coordinate system enabling cross-identity facial region alignment without face-specific training; FaRL provides semantic initialization; intermediate layers (block 18) yield strongest same-region discrimination; CLIP is less effective for fine-grained anatomy.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether frozen self-supervised vision models trained on generic objects can encode stable facial regions across identities and time, enabling zero-shot, region-level face analysis without face-specific supervision.
AI.method: Use DINOv3 ViT-L/16 patch embeddings with FaRL as a labeling interface to perform cross-identity nearest-neighbor matching and temporal label propagation on 200 CelebDF-v2 real videos. Compare region-level semantic accuracy across layers (notably block 18 vs final layer). Benchmark against a no-FaRL control and against CLIP ViT-L/14 for aggregate vs anatomical-region performance.
AI.result: Region-level semantic accuracy of 83.0% under unconstrained cross-identity matching (vs 23.0% random baseline); temporal tracking accuracy 95.5% without a temporal module; no-FaRL control collapses to 0.9%; strongest region correspondence at intermediate layer (block 18) with 4.93x same-region vs cross-region discrimination, vs 1.48x at final block; CLIP ViT-L/14 shows small aggregate advantage but a +16.8 percentage-point gain on anatomical regions when compared to DINOv3.
AI.conclusion: Frozen DINOv3 serves as a strong zero-shot representation for region-level facial correspondence; intermediate self-supervised features are most informative for dense face analysis; FaRL provides semantic initialization, while DINOv3 supplies dense spatial correspondences.

title: DRIFT: Drift and Aggregation for Motion Planning
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Under review at IEEE RAL
summary: End-to-end trajectory planners need to represent multiple plausible driving behaviors while producing a single executable trajectory under real-time constraints. Proposal-based approaches address this ambiguity by generating multiple candidates, but converting the proposal set into a final plan remains a key design problem. We present DRIFT, a fixed-depth planner that combines one-step drifting in a compact trajectory latent space with scene-aware proposal aggregation. Conditioned on features from a pretrained visual encoder, the DRIFT Decoder generates 48 proposal features in a single batched pass, with 32 samples at alpha=0.5 and 16 samples at alpha=0.9. A lightweight Aggregation Head integrates these features with scene, navigation, and ego-state information and directly predicts the final trajectory without requiring trajectory-level quality labels for aggregation. Its output is trained with expert-trajectory imitation and a map-derived boundary regularizer that penalizes waypoints outside the drivable polygon and inside waypoints near its boundary. On NAVSIM navtest, DRIFT achieves 89.6 PDMS and 90.4 EPDMS, with strong drivable-area compliance and ego progress among the methods compared. The proposal-generation and aggregation module runs in 10.82 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4090, while full-model inference including the visual backbone takes 66.43 ms. These results show that one-step latent proposal generation and direct aggregation provide an efficient design for multi-hypothesis motion planning.

AI.tldr: DRIFT introduces a fixed-depth planner that performs one-step latent proposal generation and scene-aware aggregation for multi-hypothesis motion planning, achieving fast inference and strong drivable-area compliance on NAVSIM navtest.
AI.motivation: To address ambiguity in end-to-end trajectory planning by producing multiple plausible proposals and efficiently selecting a final trajectory without trajectory-level quality labels.
AI.method: One-step drifting in a latent trajectory space conditioned on pretrained visual encoder features; DRIFT Decoder outputs 48 proposal features (32 samples at alpha=0.5, 16 at alpha=0.9); Aggregation Head fuses scene/navigation/ego-state features to directly predict the final trajectory, trained via expert-trajectory imitation and a map-derived boundary regularizer.
AI.result: NAVSIM navtest shows PDMS 89.6 and EPDMS 90.4; strong drivable-area compliance and ego progress; latency: proposal generation 10.82 ms; full-model inference 66.43 ms on RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: One-step latent proposal generation with direct aggregation is an efficient, effective design for multi-hypothesis motion planning, enabling fast inference and good adherence to drivable regions without requiring trajectory-level quality labels.

title: RxBrain: Embodied Cognition Foundation Model with Joint Language-Visual Reasoning and Imagination
summary: Embodied cognition requires agents to connect high-level task reasoning with the physical states to be achieved. We introduce Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model with joint language-visual reasoning and imagination. Unlike vision-language models that emphasize scene understanding and textual decision making, or generative world models that mainly predict future visual states, RxBrain represents embodied plans in a single planning sequence where language and visual imagination play complementary roles. Language provides the abstract structure of a plan, including task decomposition, planning primitives, constraints, temporal order, and decision logic, while visual imagination grounds this structure through world state prediction and joint subgoal planning, associating each planning step with intermediate and final physical states. RxBrain adopts a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports language, image, and video understanding and generation within one model. To train this capability, we build an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps and aligning them with visual state transitions. We further introduce RxBrain-Bench to evaluate whether models can represent embodied plans through joint textual and visual components rather than separate understanding or generation. Experiments show that RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, and produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. We also extend RxBrain to continuous robot action generation, where it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining. These results provide an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

AI.tldr: A new embodied cognition foundation model, Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, unifies language-based planning with visual imagination in a single Mixture-of-Transformers to ground abstract plans in world states. It uses an automatic video-to-planning supervision pipeline, introduces RxBrain-Bench for joint textual-visual evaluation, and demonstrates continuous robot action generation without large-scale action-data pretraining.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between high-level task reasoning and physical grounding by integrating language planning and visual imagination in one model, overcoming limitations of scene understanding-focused models and purely predictive world models.
AI.method: Develop a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers handling language, image, and video; automatically convert embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing into steps and aligning with state transitions; evaluate with RxBrain-Bench on embodied planning tasks; extend to continuous robot action generation for real robots without large action-data pretraining.
AI.result: RxBrain preserves both embodied understanding and generation capabilities; outputs plans that couple textual reasoning with world-state prediction and subgoal planning; RxBrain-Bench validates joint textual-visual planning; initial real-robot demonstrations show promise without extensive action-data pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Presents an early step toward foundation models for embodied cognition that unify planning, grounding, and action generation in a single model, enabling more integrated and scalable embodied AI.

title: Privacy Leakage in Federated Learning in Radiology Reports: A Comparative Evaluation of Tokenizer-Driven Privacy Risks
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multi-institutional training on clinical text without sharing raw data, but gradient inversion can reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates. The extent of this leakage for radiology reports, and the role of tokenizer design, remains unclear. We quantify gradient-based text reconstruction in FL and compare privacy risk across three tokenizers with the model architecture held fixed. Six FL clients trained a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on public radiology corpora (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR free-text reports) using the GPT-2, RadBERT, and LLaMA-2 tokenizers at batch sizes of 64, 128, and 256. Assuming an active malicious server that modifies the shared architecture before distribution, we applied analytic gradient inversion and measured reconstruction fidelity over five runs. Exact sentence reconstruction ranged from 31% to 44% across tokenizers (30.6-43.5% across the 27 tokenizer x dataset x batch-size cells). At batch size 64 on the Discharge dataset, accuracy was 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), decreasing to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3% at batch size 256. S-BLEU declined as batch size grew (GPT-2: 0.44 to 0.33; RadBERT: 0.48 to 0.35). RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered the most clinical terms (18.1% of a 1,440-term reference vocabulary, vs 12.5% for GPT-2 and 9.4% for LLaMA-2), yet no tokenizer prevented leakage. Substantial portions of report text are therefore recoverable from FL gradients even at larger batch sizes and with domain-specific tokenizers. Tokenizer design influences leakage severity and is a privacy-relevant decision, not only a utility one; safeguards such as secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

AI.tldr: Federated learning (FL) text leakage from gradients can reconstruct substantial radiology report content; tokenizer choice modulates leakage severity, with RadBERT showing higher reconstruction fidelity; no tokenizer prevents leakage. DP and secure aggregation likely required for HIPAA/GDPR compliance.
AI.motivation: Quantify gradient-based text reconstruction risk in FL for radiology NLP and assess how tokenizer design affects leakage.
AI.method: Six FL clients train a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on public radiology corpora totaling 468,457 reports (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR free-text reports) using three tokenizers (GPT-2, RadBERT, LLaMA-2) at batch sizes 64, 128, 256. Assuming an active malicious server that modifies the shared architecture before distribution, applied analytic gradient inversion and measured reconstruction fidelity over five runs. Evaluated exact sentence reconstruction and S-BLEU.
AI.result: Exact sentence reconstruction ranged 31%–44% across tokenizers (30.6%–43.5% across all 27 tokenizer×dataset×batch-size cells). At batch size 64 on the Discharge dataset, accuracy was 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), decreasing to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3% at batch size 256. S-BLEU declined with larger batches (GPT-2: 0.44→0.33; RadBERT: 0.48→0.35). RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered the most clinical terms (18.1% of a 1,440-term reference vocabulary, vs 12.5% for GPT-2 and 9.4% for LLaMA-2). No tokenizer prevented leakage.
AI.conclusion: Tokenizer design influences leakage severity and represents a privacy-relevant decision; safeguards such as secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

title: Cotton-SF YOLO: Learning Structural and Frequency Cues for Early Cotton Square Detection in Complex Field Environments
summary: Cotton squares are important phenotypic indicators of the early reproductive growth of cotton, and automatic field detection of cotton squares provides an important basis for cotton growth monitoring and precision cultivation management. However, early cotton square detection in complex field environments remains insufficiently explored, as cotton squares are small, frequently occluded, easily blurred, subject to illumination variations, and exhibit low contrast against surrounding cotton leaves. To address these challenges, we propose a task-oriented framework based on YOLO26m, named Cotton-SF YOLO, for cotton square detection under natural field conditions. To improve the perception of small and irregular cotton square boundaries, we introduce Dynamic Snake Convolution into the detector, enabling adaptive extraction of deformable edge features. Furthermore, a frequency-domain feature modulation module is designed by incorporating spectral enhancement into the C2f structure, which recalibrate frequency-domain representations and strengthen discriminative edge and texture cues while reducing interference from complex cotton leaf backgrounds. Trained and evaluated on our newly constructed and annotated field dataset with manually annotated cotton squares, the proposed model achieves mAP$_{50}$, mAP$_{50:95}$, and recall values of 0.8196, 0.4942, and 0.7939, improving over the baseline YOLO26m by 1.25%, 3.45%, and 2.96%, respectively. Ablation experiments and visualization demonstrate that the best performance is achieved with the complementary effects of structural and frequency cues.

AI.tldr: Cotton-SF YOLO: a task-oriented detector for cotton squares in fields, using Dynamic Snake Convolution and frequency-domain feature modulation on YOLO26m; improves small-object detection on a new field dataset.
AI.motivation: Early cotton square detection is challenging due to small size, occlusion, blur, illumination changes, and low contrast with leaves; improving detection enables better growth monitoring and precision cultivation.
AI.method: Base detector: YOLO26m. Introduces Dynamic Snake Convolution to adaptively extract deformable edge features of small squares. Adds a frequency-domain feature modulation module via spectral enhancement within the C2f structure to recalibrate frequency-domain representations and strengthen edge/texture cues while reducing leaf-background interference. Trained on a newly constructed, annotated field dataset of cotton squares.
AI.result: Performance on the dataset: mAP@50 = 0.8196, mAP@50:95 = 0.4942, recall = 0.7939. Relative gains over baseline YOLO26m: +1.25% mAP@50, +3.45% mAP@50:95, +2.96% recall.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic deformable edge modeling plus spectral-domain cue modulation improve small-object detection in challenging field conditions; the complementary structural and frequency cues yield best performance; a new field dataset underpins evaluation.

title: Communication-Efficient Relative Pose Estimation with Vision Foundation Models for Ephemeral Collaborative Perception
summary: Relative pose estimation is a fundamental capability for collaborative perception and coordination in multi-robot systems. However, robots encountering each other in real-world environments often operate in short interaction windows and must operate under limited communication bandwidth with intermittent or missing visual overlap caused by occlusions or limited fields of view. Existing approaches typically rely on global reference frames, assume sustained view overlap, or incur prohibitive communication costs, thereby limiting their applicability to ephemeral collaborative perception. To address these challenges, we introduce communication-efficient relative pose estimation (CERPE), a system-level framework that coordinates vision foundation models to jointly estimate ego-motion and inter-robot relative pose. CERPE reduces unnecessary raw-observation exchange by using continuously shared fixed-size descriptors to gate event-triggered raw-image requests independently of pose estimation. Non-overlapping encounters are handled by propagating inter-robot relative poses through metrically scaled ego-motion, thus maintaining relative pose estimates even in the absence of visual overlap. Experiments in simulation and real-world robots show that CERPE improves 6-DoF relative pose estimation over selected baselines in ephemeral collaborative perception.

AI.tldr: CERPE is a system-level framework for communication-efficient relative pose estimation in multi-robot systems. It shares fixed-size descriptors to gate event-triggered raw-image requests and propagates poses when views do not overlap, achieving improved 6-DoF relative pose estimation in ephemeral encounters.
AI.motivation: Real-world multi-robot interactions suffer from short interaction windows, limited communication bandwidth, and intermittent/missing visual overlap due to occlusions or limited fields of view. Existing methods rely on global references, sustained overlap, or high communication costs, limiting applicability to ephemeral collaboration.
AI.method: CERPE coordinates vision foundation models to jointly estimate ego-motion and inter-robot relative pose. It uses continuously shared fixed-size descriptors to gate event-triggered raw-image requests, independent of pose estimation. For non-overlapping encounters, it propagates inter-robot relative poses via metrically scaled ego-motion to maintain estimates when visual overlap is absent.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and on real robots show CERPE improves 6-DoF relative pose estimation over selected baselines in ephemeral collaborative perception.
AI.conclusion: CERPE demonstrates a practical, communication-efficient approach for maintaining reliable relative pose estimates in ephemeral encounters by descriptor-based gating and pose propagation, enabling robust collaboration under bandwidth constraints and intermittent visibility.

title: How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment? To answer, we first asked a battery of questions about 28 conflicts to five leading answer engines and scored their 5,460 answers against documented evidence. We found that the thinner the retrievable record around a given conflict, the more the engines invent, misattribute, and miscount. Thin records don't just encourage hallucination, but create structural exposure to mis- and disinformation, because they are the easiest records to warp through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to bias engine responses. Through an analysis of 1,048 websites that the AI LLMs pulled conflict facts from, we found that GEO source optimization is already happening, and while state-partisan digital capture remains incipient it is rapidly growing. We explain what these findings mean for scholarship with the rise of GEO information warfare, and for policy argue for a return to the deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate, closing with a discussion of future research opportunities and challenges in this fast-moving space.

AI.tldr: LLM-based answer engines hallucinate more on conflicts when public records are thin; current GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) practices already skew sources, with growing state-partisan digital capture. Implications demand deeper local monitoring and translation-focused research to counter GEO information warfare.
AI.motivation: To understand patterns of AI hallucinations in the conflict domain, assess reliability of AI as a source for peace and conflict information, and anticipate GEO-driven information warfare effects on scholarship and policy.
AI.method: Evaluate 28 conflicts using five leading answer engines. Collect and score 5,460 answers against documented evidence. Analyze 1,048 websites feeding the models’ facts to assess source-characteristics and potential GEO optimization.
AI.result: A negative correlation between record thickness and hallucination incidence: thinner records lead to more invention, misattribution, and miscount. Evidence of GEO source optimization in the data, with growing state-partisan digital capture. These dynamics create exposure to disinformation and bias in engine responses.
AI.conclusion: Scholarship should anticipate GEO information warfare by emphasizing deep, local monitoring and translation-based methods that AI cannot replicate. Policy should focus on countering GEO biases and preserving verifiable, richly sourced regional records; outline future research opportunities and challenges in a rapidly evolving landscape.

title: LIGO-PINN: Learned Initialization via Gated Optimization to Alleviate Convergence Failures in Physics Informed Neural Networks
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables. Code available at https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
summary:
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have had a broad research impact in modeling domains governed by partial differential equations (PDE). However, PINNs have been shown to perform poorly, sometimes even converging to trivial solutions, in challenging PDE domains, or when generalizing to unseen but related PDE domains. Previously proposed solutions detail hyperparameter tuning to reduce loss imbalance between data-driven and physics guided losses, curriculum learning based training strategies, or dynamic re-sampling of hard collocation points. These methods face certain pitfalls: hyperparameter tuning is expensive, designing a training curriculum is ambiguous in multi-parameter PDE settings, and dynamic resampling still fails in complex PDE settings. Complementary to this line of thinking, we believe the initial PINN network weights also play a crucial role in the emergence of catastrophic failures during training, yet the effect of PINN weight initialization has been surprisingly under-investigated. To this end, we propose a framework for Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization (LIGO-PINN) to overcome PINN convergence failures. Through rigorous evaluation on 1D and 2D PDE domains, including a challenging 2D fluid dynamics setting, we demonstrate that our methodology outperforms state-of-the-art methods designed to alleviate PINN failures, achieving a 91.5% average performance improvement across six baselines and 81% over the strongest baseline. We also verify that LIGO-PINN generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Finally, we analyze training dynamics across all three PDE domains to explain both LIGO-PINN's improvement and the convergence failure of traditional PINNs. Code: https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
  Keywords: Machine Learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, Deep Learning, PDE Modeling

AI.tldr: LIGO-PINN learns initialization to overcome PINN convergence failures, achieving large gains across PDE problems and enabling 3D generalization; code is provided.
AI.motivation: PINNs often fail to converge or generalize in challenging PDE domains. Prior work focuses on loss balancing, curricula, or dynamic resampling, but initialization remains underexplored. LIGO-PINN targets learned weight initialization to mitigate catastrophic failures.
AI.method: Introduce Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization (LIGO-PINN). Trainable, gated, layerwise optimization to initialize PINN weights. Evaluated on 1D and 2D PDEs, including a challenging 2D fluid dynamics case; compared against six baselines; analyzes training dynamics; demonstrates 3D unstructured domain generalization; code released.
AI.result: Reported 91.5% average performance improvement across six baselines and 81% over the strongest baseline. LIGO-PINN generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Training dynamics analysis explains improved convergence and failure modes of traditional PINNs.
AI.conclusion: LIGO-PINN is an effective strategy to alleviate PINN convergence failures by learning advantageous initializations, complementing existing loss-balancing or curriculum approaches, with strong cross-domain performance and 3D generalization; code available for reproduction.

title: G$^2$SR: Geometric Methods for Fast and Memory-Efficient Gaussian-based Surface Reconstruction
summary: Few-view surface reconstruction recovers the visible surfaces of a scene from a few posed RGB images, providing the 3D models that robots need to explore and interact online. On mobile platforms, the reconstruction must be fast and geometrically accurate while keeping a small memory footprint to ensure safe and efficient operation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offers a high-fidelity scene representation, but building it from a few views is ill-posed, as many distinct surfaces reproduce the same images, making traditional photometric methods prone to "floater" artifacts. End-to-end methods resolve the ambiguity by regressing splats with large, usually Transformer-based, networks that require heavy compute and memory while generalizing poorly to new scenes. We propose G2SR, which exploits a well-posed core of the task: given cross-view 2D splat correspondences, 3D splats follow analytically from multi-view geometry. G2SR employs a lightweight neural frontend to detect and track 2D Gaussian splats on the image plane and an analytic backend to triangulate each into a metric-scale 3D splat. On ScanNet, Replica, and DTU, G2SR matches or exceeds the geometric accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end methods while running at 69-89 reconstructions per second within 203 MB of GPU memory (5-107x less) for 2- and 3-view inputs at 384 x 512 resolution, offering a practical path to online Gaussian-based surface reconstruction.

AI.tldr: G2SR enables fast, memory-efficient few-view surface reconstruction by deriving 3D Gaussian splats analytically from cross-view 2D splat correspondences, achieving competitive accuracy with significantly lower compute/memory than end-to-end methods.
AI.motivation: Address the ill-posedness of few-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and the high computational/memory burden of end-to-end networks, to enable online, resource-constrained robotic surface reconstruction.
AI.method: A lightweight neural frontend detects and tracks 2D Gaussian splats on the image plane; an analytic backend triangulates each 2D splat into a metric-scale 3D splat using multi-view geometry, avoiding heavy transformer-based regressor networks.
AI.result: On ScanNet, Replica, and DTU, G2SR matches or exceeds the geometric accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end methods while running at 69–89 reconstructions per second with ~203 MB GPU memory (5–107x less) for 2- and 3-view inputs at 384×512 resolution.
AI.conclusion: Analytic triangulation of 2D splats yields a fast, accurate, memory-efficient surface reconstruction suitable for online deployment, offering a practical alternative to heavy end-to-end approaches.

title: SafeRelBench: A Spatial-Relation-Aware Benchmark for Process-Level Safety in VLM-Driven Embodied Agents
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as the reasoning backbone of embodied agents, enabling robots to interpret visual scenes, follow language instructions, and plan multi-step actions. In household environments, however, safety depends not only on recognizing objects, but also on how actions change the physical scene over time. Existing embodied safety evaluations largely focus on static risk recognition, unsafe instruction refusal, or final-state task completion. As a result, process-level safety failures induced by spatial relations such as support, containment, and proximity remain insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce SAFERELBENCH, a spatial-relation-aware safety benchmark with 507 executable evaluation samples, including 248 spatial-relation samples and 259 non-spatial control samples. Using SAFERELBENCH to evaluate seven open- and closed-source VLM-driven embodied agents, we find a substantial gap between task success and process-level safety compliance: models often complete the requested task while violating process-level safety constraints. Unlike prior benchmarks, SAFERELBENCH explicitly tests whether agents satisfy safety conditions before risk-prone actions, making spatial relations a core dimension in embodied safety assessment. More broadly, our results show that safe embodied intelligence requires not only stronger perception and planning, but also reliable reasoning about how object relations shape risk during interaction.

AI.tldr: SAFERELBENCH introduces a spatial-relation-aware safety benchmark for VLM-driven embodied agents, revealing that task success often coexists with safety violations and that spatial relations must be explicitly evaluated for reliable safe embodied intelligence.
AI.motivation: Address gap in embodied AI safety research: beyond static risk recognition and final-task success, there is a need to evaluate process-level safety and how spatial relations (support, containment, proximity) shape risk during interaction in household environments.
AI.method: Created SAFERELBENCH with 507 executable evaluation samples (248 spatial-relational, 259 non-spatial control). Evaluated seven open- and closed-source VLM-driven embodied agents. Benchmark tests safety compliance before risk-prone actions and focuses on spatial relations as core safety dimension.
AI.result: Found substantial gap between task success and process-level safety compliance; models often finish tasks while violating safety constraints; spatial relations are a core dimension; demonstrates the necessity to test safety reasoning explicitly.
AI.conclusion: Safe embodied intelligence requires stronger perception and planning plus reliable relational reasoning about how object relations influence risk; SAFERELBENCH provides a path toward integrating spatial-relational safety into evaluation and development.

title: Align AI to Dynamic Human-AI Workflows
summary: Current alignment approaches typically focus on emulating human behavior using static representations of human preferences, failing to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions. In this paper, we argue for a shift from static and emulative to interactive and complementary alignment, where preferences emerge through interaction and alignment is defined not by satisfying preferences alone. We first formalize this gap by contrasting existing alignment with a trajectory-level view in which human and model behavior co-evolve over time. Because these interaction dynamics have not been adequately captured within existing ML formulations, we ground this perspective in insights from an interdisciplinary workshop. We draw on lessons from social-science accounts of human-human collaboration and then argue that human-AI systems amplify these dynamics, introducing new asymmetries that make reasoning about uncertainty harder and introduce new coordination challenges. Based on these lessons and new challenges, we conclude by outlining a research agenda for developing AI systems that align with humans in interaction, requiring an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning and the social and decision sciences.

AI.tldr: Proposes interactive, complementary alignment: preferences emerge via interaction; trajectory-level co-evolution; grounded in social science; outlines interdisciplinary research agenda.
AI.motivation: Static, emulative alignment fails to capture dynamic, context-dependent human-AI interactions and uncertainty, requiring a new framework for alignment.
AI.method: Formally contrasts static/emulative alignment with a trajectory-level, co-evolution view of human and model behavior; grounds the perspective in social-science insights and an interdisciplinary workshop; derives implications for AI system design and evaluation.
AI.result: Presents a conceptual framework and initial guidance rather than empirical results; identifies interaction dynamics, asymmetries, and coordination challenges; outlines a research agenda for interactive alignment.
AI.conclusion: Advocates an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning with social and decision sciences to develop AI that aligns with humans through interaction, not merely by satisfying static preferences.

title: MIDiff: Tackling Sparsity and Imbalance in Mobile Usage Generation via Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion
summary: Mobile usage traces are critical for tasks such as user behavior prediction and app recommendation, yet their use is constrained by privacy restrictions and costly large-scale data collection. Although generative models perform well on general time series, their application to mobile usage data remains challenging because (i) limited user activity causes severe sparsity, (ii) heterogeneous variable types complicate joint modeling, and (iii) functional differences across apps create pronounced usage imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion (MIDiff), a diffusion-based framework operating in an imaging space defined by Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF). C-GASF transforms sparse multivariate sequences into correlation images, while MIDiff employs Triple Attention in a U-Net to preserve temporal consistency and variable dependencies. Experiments show that MIDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across fidelity metrics. In particular, it obtains a Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526, compared with 0.3476 for the strongest baseline, ZITS-VAE, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating realistic and diverse mobile usage traces. Our code is available at https://github.com/YilaiLiu-HKU/MIDiff.

AI.tldr: MIDiff is a diffusion-based model that converts sparse multivariate mobile usage sequences into correlation images via Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF) and uses a Triple-Attention U-Net to generate realistic, diverse traces; it reports state-of-the-art fidelity with a DA of 0.1526 vs 0.3476 for ZITS-VAE.
AI.motivation: Address privacy-driven data scarcity, severe sparsity from limited user activity, heterogeneous variable types, and app-wise usage imbalance that hinder modeling mobile usage traces.
AI.method: Diffusion-based framework MIDiff operating in imaging space created by C-GASF; transforms multivariate sequences into correlation images; employs Triple Attention in a U-Net to maintain temporal consistency and capture variable dependencies.
AI.result:
Achieves state-of-the-art fidelity across metrics; reports Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526, better than 0.3476 from the strongest baseline (ZITS-VAE);
code available at github.com/YilaiLiu-HKU/MIDiff.
AI.conclusion: MIDiff effectively generates realistic and diverse mobile usage traces, addressing sparsity, heterogeneity, and imbalance; demonstrated empirical gains on fidelity metrics with accessible code for replication.

title: Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the method of choice for reconstructing and real-time rendering of captured scenes. To capture a scene with good visual quality, continuous image sequences are usually combined with out-of-order shots for better scene coverage. Structure from motion can reconstruct such captures, but only after they are all available and often with high computational cost. Incremental reconstruction methods -- often derived from SLAM solutions -- provide immediate feedback, but cannot handle the out-of-order capture we require. We provide the first immediate feedback solution for such radiance field capture that provides global consistency. We first introduce a method for fast matching in out-of-order sequences, by repurposing visual place recognition models and a covisibility graph, and provide an efficient way to find highly connected keyframes, improving quality even for ordered sequences. We show how these steps -- together with GPU optimization and careful Gaussian primitive placement -- provide fast local reconstruction, in our challenging radiance field reconstruction case. We then introduce a novel cluster-based method, again using the covisibility graph, to provide efficient loop closure that does not require sequential input. Finally, to handle large scenes in our context, we introduce a progressive hierarchy that allows our method to scale to large environments, without compromising efficiency. Our results show we provide immediate feedback 3DGS reconstruction with good visual quality in several datasets, with up to thousands of input images.

AI.tldr: First immediate-feedback radiance-field reconstruction for 3D Gaussian Splatting that handles out-of-order captures, featuring fast matching, loop closure, and hierarchical scaling to achieve high-quality visuals on datasets with thousands of images.
AI.motivation: Need for immediate, globally consistent reconstruction in radiance-field capture. Out-of-order captures improve coverage but break incremental SLAM assumptions; full structure-from-motion is costly and not real-time.
AI.method: (1) Fast matching in out-of-order sequences by repurposing visual place recognition models and a covisibility graph to identify highly connected keyframes; (2) GPU-accelerated local reconstruction with carefully placed Gaussian primitives; (3) Cluster-based, covisibility-driven loop closure that does not rely on sequential input; (4) Progressive hierarchy to scale to large environments while maintaining efficiency.
AI.result: Demonstrates immediate-feedback 3DGS reconstructions with good visual quality across several datasets, handling up to thousands of input images; improvements occur even for ordered sequences due to better keyframe connectivity and loop closure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline delivers real-time or near-real-time, globally consistent radiance-field reconstructions for large-scale scenes, combining fast out-of-order matching, loop closure, and scalable hierarchical organization.

title: Beyond Implicit Force: Evaluating Explicit Force-Torque Proxies in Action Chunking with Transformers
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to infer interaction state from signals that are often weakly observable through vision and kinematics alone. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) has shown strong performance in fine-grained manipulation, but many deployments collect demonstrations through leader-follower teleoperation, where tracking error between commanded leader motion and executed follower motion implicitly encodes contact, resistance, and constraint violation. This paper examines whether ACT's apparent force-awareness depends on this hidden interaction cue. We introduce an observation-centric ACT variant that predicts future follower joint states instead of leader commands, thereby removing the teleoperation-induced discrepancy signal while preserving the rest of the learning pipeline. We then evaluate whether simple joint-torque proxies, derived from onboard motor current or joint effort, can recover contact-aware behavior without external force/torque sensors. Across four real-world tasks spanning surface following, insertion, stiffness discrimination, and force-based stopping, removing the implicit cue leads to severe failures in force-critical phases. In contrast, torque-augmented policies recover robust contact behavior and improve the base ACT policy. These results demonstrate that, on real hardware, the implicit teleoperation cue is a recoverable source of force-awareness, where torque signals are available, a simple proxy matches, surpasses, or further enhances it.

AI.tldr: Removing teleoperation-based cues in ACT weakens force-awareness; onboard torque proxies can recover or enhance force-aware behavior in real-world manipulation.
AI.motivation: Understand whether ACT’s purported force-awareness comes from hidden teleoperation signals and if simple torque-based cues can provide force-awareness without external sensors.
AI.method: Introduce an observation-centric ACT variant predicting follower joint states (not leader commands). Evaluate torque proxies from onboard motor current/joint effort as substitutes for force/torque sensing. Test across four real-world tasks: surface following, insertion, stiffness discrimination, and force-based stopping on real hardware.
AI.result: Removing the implicit teleoperation cue causes severe failures in force-critical phases. Torque-augmented policies restore robust contact behavior and can improve the base ACT policy, matching or surpassing the original teleoperation-derived cue.
AI.conclusion: The teleoperation cue is a recoverable source of force-awareness on real hardware. Torque signals are accessible and effective proxies, capable of matching, surpassing, or further enhancing ACT performance.

title: The Steering Budget: Examples beat Knobs
summary:
Generative models are steered with knobs -- prompts, guidance scales, property tags. Turn one as hard as you like and, past a point, it stops moving the property you care about. We find that ceiling is not a shortcoming of the model but a budget, set by the training data before the model is trained: a property's movable range splits in two -- the part a knob can reach, and a second, significant part that only examples -- concrete instances of what you want more of -- can reach. That second part is usually much larger, but not always, and the same budget says so in advance.
  Reaching that second part takes a different move: instead of turning a knob, you show the model examples, composed from what it already learned rather than added to its training. A cheap audit of the training data measures the budget; we give a recipe for building the example set that reaches all of it.
  This buys two things a knob can't. Reach: it moves a property across the whole budget, not just the part a knob reaches. Expressiveness: it steers toward targets you can only specify by example -- including ones you can't put into words. We turn these into a handful of falsifiable claims and verify them in two unrelated domains, image and crystal-structure generation -- marking where a knob is enough, and where only examples will do.

AI.tldr: Generative-model controllability is limited by a training-data budget that splits the space into knob-reachable and example-reachable regions; to reach the full budget, use example-based editing guided by a budget-aware audit of training data. The authors validate this in image and crystal-structure generation.
AI.motivation: Explain why prompts and guidance scales saturate and propose a principled way to expand controllability by exploiting examples derived from learned data, not new training.
AI.method: Analyze several generative systems to show a budgeted control space. Define a cheap training-data audit to measure the budget. Propose a recipe for constructing example sets that reach the entire budget. Validate claims in two unrelated domains (image and crystal-structure generation).
AI.result: Two-part controllability: part reachable by knobs is smaller than the total budget; remaining part requires example-based guidance. An audit recipe yields full budget reach; example sets outperform knobs in expressing certain targets; clears where knobs suffice and where examples are necessary.
AI.conclusion: Knobs alone cannot fully control generative models due to a data-imposed budget; combining knob-based control with example-based guidance yields broader reach and expressiveness, enabling targets describable only by examples and providing falsifiable claims verified across domains.

title: Local Additive Feature Attribution: A Mathematical Taxonomy and Reporting Checklist
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, and 19 tables. Ancillary files include the axiom matrix, reporting checklist, related-survey scoring, and review-corpus summary
summary: Feature-attribution methods are central to explainable artificial intelligence. Their assumptions are expressed in several mathematical languages: cooperative-game values, path integrals, gradient operators, perturbation distributions, and backpropagation rules. This survey proposes a common framework for local additive feature attribution. It organizes Shapley, path-based, gradient/backpropagation, perturbation, and CAM-style methods around five specification choices: value function, reference, path, perturbation distribution, and conservation rule. It then compares these methods through an axiom-by-method matrix and links common failure modes, including baseline sensitivity, off-manifold perturbations, sanity-check failures, adversarial manipulation, and method disagreement, to the assumptions that produce them. Finally, the survey proposes a ten-item reporting checklist for studies that use local additive attributions. The central message is that attribution results are meaningful only relative to the mathematical assumptions under which they are defined, and that those assumptions should be reported.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for local additive feature attribution is proposed, organizing Shapley, path-based, gradient/backprop, perturbation, and CAM-style methods around five specification choices; it analyzes methods with an axiom-by-method matrix, links failure modes to assumptions, and offers a ten-item reporting checklist; the core message is that attribution meaning depends on underlying mathematical assumptions that should be disclosed.
AI.motivation: Clarify relationships among feature-attribution methods, expose underlying assumptions, and improve reporting and evaluation in explainable AI.
AI.method: A conceptual framework that classifies local additive attribution methods by five dimensions (value function, reference, path, perturbation distribution, conservation rule), followed by an axiom-by-method comparison, analysis of common failure modes, and a 10-item reporting checklist.
AI.result: A comprehensive taxonomy connecting Shapley, path-based, gradient/backprop, perturbation, and CAM-style attributions; identification of common failure modes tied to assumptions; practical reporting guidelines for studies using local additive attributions.
AI.conclusion: Attribution results gain meaning only under specified mathematical assumptions, and those assumptions must be explicitly reported to enable valid interpretation and comparison.

title: Reinforcing Egocentric Spatial Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ego Scene Augmentation
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Chi Kit Wong and Ye Pan contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/Chikit-WONG/spatialGraph
summary: Egocentric Visual Question Answering (VQA) has attracted widespread attention as an important task for enabling Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to interact with the real world. However, existing MLLMs struggle to perform effective spatial reasoning in complex egocentric scenes due to their limited spatial perception capabilities. To this end, we introduce Ego Scene Augmentation (ESA), an egocentric spatial perception framework, which actively enhances the spatial perception capabilities from the egocentric perspective, powered by the proposed Ego-element Graph. Our core insight is leveraging the Ego-element Graph as an intermediary representation to augment the egocentric spatial perception of MLLMs via visual foundational models. Specifically, we 1) construct the Ego-element Graph, which encapsulates and integrates egocentric spatial features enabled by visual foundational models; 2) enhance the spatial perception capabilities of MLLMs via the Ego-element Graph for ego-perspective scenes. Our proposed ESA framework presents significant performance improvement on the EgoTextVQA benchmark. We achieve an 8.14% gain on the indoor setting and an 8.72% gain on the outdoor setting. Furthermore, our ESA shows the most impressive performance improvement in the shopping subset of the indoor setting. The project code is publicly available.

AI.tldr: ESA introduces Ego-element Graph to augment egocentric spatial perception in MLLMs for VQA, improving performance on EgoTextVQA (8.14% indoor, 8.72% outdoor; strong gain in shopping subset), with public code.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs have limited spatial perception, hindering effective spatial reasoning in complex egocentric scenes; there is a need to enhance egocentric spatial awareness for better VQA performance.
AI.method: Construct an Ego-element Graph as an intermediary representation powered by visual foundational models; encode and integrate egocentric spatial features in the graph; leverage this graph to augment MLLMs for ego-perspective VQA tasks.
AI.result: Significant improvements on EgoTextVQA: +8.14% indoor, +8.72% outdoor; largest gains in shopping subset; code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: ESA effectively enhances egocentric spatial perception in MLLMs through the Ego-element Graph, yielding notable performance gains on egocentric VQA benchmarks; the framework demonstrates the potential of intermediary spatial representations in multimodal models.

title: SoftNav: Injecting 3D Scene Tokens into VLMs for Embodied Navigation
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: In goal-directed embodied navigation, where an agent must locate a specified target in an unseen environment, 3D scene understanding and navigation reasoning must work in concert. Current approaches transmit 3D scene information to vision-language models (VLMs) through text, suggesting a representation gap in our tested configurations; a controlled ablation confirms that direct embedding-level transfer significantly outperforms the evaluated text serialization formats. We introduce SoftNav, which injects entity-level 3D continuous representations -- one token per detected object or frontier -- into a VLM's hidden space as soft tokens through a lightweight projector. With the 3D encoder and VLM frozen, only ~1,200 samples and ~17M trainable parameters are needed. On HM3D-OVON, SoftNav achieves 74.2%/68.3%/66.7% SR across three splits, surpassing all prior methods in both SR and SPL; the same navigation policy transfers zero-shot to GOAT-Bench (67.2% SR), SG3D (47.2% s-SR), and real-world robot deployment without retraining or architectural modification. Injecting 3D scene tokens directly into VLMs bridges the representation gap, enabling transferable navigation with minimal training.

AI.tldr: SoftNav injects 3D object-level tokens into a frozen VLM to bridge the 3D–language representation gap, enabling transferable goal-directed navigation with minimal training.
AI.motivation: To overcome the representation gap between 3D scene understanding and vision-language models, enabling robust, transferable navigation across unseen environments with limited labeled data.
AI.method: Introduce SoftNav: construct entity-level 3D continuous representations (one token per detected object or frontier) and inject them as soft tokens into a VLM's hidden space via a lightweight projector, while keeping the 3D encoder and VLM frozen; training requires ~1,200 samples and ~17M trainable parameters.
AI.result: On HM3D-OVON, SoftNav achieves 74.2%/68.3%/66.7% SR across three splits, surpassing prior methods in SR and SPL; the policy transfers zero-shot to GOAT-Bench (67.2% SR), SG3D (47.2% s-SR), and real-world deployment without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Embedding 3D scene tokens directly into VLMs closes the representation gap and enables transferable navigation with minimal training, achieving state-of-the-art results and zero-shot transfer.

title: Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed for nuanced content safety and moderation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation fail to scale against the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats. In this paper, we propose an automated, agentic red-teaming framework that systematically synthesizes difficult examples using an iterative strategy that proposes novel hypotheses as well as mutating on past attempts. Leveraging a multi-agent architecture that consists of a high-reasoning Architect agent, an advanced image generator, and a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters, our system autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases without any human intervention. By employing these carefully synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time Retrieval, we substantially improve the target model's robustness, reducing the False Negative Rate (FNR) from 41.2% to 24.5% in a public image safety benchmark without relying on any human labeling.

AI.tldr: Automated agentic red-teaming with a multi-agent system (Architect, image generator, LLM raters) to generate adversarial multimodal examples; reduces FNR from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image-safety benchmark without human labeling.
AI.motivation: Scalability limits of traditional active learning and manual annotation for multimodal threats; need autonomous discovery of novel, boundary-pushing edge cases to improve content safety.
AI.method: Iterative strategy of proposing novel hypotheses and mutating past attempts, orchestrated by a high-reasoning Architect, an advanced image generator, and a multi-level verification committee of LLMs; uses in-context demonstrations via test-time retrieval; no human labeling.
AI.result: Significant robustness gain; FNR reduced from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Agentic red-teaming can autonomously uncover boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases, improving safety without human annotation; potential applicability to broader multimodal safety tasks.

title: Lyapunov Guidance: A Unified Framework for Stabilizing Generative Flows
summary: Flow matching has emerged as an effective framework for learning complex data distributions, but adapting pretrained flow models to new tasks often requires computationally expensive retraining. Post-training guidance provides a more efficient alternative, but existing methods are largely heuristic and offer no explicit stability guarantees. We address this limitation by proposing LyaGuide, a unified Lyapunov-guided framework that formulates flow guidance as a Lyapunov control problem. Our main theoretical result establishes an equivalence between guided flow matching and Lyapunov control, thereby unifying common guidance strategies, such as classifier guidance, reward guidance, and energy-based guidance, within a single control-theoretic framework. To enforce the Lyapunov condition, we introduce a pseudo-projection operator with a closed-form expression that endows learned or heuristic guidance terms with explicit stability guarantees. LyaGuide supports two practical settings: a model-driven setting, where the target guidance distribution is specified through a known Lyapunov function, and a data-driven setting, where the guidance is adapted from task-specific downstream data. LyaGuide is compatible with existing guidance methods, introduces minimal additional computational overhead, and is straightforward to integrate in practice. Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks, image inverse problems, reinforcement learning planning, and energy-based modeling demonstrate consistent improvements in sample quality, guidance fidelity, and robustness, while maintaining computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Unifies guidance for pretrained flow models under a Lyapunov control framework (LyaGuide), providing explicit stability guarantees via a pseudo-projection operator; supports model-driven and data-driven guidance with minimal overhead and strong empirical performance across domains.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained flow models to new tasks via retraining is costly; existing post-training guidance lacks formal stability guarantees and a unified theory.
AI.method: Formulate flow guidance as a Lyapunov control problem, prove equivalence between guided flow matching and Lyapunov control, introduce a closed-form pseudo-projection operator to enforce the Lyapunov condition, and support two settings: model-driven (known Lyapunov function) and data-driven (downstream data).
AI.result: Theoretical equivalence between guided flow matching and Lyapunov control is established; the pseudo-projection operator ensures stability; empirical results across synthetic benchmarks, image inverse problems, RL planning, and energy-based modeling show improved sample quality, guidance fidelity, and robustness with low overhead.
AI.conclusion: LyaGuide provides explicit stability guarantees, unifies diverse guidance strategies under a single control-theoretic framework, and is practical to adopt with broad applicability and efficiency gains.

title: Multi-Scale ViT Inference with Habitat-Fit Priors and kNN Retrieval for Multi-Species Plant Identification
summary: This paper describes DS@GT ARC's third-place solution to the PlantCLEF 2026 challenge on multi-species plant identification in vegetation quadrat images, where systems must predict every species present in high-resolution (~3000 x 3000 pixel) plot photographs while training only on single-label images of individual plants. The pipeline is built around a fine-tuned DINOv2 ViT-L/14 classifier applied over a multi-scale tile decomposition of each quadrat, with per-tile predictions blended with a FAISS kNN retriever and post-processed by source-aware temporal fusion across repeated plot visits, a habitat-fit demotion that injects geographic and altitude priors from the training data, and a South-Western Europe geographic mask. Habitat-fit demotion and multi-scale aggregation are the largest individual contributors in the ablations. Two complementary training-centric directions, a cross-region transformer with noisy-student distillation on the LUCAS dataset and a label-as-query transformer decoder over synthetic CLS-domain pseudo-quadrats, yielded null results. An inference-time augmentation with instance-aware segmentation crops also did not improve performance. The selected submission reaches a private-leaderboard macro-F1 of 0.43902 (third place; public 0.51096); an unselected configuration of the same pipeline scored above 0.45 on the private set. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/plantclef-2026.

AI.tldr: Applied DS@GT ARC's PlantCLEF 2026 entry: a multi-scale, tile-based DINOv2 ViT-L/14 classifier with FAISS kNN integration, temporal fusion, and habitat priors; achieved 3rd place on private leaderboard (macro-F1 0.43902), with habitat-fit demotion and multi-scale aggregation driving most gains.
AI.motivation: Address multi-species plant identification in high-resolution quadrats while training only on single-label plant images; leverage spatial granularity and geog priors to bridge label gaps and improve performance in complex vegetation scenes.
AI.method: Fine-tuned DINOv2 ViT-L/14 classifier applied to a multi-scale tile decomposition of quadrats; per-tile predictions blended with FAISS kNN retrieval; source-aware temporal fusion across repeated plot visits; habitat-fit demotion injecting geographic and altitude priors from training data; South-Western Europe geographic mask. Ablation shows habitat-fit demotion and multi-scale aggregation are the largest contributors. Two additional training-centric approaches (cross-region transformer with noisy-student distillation on LUCAS; label-as-query transformer decoder on synthetic pseudo-quadrats) yielded null results. Inference-time augmentation with instance-aware segmentation crops provided no improvement.
AI.result: Selected submission achieved private-leaderboard macro-F1 of 0.43902 (3rd place; public 0.51096). An unselected configuration of the same pipeline scored above 0.45 on the private set.
AI.conclusion: The combination of multi-scale tile-based classification with habitat priors and temporal fusion yields competitive results for multi-species plant ID in quadrats, with habitat-fit demotion and multi-scale aggregation being the dominant contributors; competing training strategies did not improve performance; code is publicly available.

title: Representation-Aligned Tactile Grounding for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
summary: Tactile-enhanced vision-language-action (VLA) policies have been introduced for contact-rich manipulation, where critical interaction states are often hidden from vision. Future tactile prediction is a promising way to use touch because it turns tactile outcomes into supervision for action-induced contact dynamics. Yet VLA policies contain representations with different roles, from perceptual encoding to motor prediction, making it unclear where this supervision should be applied. We study this as a representation-alignment problem. Through a linear probe analysis, we find that future tactile states are most predictable from intermediate action-expert features, rather than from vision-language features or final action states.
