AI.method: Construct a tractable framework for LLM serving that links statistical signals (pretraining coverage and data SNR) to economic incentives; analyze equilibrium resource use and dominance regimes; prove that offering both personalization methods never lowers maximal profits; validate with GPT-2 experiments on linear regression and a survey of 21 platforms’ documentation.
AI.result: ICL and SFT dominate in different regimes determined by pretraining coverage and data SNR; congestion can flip dominance between ICL and SFT; equilibrium congestion is non-monotone with respect to pretraining precision, coverage, and task difficulty; offering both methods never hurts platform profits; GPT-2 experiments corroborate predictions; platform survey shows dual-offering increased from 9.5% (2021) to 71.4% (2025).
AI.conclusion: Platforms should offer multiple personalization algorithms to maximize profits and adapt to task characteristics and congestion; design strategies must consider the non-monotone effects of pretraining and data signals on congestion; these results generalize to broader LLM-serving settings and user ecosystems.

title: HyMobileAgent: Data-Environment Co-Scaling for Efficient GUI Agents
summary:
As large multimodal models move from understanding content to operating on digital environments, mobile GUI has emerged as a challenging and consequential testbed for digital embodied intelligence. Mobile agents operate under three coupled constraints: precise perception of complex interfaces, scalable acquisition of high-quality interaction data, and robust long-horizon decision making under compounding execution errors. This report presents HyMobileAgent, a mobile GUI agent built on Hy3.0-VL-A3B, a vision-native foundation model featuring native any-resolution input, an A3B-scale deployment budget, and a 32K context window to model extended interaction histories. Rather than relying solely on model scaling, we develop a joint data and environment centric scaling framework to address the key bottlenecks of mobile interaction.
  Our framework integrates a GUI perception flywheel combining mock-interface synthesis, rejection sampling, and icon-specific augmentation; a knowledge pipeline that transforms tutorial videos into structured interaction data; a million-scale action data pipeline deployed across more than 2000 sandbox and real-device instances with automated failure attribution; the PhoneWorld Mock App Factory, providing a resettable training environment with 34 mock applications and over 34000 tasks; and a structured Planning-and-Reflection mechanism with explicit dead-loop detection for reliable long-horizon execution.
  We also introduce a progressive training recipe consisting of mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with task-specific reward designs.

AI.tldr: HyMobileAgent presents a joint data-and-environment scaling framework for mobile GUI agents, built on Hy3.0-VL-A3B with a 32K context. It integrates a GUI perception flywheel, a knowledge pipeline converting tutorial videos, a million-scale action data pipeline across 2,000 devices, a PhoneWorld Mock App Factory (34 apps, 34,000 tasks), and a Planning-and-Reflection mechanism, together with a progressive training recipe (mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, RL with task-specific rewards) to enable robust, long-horizon mobile interaction.
AI.motivation: Address the three coupled bottlenecks in mobile GUI agents: precise perception of complex interfaces, scalable acquisition of high-quality interaction data, and robust long-horizon decision making under compounding execution errors. Scaling model size alone is insufficient; a joint data- and environment-centric scaling framework is needed to close the gap between perception, data, and planning in embodied mobile interactions.
AI.method: - GUI perception flywheel: mock-interface synthesis, rejection sampling, and icon-specific augmentation. - Knowledge pipeline: convert tutorial videos into structured interaction data. - Million-scale action data pipeline: deployed across 2,000 sandbox and real-device instances with automated failure attribution. - PhoneWorld Mock App Factory: resettable training environment with 34 mock apps and over 34,000 tasks. - Planning-and-Reflection: explicit dead-loop detection for reliable long-horizon execution. - Progressive training: mid-training, supervised fine-tuning, and RL with task-specific reward designs.
AI.result: An end-to-end framework that demonstrates scalable data and environment scaling for mobile GUI agents, enabling robust long-horizon planning and execution. The integration across perception, data pipelines, mock environments, and planning yields improved reliability and scalability for mobile interaction tasks, supported by a large-scale deployment footprint.
AI.conclusion: The work argues that joint data- and environment-scale strategies are essential for advancing embodied mobile GUI intelligence. The proposed components collectively address perception, data, and planning bottlenecks and offer a scalable path toward robust, long-horizon mobile agent operation, with potential for broader applicability and future enhancements.

title: Reinforcement Learning for the Full Strawberry Harvesting Process: Obstacle Separation, Detachment, and Placement
summary: Severe occlusions and deformable plant structures introduce complex contact dynamics that challenge robotic strawberry harvesting. A policy-driven reinforcement learning (RL) framework with heuristic phase coordination was developed, in which obstacle separation, fruit detachment, and placement were formulated as a sequential decision-making task. A shared interaction-aware policy generated Cartesian motions across all task phases, while lightweight heuristic logic coordinated task progression and gripper events. A shared structured observation space was used to represent target, obstacle, end-effector, and task-context information. A hierarchical architecture combined the high-level policy with low-level Cartesian impedance control for compliant interaction. To support zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, feasibility-first observation alignment and domain randomization were adopted. The policy achieved success rates of 89.7% in simulation and 82.0% in real-world experiments. As the occlusion level increased from 1 to 5, the average execution time increased from 12.99 s to 21.73 s, reflecting greater interaction complexity. These results demonstrated effective transfer of interaction-aware harvesting behaviors to a structurally different robotic platform.

AI.tldr: A policy-driven RL framework with heuristic phase coordination enables interaction-aware robotic strawberry harvesting, achieving strong sim-to-real transfer and robust performance under occlusions using a shared policy, hierarchical control, and structured observations.
AI.motivation: Handling severe occlusions and deformable plant structures creates challenging contact dynamics for autonomous harvesting; robust, transferable control policies are required to operate across different robotic platforms.
AI.method: Formulated obstacle separation, fruit detachment, and placement as sequential decisions within a policy-driven RL framework. A shared interaction-aware policy generates Cartesian motions for all task phases, with lightweight heuristic logic coordinating task progression and gripper events. A structured observation space represents target, obstacle, end-effector, and task-context information. A hierarchical architecture combines a high-level policy with low-level Cartesian impedance control for compliant interaction. Feasibility-first observation alignment and domain randomization support zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: The policy achieved 89.7% success in simulation and 82.0% in real-world experiments. Occlusion level increased from 1 to 5, and average execution time rose from 12.99 s to 21.73 s, indicating greater interaction complexity.
AI.conclusion: Interaction-aware harvesting policies can transfer across structurally different robotic platforms and maintain robust performance under occlusion. The approach leveraging observation alignment and domain randomization enables zero-shot transfer, with hierarchical control ensuring compliant, coordinated manipulation during complex contact tasks.

title: CatalogAgent: A Supervisor-mediated Self-Learning System Enabling Context Engineering for GenAI Models
summary: Product catalogs are the backbone of e-commerce sites, yet a large number of structured attributes (SAs) -- such as material, color, and shape -- often have missing values. Typically, SA values are extracted from product information, including titles and descriptions. While LLM-based generator-evaluator frameworks have demonstrated effectiveness for SA prediction -- where an LLM generates SA values and another evaluates them -- they face challenges when the Generator and Evaluator produce conflicting outputs, as either component can make mistakes. We introduce \texttt{CatalogAgent}, a novel agentic system that continuously improves Generator and Evaluator models for e-commerce catalog enrichment. When disagreements arise from (1) internal conflicts between the LLM-based Generator and Evaluator, or (2) external feedback from sellers on LLM outputs, a Supervisor Agent intervenes to mediate these conflicts and make final decisions. The system also incorporates a Memory Base and a Memory Summarizer that stores Supervisor Agent activities from individual cases and aggregates patterns into learnings. These learnings are fed back to the worker Generator and Evaluator LLMs, enabling self-improvement without human intervention. Through context engineering -- injecting learnings and insights into worker LLMs' contexts -- the system successfully transfers the Supervisor's capabilities to the Generator and Evaluator, improving their performance by 15.24\% and 13.98\%, respectively. Our experiments demonstrate a new paradigm of Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning systems for improving generative AI model accuracy.

AI.tldr: CatalogAgent introduces a Supervisor Agent to mediate conflicts between an LLM-based Generator and Evaluator for product-attribute prediction, augmented by a Memory Base and Memory Summarizer. It uses context engineering to inject learned patterns back into worker models, achieving ~15% improvements for Generator and ~14% for Evaluator, demonstrating a self-learning, Supervisor-mediated paradigm for SA enrichment in e-commerce catalogs.
AI.motivation: Structured attributes in product catalogs are often incomplete. LLM-based Generator-Evaluator setups can generate and verify SA values, but disagreements between components or external seller feedback can degrade accuracy. A supervisory mediation layer and memory-driven feedback aim to stabilize and improve the system without human intervention.
AI.method: A multi-agent architecture: Generator (LLM), Evaluator (LLM), and Supervisor Agent. When disagreements occur or external feedback arises, the Supervisor mediates to reach final decisions. A Memory Base stores case-level activities; a Memory Summarizer aggregates patterns into learnings. These learnings are injected into worker LLM contexts (context engineering) to enable self-improvement. The cycle repeats, enabling continuous improvement.
AI.result: Empirical results show improvements of 15.24% for the Generator and 13.98% for the Evaluator. The experiments demonstrate a new paradigm: Supervisor Agent-mediated self-learning to enhance generative AI accuracy in catalog enrichment.
AI.conclusion: Supervisor-mediated, memory-informed self-learning can transfer supervisory capabilities into generator and evaluator components through context engineering, yielding significant accuracy gains and establishing a scalable paradigm for SA completion in e-commerce catalogs.

title: A Noise-Robust Elicit-to-Optimize Framework for Distortion Riskmetrics via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: We propose a noise-robust elicit-to-optimize framework that integrates inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and reinforcement learning (RL) for eliciting agents' risk preferences and optimizing policies under a broad class of risk objectives characterized by distortion riskmetrics. On the elicitation side, we propose an adaptive Bayesian IRL method that infers agents' latent risk objectives from their noisy observed decisions, explicitly allowing agents to take stochastic and suboptimal actions. We establish the existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions that identifies the preferred distortion riskmetric within the candidate class and prove that the convergence rate of the algorithm is of order $O(\exp(-cm+O(\sqrt{m\log m})))$ under general settings, where $c>0$ is a constant and $m$ denotes the number of algorithm iterations. On the optimization side, we develop a model-free RL algorithm for optimizing policies under conditional distortion riskmetrics. By representing the objective as an integral of the conditional cost quantile function with respect to the distortion function, the method unifies distortion-riskmetric objectives. We optimize diverse risk objectives by extending the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm with policy, value, and quantile neural networks, where the quantile network estimates the full conditional cost quantile function and enables numerical evaluation of general risk objectives. A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates the framework's elicitation accuracy and effectiveness in complex financial environments.

AI.tldr: A noise-robust elicitation-to-optimization framework that combines adaptive Bayesian IRL with model-free RL to handle distortion-riskmetric objectives; provides theoretical guarantees and empirical validation in finance.
AI.motivation: To recover latent risk preferences from noisy, potentially suboptimal decisions and to optimize policies under a broad class of distortion riskmetrics with robustness to noise.
AI.method: Elicitation: adaptive Bayesian IRL with a finite set of distinguishing questions and a proven convergence rate O(exp(-c m + O(sqrt(m log m)))); Optimization: model-free RL (PPO) extended with policy, value, and quantile neural networks, representing the objective as an integral of the conditional cost quantile function with respect to the distortion function to handle conditional distortion riskmetrics.
AI.result: Proves existence of a finite set of distinguishing questions for identifying the preferred distortion riskmetric; establishes a convergence rate for the elicitation algorithm; develops a PPO-based RL method with quantile networks to handle distortion riskmetrics; empirical study shows elicitation accuracy and policy performance in complex financial settings.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified, robust approach for eliciting risk preferences and optimizing risk-aware policies under a broad class of distortion riskmetrics, with strong theoretical guarantees and practical efficacy in finance; opens avenues for extending to other risk measures and domains.

title: Breaking the Model Forgetting Cycle in Long-Incremental 3D Object Detection
summary: Incremental 3D object detection requires a detector to learn novel object classes while remembering previously learned ones over sequentially arriving data. Previous methods, primarily based on pseudo-labeling, perform reasonably in short-incremental stages but still suffer from severe model forgetting when dealing with long-incremental sequences. We investigate this failure and reveal a detrimental self-reinforcing cycle: data distribution shift of novel classes causes model forgetting on old classes, which further produces accumulated error in pseudo-labeling that exacerbates model degradation. To address this issue, we draw inspiration from the human learning process and propose the \emph{Learning-Dynamics-driven Memory and Review} (LDMR) framework. LDMR monitors per-class detection quality at periodic training checkpoints and uses these learning-dynamics signals to drive two innovative mechanisms, namely (i) human-like intra-stage review that divides each incremental stage into multiple sub-stages' training and concentrates on remembering the most-forgotten objects, and (ii) scene-aware cross-stage memory evolution that evolves a memory bank to transfer knowledge between two consecutive stages by jointly considering scene learnability and diversity. Extensive experiments across multiple long-incremental protocols on indoor benchmarks SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 show that LDMR substantially mitigates the model forgetting and outperforms all baselines by a clear margin. Code is available at https://github.com/qianpeisheng/LDMR.

AI.tldr: Proposes LDMR to mitigate forgetting in long-incremental 3D object detection by using learning-dynamics-driven memory and review, with intra-stage sub-stage training and cross-stage memory evolution; achieves strong gains on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2; code released.
AI.motivation: Incremental 3D object detectors suffer severe forgetting due to distribution shift for novel classes and error accumulation from pseudo-labeling; existing methods fail in long sequences; need to model learning dynamics to break the self-reinforcing cycle.
AI.method: LDMR monitors per-class detection quality at training checkpoints; introduces two mechanisms: (i) intra-stage review that partitions each incremental stage into sub-stages focusing on most-forgotten objects; (ii) scene-aware cross-stage memory evolution that updates a memory bank to transfer knowledge between stages by jointly considering scene learnability and diversity.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 show LDMR substantially mitigates forgetting and outperforms baselines by margin; code at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Learning-dynamics-driven memory and review effectively reduces forgetting in long-incremental 3D object detection and provides a practical framework with memory management guided by detection-quality dynamics; potential for broader application and extension.

title: BridgeFlow: Fast and Robust SE(2)-Equivariant Motion Planning with Flow Matching
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). 8 pages, 7 figures
summary: In robotic motion planning, equivariance to rigid body transformations is crucial for robust spatial generalization. However, current learning-based planners face a critical dilemma: they either lack inherent equivariance, treating transformed tasks as novel scenarios, or enforce it via computationally expensive specialized architectures that bottleneck real-time inference. To break this trade-off, we propose BridgeFlow, a fast and strictly SE(2)-equivariant generative motion planning framework. Rather than relying on heavy equivariant networks, BridgeFlow achieves exact spatial equivariance via a lightweight task-centric canonicalization module, enabling generalization using standard architectures. To further accelerate inference, we pair a Brownian bridge informative prior with context-aware mini-batch optimal transport. This constructs a straightened vector field that minimizes transport costs and stabilizes training. Furthermore, environmental awareness is explicitly embedded via Classifier-Free Guidance. Evaluations in dense 2D environments and on a 7-DoF Franka manipulator demonstrate that BridgeFlow achieves up to a 15x inference speedup and a 2x higher valid trajectory rate over state-of-the-art diffusion baselines, alongside robust generalization to entirely unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.

AI.tldr: BridgeFlow delivers fast, strictly SE(2)-equivariant generative motion planning by replacing heavy equivariant networks with a task-centric canonicalization module, plus a Brownian-bridge prior and context-aware optimal transport; it achieves up to 15x speedups and 2x higher valid trajectory rates, with strong generalization to unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.
AI.motivation: Current learning-based planners face a trade-off between inherent equivariance (robust spatial generalization) and real-time inference, as enforcing equivariance via specialized architectures is computationally expensive. There is a need for exact spatial equivariance without sacrificing inference speed.
AI.method: Key components include a lightweight task-centric canonicalization module to achieve exact SE(2) equivariance without heavy networks, a Brownian-bridge informative prior, context-aware mini-batch optimal transport to construct a straightened vector field with lower transport costs, and classifier-free guidance to inject environmental awareness. The framework operates as a generative diffusion-based planner evaluated on dense 2D environments and a 7-DoF Franka manipulator.
AI.result: Empirical results show up to 15x faster inference and 2x higher valid trajectory rate compared with state-of-the-art diffusion baselines. BridgeFlow generalizes robustly to unseen environments and arbitrary spatial transformations.
AI.conclusion: BridgeFlow demonstrates that exact SE(2) equivariance can be achieved with a lightweight canonicalization module, avoiding heavy equivariant architectures while delivering strong generalization and real-time performance in diffusion-based motion planning.

title: Instrument Effects in Language-Model Honesty Evaluation: An Auditable Single-System Demonstration
summary: Evaluations of language-model honesty read the model's verdicts as evidence about the model. We test the instrument instead. We built a text-adventure world where the game engine, not any model, knows whether the quest can be completed. A language model plays under a budget and must eventually declare its quest complete, unreachable, or not yet decidable; the engine scores every verdict. Decision rules were recorded before results were read, and run artifacts bind the revisions they executed; the strength of preregistration varies by series and is disclosed. With the player held fixed, instrument choices substantially changed measured behavior. On four byte-identical anchors, expanding a two-verdict grammar to three verdicts moved strong claims from 38/40 to 7/40, while the new incomplete verdict took 28/40 outcomes; across series 2, 93/158 valid games ended incomplete. One sentence disclosing the success criterion took matched-instance false verdicts from 18/59 to 0/58, through fewer decision points and cleaner decisions. Repeated runs of one fixed configuration produced non-stable verdict distributions on 3 of 4 instances: single runs report samples as dispositions. A formally preregistered narrative-register gradient was falsified; two post-hoc, hypothesis-generating patterns remain: register presence roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering moved verdicts more than register content (.383 meter vs .150 lantern). The narrator compressed abundant budgets toward scarcity landmarks, yet the registered mediation test returned a null. We propose a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments.

AI.tldr: Instrument choices heavily shape language-model verdicts in a controlled text-adventure evaluation; preregistration can be falsified; results show instability and post-hoc patterns; a four-check integrity protocol is proposed.
AI.motivation: To assess whether language-model honesty evaluations are reliable when the evaluation instrument itself may bias the verdicts, highlighting issues with preregistration, stability, and interpretability.
AI.method: Create a complete text-adventure environment where the engine knows solvability; have a language model operate under a budget and declare quest status; test different verdict grammars; preregister analysis plans; run multiple series with fixed player and random seeds; compare results across instrument variants; examine stability with repeated runs; analyze whether narrative or budget cues correlate with verdicts; propose integrity checks.
AI.result: Instrument design choices (e.g., verdict grammar, budget manipulation, disclosure of success criteria) substantially affect outcomes; many results show pronounced shifts in strong-claim frequencies and incomplete verdicts; results exhibit unstable distributions across runs; preregistered analyses can be falsified; some post-hoc patterns emerge (register presence, budget effects) but mediation tests fail; many games remain incomplete; overall, evaluation reliability is in question.
AI.conclusion: The current evaluation instruments for model honesty are fragile and heavily instrument-dependent; to improve reliability, a four-check integrity protocol for eval instruments should be adopted to detect and mitigate instrument-driven biases.

title: Integration Matters: Rollout-Based Training for Constrained Diffusion Models
summary: Constrained generative models aim to produce samples that satisfy complex feasibility constraints while remaining faithful to the data distribution. Existing constrained generation methods typically enforce constraints either through training-time optimization or sampling-time correction. Training-time optimization approaches optimize on states induced by the training distribution, which can differ substantially from those encountered during sampling. Sampling-time correction methods instead modify the sampling process at inference, introducing distribution shift and requiring expensive tuning, particularly for few-step sampling. We propose a fine-tuning framework that incorporates constraint guidance obtained through online rollout into the training process, which aligns training with sampling by differentiating through the fixed noise schedule used to numerically integrate the denoising process. This exposes the model to violations that arise along the denoising trajectory and aligns diffusion learning with the sampling process. Experiments across multiple tasks show that our method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior methods.

AI.tldr: A diffusion model is fine-tuned with constraint guidance from online rollouts, differentiating through the denoising schedule to align training with sampling, improving constraint satisfaction without harming sampling quality.
AI.motivation: Constrained generation often suffers from training-time optimization on distributions that differ from sampling-time distributions, or from sampling-time corrections that shift the distribution and require tuning. A method that aligns training with the sampling process can reduce mismatch and improve feasibility adherence.
AI.method: Introduce a fine-tuning framework that uses online rollout for constraint guidance during training. The approach differentiates through the fixed noise schedule used in the diffusion denoising process, exposing the model to constraint violations along the denoising trajectory and aligning diffusion learning with sampling.
AI.result: Across multiple tasks, the method improves constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive sampling quality compared to prior constrained-generation approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed technique reduces training-sampling mismatch in constrained diffusion models by integrating rollout-based constraint guidance into training, yielding better feasibility adherence with minimal sacrifice to sampling performance.

title: Advanced Image Generation: Negative Prompt Optimization and Latent Classifier Guidance
summary: We present a novel system that integrates negative prompt optimization via a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence LLM and latent-space classifier guidance to improve the quality of images generated by Stable Diffusion. Our approach automatically generates optimized negative prompts, and employs a CNN-RNN hybrid classifier to evaluate and guide diffusion steps, rolling back low-quality latent updates. Experimental results demonstrate that our dual-guidance framework reduces artifacts and improves semantic fidelity compared to baseline diffusion.

AI.tldr: Dual-guidance for Stable Diffusion using automatic negative-prompt optimization via a fine-tuned seq-to-seq LLM and latent-space classifier guidance (CNN-RNN) to roll back low-quality latent updates, reducing artifacts and improving semantic fidelity.
AI.motivation: Address artifacts and semantic drift in diffusion-based image synthesis by jointly optimizing negative prompts and constraining latent updates during diffusion to improve output quality.
AI.method: 1) Fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence LLM generates optimized negative prompts automatically. 2) A CNN-RNN hybrid classifier evaluates latent updates and guides diffusion steps via latent-space feedback, rolling back low-quality updates. 3) Integrates these two components as dual-guidance within Stable Diffusion to steer generation.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate reduced artifacts and higher semantic fidelity relative to baseline diffusion methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of dual-guidance with automatic negative prompts and latent-space classification.
AI.conclusion: A dual-guidance framework combining automatic negative-prompt optimization and latent-space classifier guidance enhances diffusion quality beyond baseline Stable Diffusion by mitigating artifacts and preserving semantic content.

title: Hybrid Rigid-Soft Robotic Gripper with Shape Adaptation, Uniform Force Distribution, and Self-Locking Capabilities
summary: Conventional robotic grippers face a significant challenge in agricultural automation: the trade-off between compliant, adaptive grasping, pressure balancing among all joints, and high load capacity, often at the cost of high energy consumption. This paper presents a novel hybrid rigid-soft gripper that integrated low-cost, membrane-based pneumatic actuators with 3D-printed dual ratchet-pawl mechanisms to simultaneously achieve shape adaptation, uniform force distribution, and energy-free self-locking. The dual-ratchet structure assembled in an offset configuration significantly increased the angular resolution of the joint locking mechanism. Key experimental results demonstrated the gripper's superior performance: a remarkable maximum load capacity of 4200 g, far exceeding that of conventional soft grippers (45-210 g); more uniform force distribution across object sizes (1.75-35.29% difference ratio) compared to a rigid gripper (56.77-66.44%), with peak contact forces remaining below surface damage thresholds; and a 50.05% reduction in total energy consumption to 42.6 J per grasp cycle, achieved by eliminating the need for continuous pneumatic pressure through the self-locking mechanism, compared to 85.28 J for a conventional soft gripper. The combination of additive manufacturing for ratchets and commercially available materials for pneumatic chambers ensured a low-cost and easily fabricated design. These findings validated that the proposed gripper successfully bridged the gap between soft compliance and rigid reliability, offering a robust and efficient solution for scalable agricultural harvesting and manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Hybrid rigid-soft gripper with dual ratchet-pawl self-locking achieves high payload, uniform force distribution, and energy efficiency, bridging soft compliance and rigid reliability.
AI.motivation: To overcome the typical trade-offs in agricultural grippers among compliance, force distribution, load capacity, and energy consumption.
AI.method: Fabricate a hybrid gripper by integrating membrane-based pneumatic actuators with 3D-printed dual ratchet-pawl mechanisms. Use an offset dual-ratchet configuration to enhance angular resolution of joint locking. Employ additive manufacturing for ratchets and commercially available pneumatic chambers. Evaluate performance against conventional soft and rigid grippers using metrics: maximum load, force distribution across object sizes, surface damage thresholds, and energy per grasp.
AI.result: Maximum load of 4200 g; more uniform force distribution across object sizes (1.75–35.29% difference) versus rigid grippers (56.77–66.44%); peak contact forces below surface damage thresholds; energy per grasp reduced by 50.05% to 42.6 J (vs 85.28 J for conventional soft gripper). Energy-free self-locking eliminates continuous pneumatic actuation.
AI.conclusion: The gripper effectively bridges soft compliance with rigid reliability, offering a robust, low-cost, and energy-efficient solution for scalable agricultural harvesting and manipulation tasks.

title: Reward-Free Evolving Agents via Pairwise Validator
summary: A self-evolving agentic loop repeatedly proposes a tweaked version of an agent (its prompt template or program) and accepts or rejects the change based on a per-iteration quality signal. Designing that signal is often the costly part of the project: a reliable scalar reward requires domain expertise and labeled examples that are themselves as expensive to assemble as the agent's underlying task. We propose replacing the scalar at the accept/reject gate with a pairwise validator: a frozen LLM that, given the parent and child candidate, returns a binary verdict on which is better. Pairwise judgment is generally easier and more stable than absolute scoring, due to its contrastive nature, which mitigates the need for strict scale calibration. The validator also requires no training of its own. We integrate the validator into three published self-evolving engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and report two flavors: Adaptive Focus, which retains the engine's existing val-set parent selection, and Soft Elo, which lets the validator's verdicts drive parent selection so that val-set rewards drop as well. Across multiple agents and two artifact substrates (prompt and code), our method matches or exceeds the full-reward baseline on the majority of settings we evaluate, and the pattern survives a cross-family validator swap. The pairwise gate is thus a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design at competitive task accuracy without the labeling cost.

AI.tldr: A pairwise, frozen LLM validator replaces scalar reward signals in self-evolving agent loops, enabling a drop-in gate that compares parent vs child prompts/colicies. It matches or exceeds full-reward baselines across multiple engines and substrates, using Adaptive Focus or Soft Elo styles, with no additional training or labeled data.
AI.motivation: Scalar reward design for self-evolving agents is costly and requires labeled data and domain expertise. A stable, calibration-free alternative is a pairwise, contrastive evaluation that determines which option is better without absolute scoring.
AI.method: Introduce a frozen LLM that performs pairwise judgment between a parent and a child candidate. Integrate this pairwise validator into three engines (GEPA, ADRS, ShinkaEvolve) and implement two strategies: Adaptive Focus (keep existing val-set-based parent selection) and Soft Elo (validator verdicts influence parent selection, reducing val-set rewards). Evaluate across multiple agents and two substrates (prompt and code).
AI.result: The pairwise gate achieves equal or superior performance to full-reward baselines in a majority of settings. It remains effective under cross-family validator swaps, indicating robustness and generality. It serves as a drop-in replacement for per-step reward design while eliminating labeling cost.
AI.conclusion: Pairwise validation provides a stable, training-free mechanism to guide self-evolving agents, delivering competitive task accuracy without the expense of absolute reward labeling and is broadly applicable across engines and substrates.

title: LATTICE: Graph Self-Supervised Learning for Multimodal Spatial Omics Integration
summary: Spatially resolved omics studies increasingly combine transcriptomic and epigenomic assays, yet downstream analysis is often still performed using single-modality pipelines. We present LATTICE (Latent Alignment of Tissue-level and Transcriptomic Information for Cross-modal Embedding), a graph-based self-supervised framework that learns spot-level representations from harmonized multimodal features. LATTICE integrates five aligned modality blocks per Visium spot: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT\&Tag. These modalities capture spatial transcriptomic measurements, single-cell inferred regulatory activity, and in situ chromatin and histone states within a unified lattice representation. LATTICE constructs a spatial neighborhood graph and trains a TransformerConv encoder using masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness objectives. On a private 11-sample melanoma cohort from an anonymized clinical collaborator comprising 54{,}912 total spots, LATTICE demonstrated stable optimization behavior, reproducible embeddings across analysis seeds, and complete multimodal integration across all samples. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA alone substantially improved concordance with Space Ranger clusters across 11 runs (adjusted Rand index [ARI] +0.157, normalized mutual information [NMI] +0.143, and spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved spatial contiguity and multimodal utility score (MUS), although they sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived reference labels, likely because the learned embeddings captured chromatin and regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity alone. These results position LATTICE as a practical and empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, while also highlighting the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking.

AI.tldr: LATTICE is a graph-based, self-supervised multimodal spatial-omics framework that harmonizes five modalities per Visium spot, uses a TransformerConv encoder with masked reconstruction, cross-modal alignment, and spatial smoothness, and achieves improved alignment with RNA-derived clusters and enhanced spatial contiguity and multimodal utility on a melanoma dataset, with trade-offs in RNA-label concordance and a need for stronger supervision and external benchmarking.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of single-modality pipelines in spatial omics by learning integrated spot-level representations across transcriptomic and epigenomic modalities, capturing regulatory and chromatin information in a unified spatial framework.
AI.method: Construct a spatial neighborhood graph over Visium spots and train a TransformerConv encoder in a graph-based, self-supervised setting using (1) masked reconstruction, (2) cross-modal alignment, and (3) spatial smoothness objectives. Five aligned modality blocks per spot are used: Visium RNA, scMultiome RNA, scMultiome ATAC, spatial ATAC, and spatial CUT&Tag, enabling a lattice representation that blends spatial transcriptomics, regulatory activity, and in situ chromatin/histone state.
AI.result: On an anonymized melanoma cohort of 11 samples (54,912 spots), LATTICE showed stable optimization, reproducible embeddings across seeds, and complete multimodal integration. Adding scMultiome RNA to Visium RNA markedly increased concordance with Space Ranger clusters across 11 runs (AR I +0.157, NMI +0.143, spatial contiguity +0.174). Additional modalities further improved contiguity and the multimodal utility score (MUS), though they sometimes reduced agreement with RNA-derived labels, likely because the embeddings captured chromatin/regulatory structure beyond transcriptomic similarity.
AI.conclusion: LATTICE offers a practical, empirically grounded framework for multimodal spatial omics integration, demonstrating robust multimodal embedding across samples and modalities, while highlighting the need for stronger supervision and broader external benchmarking to ensure generalization and interpretability.

title: MagicPrompt: Ultra-Lightweight Prompt Tuning for Video Generation
summary: Large-scale video diffusion models (VDMs) deliver strong generation performance, but full fine-tuning for downstream tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have two critical flaws on billion-scale models: they still require substantial trainable parameters, and reward-based training suffers from noise-induced optimization instability in condition-guided tasks. We propose MagicPrompt, a lightweight framework that achieves extreme parameter efficiency and stable reward optimization. It first adopts Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning, which steers generation via lightweight soft prompts with orders of magnitude fewer parameters while preserving pre-trained knowledge. It further introduces Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization, which uses self-supervised latent objectives to improve condition-guided reward training. Experiments show MagicPrompt reaches competitive performance with less than 1\% trainable parameters and notably reduces training costs.

AI.tldr: MagicPrompt achieves extreme parameter efficiency in large-scale video diffusion models by combining Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning with Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization, attaining competitive results with <1% trainable parameters and reduced training cost.
AI.motivation: Large-scale video diffusion models deliver strong generation performance, but full fine-tuning is computationally prohibitive. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods on billion-scale models suffer from two flaws: substantial trainable parameter requirements and instability in reward-based training for condition-guided tasks.
AI.method: Attention-Embedded Prompt Tuning: lightweight soft prompts steer generation while preserving pre-trained knowledge. Dual-Space Reward Feedback Optimization: self-supervised latent objectives enhance condition-guided reward training and stabilize optimization.
AI.result: Experiments show MagicPrompt achieves competitive performance with less than 1% trainable parameters and significantly reduced training costs.
AI.conclusion: MagicPrompt provides an extremely parameter-efficient and stable framework for adapting large video diffusion models to downstream tasks, enabling cost-effective deployment with minimal trainable parameters.

title: Curvature-Constrained and Constant-Speed Distributed Simultaneous Arrival Control for Multi-Robot Systems
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
summary: The simultaneous arrival of multiple mobile robots at a target point is crucial for cooperation tasks such as cooperative encirclement, disaster relief, and environmental monitoring. Although the simultaneous arrival problem itself is already complex, the problem becomes more challenging when there are constraints on the robot trajectory curvatures and the speeds are required to be constant (possibly different for different robots), and the control law for robots needs to be distributed. These constraints are typical for a multi-robot system consisting of, e.g., fixed-wing UAVs. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a distributed switching control method based on the maximum consensus protocol. By exploiting the geometric properties of Dubins paths along with optimization principles, a virtual time variable is introduced, and a hybrid control law that combines optimal control with saturated proportional control is designed. Under the proposed control law, each robot is driven to approach the maximum virtual time among its neighbors, thereby achieving simultaneous arrival under some mild conditions. Furthermore, we prove that in certain cases the proposed method attains a theoretically optimal arrival time. The approach is scalable and real-time, with low communication overhead. Its effectiveness and robustness are validated through extensive simulations and experiments.

AI.tldr: A distributed, curvature-constrained, fixed-speed Dubins-robot coordination method that uses a maximum-consensus switching controller with a virtual time to achieve simultaneous arrival, with optimality in some cases, scalable and validated by simulations/experiments.
AI.motivation: To solve simultaneous arrival for multiple mobile robots under curvature constraints and constant speeds, enabling distributed control suitable for fixed-wing UAVs with low communication overhead.
AI.method: Distributed switching control based on maximum consensus; leverage Dubins path geometry; introduce a virtual time variable; design a hybrid controller combining optimal control with saturated proportional control; drive each agent toward the maximum virtual time among neighbors.
AI.result: Under mild conditions, achieves simultaneous arrival; in certain scenarios, it attains theoretically optimal arrival time; scalable, real-time, with low communication requirements; validated by extensive simulations and experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical, robust, and scalable solution for coordinated arrival under trajectory curvature and speed constraints, with potential optimality guarantees and real-time applicability.

title: CausalGraphX: A Counterfactual Graph Neural Network Framework for Explainable Systemic Risk Assessment
comment: Accepted in AAAI'26 Workshop, Agentic AI in Financial Services
summary: The interconnected nature of global financial systems makes them vulnerable to systemic risks, where the failure of a few institutions can trigger catastrophic cascading defaults. Traditional risk models often fail to capture the complex, non-linear dynamics of these networks. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promise in modeling relational data, they primarily learn correlative patterns and function as black boxes, offering little insight into the causal mechanisms of shock propagation. This limitation is critical for regulators who require explainable models to perform stress tests and devise effective interventions. We introduce CausalGraphX, a novel framework that integrates GNNs with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable assessments of systemic risk. CausalGraphX employs a Graph Attention mechanism to learn representations of institutional vulnerability and uses an adversarial regularization technique to ensure these representations capture causal drivers rather than spurious correlations. Furthermore, we propose an optimization-based approach to generate counterfactual explanations, answering questions such as, "What minimum capital injection would have prevented Bank A's default under a specific stress scenario?" We validate CausalGraphX on large-scale synthetic financial networks. Our results demonstrate that CausalGraphX significantly outperforms traditional and deep learning baselines in predicting cascading defaults while providing sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.

AI.tldr: CausalGraphX integrates Graph Attention Networks with counterfactual reasoning to provide explainable systemic risk assessments and minimal intervention strategies; validated on large synthetic financial networks, it outperforms baselines and yields sparse, actionable counterfactual explanations.
AI.motivation: Regulators need explainable, causal insights into shock propagation and stress testing; traditional risk models are opaque and fail to capture non-linear network dynamics, while GNNs capture relations but not causal mechanisms.
AI.method: Use Graph Attention to learn institutional vulnerability representations; apply adversarial regularization to emphasize causal drivers over spurious correlations; formulate optimization-based counterfactuals to identify minimal capital injections that prevent defaults under given stress scenarios; evaluate on large-scale synthetic financial networks; compare against traditional and deep-learning baselines.
AI.result: CausalGraphX significantly outperforms baselines in predicting cascading defaults and provides sparse, plausible, and actionable counterfactual explanations.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers explainable, causally informed systemic risk assessment by marrying GNN representations with counterfactual reasoning, showing strong performance on synthetic data and providing practical guidance for stress testing and intervention planning.

title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
summary: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee for the e-LAAL architecture. In a platform-level production deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches, e-LAAL improves the empirical revenue--conversion trade-off relative to deployed static benchmarks and outperforms uniform and historical query-dependent static benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Large-scale randomized field experiment shows higher ad load boosts revenue but reduces conversions and engagement; introduces adaptive e-LAAL algorithm combining a model-free LAAL rule with exploration arms, backed by finite-time regret guarantees, and proven to improve the revenue–conversion trade-off in production.
AI.motivation: Quantify the revenue–user outcome trade-off of ad load in sponsored search and address heterogeneity across queries and advertiser mixes; design an adaptive policy with provable guarantees to navigate this trade-off at scale.
AI.method: Field experiment on an Android app store with 1–6 sponsored slots across over 5 million users; development of e-LAAL (exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load) combining LAAL with static exploration arms; finite-time dynamic-regret analysis; platform deployment serving 22.3 million users and 77.6 million searches; comparison against static benchmarks (uniform and historical query-dependent).
AI.result: Ad load increases revenue up to 43% but reduces total search conversions up to 5% and daily engagement up to 2.2%; substantial heterogeneity: high-ad-conversion queries gain more revenue with extra slots; low-conversion queries gain little or negative revenue; advertiser composition shifts effects; e-LAAL improves the revenue–conversion trade-off relative to static benchmarks and outperforms baseline policies in production.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive exploration-augmented LAAL effectively manages the ad-load decision to improve revenue while maintaining acceptable user outcomes; production deployment with regret guarantees demonstrates practical viability for large-scale platforms.

title: Hough-SIFT: Robust Image Registration for Linear Structures via Hough Space
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Supplementary video is available as an ancillary file. Accepted for oral presentation at the 29th Meeting on Image Recognition and Understanding (MIRU2026)
summary: Image registration is essential in applications such as electronic image stabilization. Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), a widely used local keypoint detector and descriptor, typically provides accurate registration; however, it often fails in scenes with strong linear structures (e.g., shutters), where local features become ambiguous. We propose Hough-SIFT, a robust registration method that performs SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space. In this domain, linear structures form distinctive peaks that restore descriptor discriminability. Experiments demonstrate that Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT frequently fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in normal scenes.

AI.tldr: Hough-SIFT uses SIFT descriptor matching in Hough space to exploit linear-structure peaks, improving robustness for image registration without sacrificing SIFT-level accuracy in normal scenes.
AI.motivation: SIFT provides accurate registration but struggles in scenes with strong linear structures, causing ambiguity in local features, which is problematic for applications like electronic image stabilization.
AI.method: Compute SIFT keypoints and descriptors and perform descriptor matching in Hough space, where linear structures generate distinctive peaks that restore descriptor discriminability and guide robust correspondences and registration.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that Hough-SIFT is robust in linear scenes where SIFT often fails, while maintaining accuracy comparable to SIFT in typical, non-linear scenes.
AI.conclusion: Hough-SIFT enhances SIFT-based registration in challenging linear-structure environments and preserves performance in normal scenes, making it suitable for stabilization and similar applications.

title: Interventional Causal Circuits for Safe Robot Action Testing and Failure Recovery
comment: 1st IJCAI Workshop on Safe Physical AI IJCAI 2026 workshop on Safe Physical AI
summary: Safe physical AI for robot actions are required not only likely to succeed but tested to be safe before execution. In practice, however, formal testing of motion parameters is computationally expensive, and the cost scales poorly with the dimensionality of the action space. When a proposed action is rejected by a tester, the naive response is to resample blindly until a passing candidate is found. This is wasteful, uninformative, and offers no convergence. We argue that rejection should instead trigger causal diagnosis: a principled identification of which action parameter caused the failure and what corrective value maximises the probability of passing testing under the interventional probability distribution. We propose a closed-loop framework that couples a Joint Probability Tree (JPT) with a Causal Circuit derived from a Marginal-Deterministic Variable Tree, enabling exact polytime computation without retraining, or additional data collection. The framework validates tractability of all interventional queries before the robot begins operating, and out-of-support candidates are detected and excluded from correction automatically. We perform experiments in a ROS2 simulation environment, and the framework demonstrates complementary roles across quality of distribution: under a high-quality JPT, the Causal Circuit reduces failed attempts by 10.3% and under a degraded JPT, it reduces total failed attempts by 37%. Every rejected plan produces a structured, interpretable causal report naming the primary cause variable, its observed value, and the recommended corrective region, supporting operator oversight and autonomous recovery without a separately trained failure model.

AI.tldr: A closed-loop JPT-Causal Circuit framework enables causal diagnosis of rejected robot actions, ensuring polynomial-time interventional reasoning, automatic out-of-support handling, and interpretable corrective guidance; it reduces failed attempts in simulation, with performance dependent on JPT quality.
AI.motivation: Formal testing of motion parameters is expensive and scales poorly with action-space dimensionality; naive resampling wastes attempts and provides no convergence; need principled diagnosis to maximize pass probability under interventional distribution.
AI.method: Couple a Joint Probability Tree (JPT) with a Causal Circuit derived from a Marginal-Deterministic Variable Tree; perform exact polynomial-time interventional queries without retraining; detect out-of-support actions; generate structured causal reports; validate in ROS2 simulation.
AI.result: Under high-quality JPT, failed attempts reduced by 10.3%; under degraded JPT, reduced by 37%; reports identify primary cause variable, observed value, and recommended corrective region; no separate failure model needed.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables tractable, interpretable causal diagnosis for safe robot actions, supports operator oversight and autonomous recovery, and avoids retraining or extra data collection while providing early detection of unanswerable interventions.

title: Per-Token Fixed-Point Convergence in Depth-Recurrent Transformers
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Code, configs, experiment log, and checkpoint at https://github.com/jlognn/depth-recurrent-convergence
summary: A depth-recurrent transformer applies a weight-tied core a variable number of times, and prior work has shown that training with a randomized recursion count yields one checkpoint usable across a range of inference depths. We ask what such a model actually computes per token, and measure it directly. On a 135M-class model trained on FineWeb-Edu, the recurrent state converges to a per-token fixed point: mean successive-output KL divergence falls from 3.9e-1 at the second loop to 8.5e-6 by the sixteenth, and per-token state change decays in step. Crucially, this convergence is not uniform across tokens. The median token converges by loop six, while approximately 10 percent of tokens continue to update at the training-mean depth of eight, and mean convergence depth is ordered by token type (whitespace shallowest, content words deepest). This per-token variation is the central object of the paper. We show it is directly readable and that reading it outperforms learning to predict it: a training-free rule that halts each token once its output stabilizes attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (a 38 percent reduction in average depth) and matches uniform depth across the average-depth range, whereas a linear router trained on convergence labels harvested from the same model requires nearly full depth and yields no reduction. The elasticity that makes this possible reproduces here as background (validation loss decreases monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight and remains stable to 32 loops). We report average depth as a FLOP proxy with a three-point wall-clock bracket rather than a realized speedup, make no FLOP-matched parity claim, and note that the allocation results are established at a single scale and seed. The complete study runs on a single RTX 4090 in approximately 100 GPU-hours.

AI.tldr: Per-token convergence depth in a depth-recurrent transformer is not uniform; tokens vary in how many loops are needed to stabilize. A simple, training-free halting rule based on per-token stabilization achieves uniform depth-8 quality and reduces average depth by ~38%, outperforming a learned linear router. The phenomenon is observable, scalable to a 135M-class model on FineWeb-Edu, and the convergence correlates with token type (whitespace shallower, content words deeper).
AI.motivation: To understand what a depth-recurrent transformer computes per token, quantify per-token variability in convergence depth, and evaluate simple strategies to exploit this variability for efficiency without retraining.
AI.method: Analyze a 135M-class depth-recurrent transformer trained on FineWeb-Edu. Measure per-token convergence by tracking the KL divergence between successive token outputs and the per-token state change across recursion loops. Identify the loop at which each token stabilizes, assess dependence on token type, and compare a training-free halting rule (stop when stabilized) against a learned linear router trained on convergence labels. Report average-depth as a FLOP proxy and provide hardware/time context (RTX 4090, ~100 GPU-hours).
AI.result: Convergence converges to a per-token fixed point, with mean successive-output KL divergence decaying from 0.39 at loop 2 to 8.5e-6 by loop 16. Approximately 10% of tokens continue to update at training-mean depth (8). Median token stabilizes by loop 6; token-type depth order: whitespace shallower, content words deeper. A training-free halting rule that stops tokens once stabilized attains uniform depth-8 quality at 4.94 average loops (38% reduction in average depth) and matches uniform depth across the range. A linear router trained on convergence labels yields nearly full depth and no reduction. Validation loss decreases monotonically from 3.80 at one loop to 3.20 at eight and remains stable up to 32 loops. The study is single-scale/seed and runs ~100 GPU-hours on RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: Per-token convergence depth is a central, observable property of depth-recurrent transformers. A simple, training-free halting strategy can leverage per-token stability to achieve substantial efficiency gains (lower average depth) without retraining, whereas learned routing offers no comparable benefit in this setting. The elasticity of the model’s computation manifests as token-type dependent convergence, suggesting targeted efficiency strategies and further study of per-token dynamics.

title: Knowing You at First Glance: Inferring Apparent Personality from Faces
comment: Accepted by The 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision, PRCV2026
summary: Inferring apparent personality from facial images is important in social scenarios for embodied agents in human-robot interaction. Unlike inferring intrinsic personality traits via conversation, this task models first-impression personality perception based solely on facial appearance before interaction begins. Existing studies mainly focus on the Big Five personality model and often rely on language or multimodal inputs. As a result, it remains unclear whether facial cues alone can support meaningful associations with perceived personality traits. This question is particularly relevant for MBTI types, which are widely used in practice and more readily interpretable by large language models. To this end, we propose \textbf{GlanceFace}, an end-to-end framework for apparent personality inference leveraging vision-language models to introduce semantic priors and a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture subtle personality-related cues, together with an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy and subjective annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks and reveal relationships between facial characteristics and perceived personality traits, highlighting its potential to support adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/MrHuan3/GlanceFace.

AI.tldr: GlanceFace is an end-to-end framework that infers apparent MBTI personality from facial images using vision-language priors and a semantic-enhanced facial representation, with uncertainty-aware learning to handle subjective noise; it shows strong performance on MBTI-based benchmarks and supports adaptive interaction for embodied agents; code/dataset released.
AI.motivation: To determine whether facial cues alone can support meaningful MBTI-based apparent personality inference, addressing the gap left by studies focusing on Big Five or relying on language/multimodal inputs, and to enable adaptive initial interactions for embodied agents.
AI.method: An end-to-end model (GlanceFace) that leverages vision-language models to inject semantic priors, includes a semantic-enhanced facial representation module to capture subtle cues, and employs an uncertainty-aware learning strategy to handle noisy, subjective annotations; trained and evaluated on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance on MBTI-based apparent personality benchmarks and reveal relationships between facial characteristics and perceived personality traits, indicating the model’s effectiveness and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The approach supports adaptive initial interaction strategies for embodied agents by providing MBTI-based apparent personality inference from facial appearance, and provides a publicly available code and dataset to facilitate further research.

title: KineFuse: Kinematic-Aware Haptic Fusion for In-Hand Occluded-Object Pose Tracking
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires continuous 6D pose tracking, yet the manipulating fingers inevitably occlude the object from the camera. We study how to structure the sparse haptic signals already available on multi-fingered hands, including proprioception, proximal force/torque, and binary contact, to complement a pretrained visual pose tracker under occlusion. We propose a kinematic-aware finger-level encoder and systematically compare it against four alternative designs through three levels of evaluation: per-frame refinement, sequential open-loop tracking, and closed-loop manipulation. Our experiments reveal that (i) per-frame evaluation cannot distinguish encoder quality, while sequential tracking amplifies architectural differences by up to 15 times; (ii) the structured encoder learns task-specific cross-modal gating, using vision exclusively for translation and dedicating one attention head to haptics for rotation, without explicit supervision; and (iii) compact finger-level tokenization with 4 tokens outperforms both flat fusion and joint-level representations, which suppress vision through norm dominance. We validate that improved tracking yields higher success in a downstream reorientation task and provide qualitative real-world demonstrations. Our project page is available at https://cold-young.github.io/kine-fuse/.

AI.tldr: A compact finger-level, kinematic-aware encoder fuses sparse haptics with a pretrained visual pose tracker to improve 6D pose tracking under occlusion in dexterous in-hand manipulation; sequential evaluation amplifies architectural differences; a 4-token finger-level representation with cross-modal gating (vision for translation, haptics for rotation) outperforms flat fusion and joint-level methods; improved tracking boosts downstream task success; code and demos available on the project page.
AI.motivation: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires continuous 6D pose tracking, but visual tracking is often occluded by the manipulating fingers. Existing cues—proprioception, proximal force/torque, and contact—are sparse and underutilized. A structured, artifact-aware fusion strategy could leverage these signals to complement vision, enabling robust tracking and manipulation.
AI.method: Introduce a kinematic-aware finger-level encoder that tokenizes per-finger haptic signals into a small set of tokens. Compare this encoder against four alternative fusion designs across three evaluation regimes: per-frame refinement, sequential open-loop tracking, and closed-loop manipulation. Assess cross-modal gating to reveal how vision and haptics contribute to translation vs rotation without explicit supervision. Use a constant-parameter pretrained visual tracker and evaluate on synthetic and real-world dexterous tasks with occlusion.
AI.result: The structured finger-level encoder enables task-specific cross-modal gating: vision handles translation while a dedicated haptic-attention head handles rotation, learned without supervision. A compact 4-token finger-level representation outperforms flat fusion and joint-level representations, which suppress vision via norm dominance. Sequential tracking amplifies architectural differences (up to ~15x). Improved tracking yields higher success in a downstream reorientation task and is demonstrated with qualitative real-world results.
AI.conclusion: A compact, kinematic-aware finger-level tokenization for multimodal fusion with a pretrained visual tracker improves 6D pose tracking under occlusion in dexterous manipulation. The approach reveals task-specific cross-modal gating and outperforms alternative fusion schemes, suggesting robust, scalable in-hand sensing. The project page provides implementation details and demos.

title: Tactile: Giving Computer-Using Agents Hands and Feet
summary: Computer-use agents are becoming capable software operators, but their interface to desktop applications is still often a brittle motor layer: they look at screenshots, predict coordinates, click, and hope that the visible state changed as intended. This collapses target grounding, action execution, and outcome verification into a single ambiguous operation. We present Tactile, an open-source tool layer that gives agents a more reliable "hands and feet" for desktop use. Tactile converts heterogeneous UI evidence--operating-system accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual fallback regions--into action-grounded interface states: compact target candidates with source labels, roles or text, state, geometry, executable affordances, and verification cues. Agents operate through an observe-ground-act-verify loop that prefers native semantic actions when available, falls back to OCR-grounded coordinates when visible text is the best evidence, and keeps full provenance for replay and failure attribution. On macOSWorld-style tasks, adding Tactile improves Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks; a 96-task cross-agent subset shows consistent gains across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose. These results suggest that reliable computer use requires not only stronger models, but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

AI.tldr: Tactile provides a reusable, verifiable execution layer for desktop automation that grounds actions in semantic UI evidence (OS semantics, OCR, visuals) rather than screen coordinates, improving model-assisted task success.
AI.motivation: Current agent interactions with desktop apps rely on brittle, coordinate-based actions grounded in screen pixels. There is a need for a grounded, auditable action substrate that can verify outcomes and support provenance tracing.
AI.method: Incorporates operating-system accessibility semantics, OCR-derived text, and visual regions to produce action-grounded interface states (target candidates with labels, roles/text, state, geometry, executable affordances, verification cues). Uses an observe-ground-act-verify loop; prioritizes native semantic actions, falls back to OCR-based coordinates when necessary; preserves provenance for replay and error attribution; implemented as an open-source tool layer (Tactile).
AI.result: On macOS World-style tasks, integrating Tactile raised Codex Success@100 from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks. In a 96-task cross-agent subset, gains were consistent across Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose.
AI.conclusion: Reliable computer use requires not only stronger models but also a reusable, semantic, auditable execution substrate that exposes software actions as verifiable objects instead of opaque screen coordinates; Tactile demonstrates robust improvements by grounding automation in diverse UI evidence.

title: Active Real-World Factor-Based Evaluation for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Generalist robot manipulation policies trained on large, diverse datasets have shown remarkable promise across a wide range of tasks. However, rigorously evaluating these policies remains a fundamental challenge. Real-world performance depends on a large combinatorial space of task factors including object poses and camera viewpoints, making full, exhaustive evaluation intractable. Additionally, real hardware evaluation is slow and resource-intensive, so current practice is to use narrow test suites that can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent true deployment readiness. We propose an active evaluation framework that addresses this challenge by treating policy evaluation as a sequential experimental design problem. Our approach fits a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors and adaptively selects evaluation configurations to maximize information gain over the policy's performance distribution, allowing for sample-efficient characterization of policy behavior across unseen conditions and a systematic identification of failure-prone regions. We conduct 2331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations and find that our approach typically saves the evaluator at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing.

AI.tldr: An active evaluation framework for generalist robot manipulation policies that uses a probabilistic surrogate model over task factors and sequential experimental design to efficiently characterize performance and identify failure-prone regions; demonstrated with 2,331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks and 3 factor variations, saving 20-40% of trials vs random testing.
AI.motivation: Rigorous, broad evaluation is intractable due to combinatorial task factors (e.g., object pose, camera viewpoint) and slow real-world testing. Narrow test suites can miss critical failure modes and misrepresent deployment readiness, so a sample-efficient method to cover unseen conditions is needed.
AI.method: Build a probabilistic surrogate model over a structured space of task factors (poses, viewpoints, etc.) and apply sequential experimental design to adaptively select evaluation configurations that maximize information gain about the policy's performance distribution, enabling efficient mapping of performance across conditions and identification of failure-prone regions.
AI.result: Conducted 2,331 real-world evaluations across 3 tasks with 3 factor variations; observed that the active evaluation approach saves at least 20-40% of trials compared to typical random testing, enabling more efficient and reliable evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Active evaluation significantly improves the efficiency and reliability of evaluating generalist manipulation policies, by providing broad, informative coverage of task factors, reducing evaluation cost, and enabling systematic detection of failure-prone regions for deployment readiness.

title: Autoregressive Modeling of Film with Applications in Video Montage
summary: This work introduces FilmGPT, an autoregressive transformer designed to address the challenge of video montage--turning a collection of raw, "unwatchable" footage into coherent cinematic sequences. Inspired by language learning in modern LLMs, we train a long-context autoregressive transformer on a large corpus of movies. The aim is to implicitly capture the "grammar" of film directly from data rather than from hand-coded rules. Unlike other generative models, FilmGPT does not generate any new video frames. Instead, at inference time, we introduce a footage-constrained decoding algorithm to select the best next shot from the input raw footage according to the statistical patterns learned from films. We first evaluate these learned statistics directly by using the FilmGPT autoregressive model for next shot prediction on a standard benchmark of shot sequence ordering, outperforming the previous state of the art. We then evaluate our footage-constrained decoding algorithm on the full film editing task via a user study, and find that our FilmGPT-based editing significantly outperforms previous approaches. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of FilmGPT to a wide range of applications in video montage, from automatic video segment trimming to human-in-the-loop film editing.

AI.tldr: FilmGPT learns the film 'grammar' from a large movie corpus with a long-context transformer; it does not synthesize frames but uses a footage-constrained decoding strategy to select the next shot from raw footage, achieving state-of-the-art results on shot-order benchmarks and in user studies for editing quality.
AI.motivation: Capture the implicit cinematic structure from data to enable coherent editing without hand-coded rules, addressing the challenge of turning unwatchable raw footage into coherent sequences.
AI.method: Train a long-context autoregressive transformer on a large corpus of films; at inference, apply a footage-constrained decoding algorithm to pick the next shot from input footage based on learned statistical patterns; evaluate on a shot-sequence ordering benchmark and through a user study of full editing; demonstrate broad applicability.
AI.result: Outperforms prior state-of-the-art on shot-sequence ordering; the footage-constrained decoding yields significantly better editing in user studies; demonstrates applicability to automatic trimming and human-in-the-loop editing.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven learning of film grammar enables effective video montage without generating new frames, offering a versatile framework for automated and assisted film editing.

title: Towards Human-like Physical Intelligence: LifelongVision-Language-Action Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Similar to the natural capabilities of humans to sequentially learn new tasks, robots with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models should possess lifelong learning ability to learn a new task when deployed in open-world environments. However, most recently proposed lifelong learning models aim to effectively learn the current task (plasticity) or maintain high accuracy on previous tasks (stability), while the plasticity-stability trade-off remains largely unsolved in robotic manipulation models. To address this fundamental challenge, we propose a cache-efficient lifelong Vision-Language-Action learning framework for robotic manipulation (i.e., LifelongVLA), which alleviates the plasticity-stability trade-off with a dual-timescale adaptation mechanism while achieving low-cost robotic deployment with a cache-efficient replay strategy. More concretely, we propose a dual-timescale LoRA gating module to decompose VLA adaptation into two lightweight pathways: a short-term adapter for plasticity and a long-term adapter for stable consolidation. These pathways are integrated via a task-aware gate, enabling explicit control of the plasticity-stability trade-off. In the skill replay phase, a cache-efficient stochastic replay strategy is proposed to preserve more balanced retention signals without full-trajectory storage. Finally, experiments show that LifelongVLA outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating efficient skill expansion, robust retention of learned manipulation behaviors, and reduced reliance on retraining for real-world deployment on an xArm robot.

AI.tldr: LifelongVLA presents a dual-timescale adaptation with LoRA gates and a cache-efficient replay to tackle plasticity-stability in lifelong Vision-Language-Action learning for robotic manipulation, showing improved continual skill acquisition and retention on an xArm with lower retraining needs.
AI.motivation: To overcome the plasticity-stability trade-off in lifelong VLA learning for robotic manipulation in open-world environments, enabling efficient, scalable, and robust continual skill learning for real robots.
