AI.method: Introduce a dual-timescale LoRA gating module that splits VLA adaptation into a short-term (plastic) and a long-term (stable) pathway, controlled by a task-aware gate. Implement a cache-efficient stochastic replay strategy to retain diverse learning signals without storing full trajectories, reducing memory and computational costs.
AI.result: Empirical results show LifelongVLA outperforms baselines in efficient skill expansion, robust retention of manipulated behaviors, and reduced retraining requirements, demonstrated on a xArm robot.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-timescale adaptation with cache-efficient replay effectively mitigates the plasticity-stability trade-off in lifelong VLA for robotic manipulation, enabling scalable, real-world deployment with improved continual learning performance.

title: Step-Level Preference Learning for Generative Agents in Social Simulations
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based generative agents simulate human behavior through long-horizon decision-making processes that comprise intermediate steps such as planning, memory retrieval, reflection, and action selection. However, fine-grained human annotations of these intermediate steps remain scarce, and existing agents are not grounded in human preferences over such intermediate decisions. To address this gap, we introduce \method, an interactive simulation interface that enables us to collect step-level human preference supervision over agent decision trajectories, leading to a dataset of 57K fine-grained annotations. We conduct step-level preference learning on open-weight language models using supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on this data, consistently improving simulation fidelity, coordination, and interaction quality, and inducing more socially effective agent behavior. Our results show that step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.

AI.tldr: Introduces an interactive interface to collect step-level human preferences for LLM agent decision trajectories (57K annotations); through supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization on open-weight LMs, it improves simulation fidelity, coordination, interaction quality, and socially effective behavior, showing step-level supervision benefits both local decisions and long-horizon behavior.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of fine-grained annotations for intermediate decision steps in LLM-based generative agents and the absence of grounding in human preferences over those steps, aiming to improve long-horizon simulation quality and social outcomes.
AI.method: Proposes an interactive simulation interface (\method) to collect step-level preference supervision, yielding 57K annotations. Trains open-weight language models with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on this data to align agent decision trajectories with human preferences.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in simulation fidelity, agent coordination, interaction quality, and socially effective behavior. Step-level supervision enhances both local decision quality and long-horizon agent behavior.
AI.conclusion: Step-level human supervision is an effective training signal for improving micro-level decision quality and macro-level long-horizon agent behavior in LLM-based agents.

title: Depth-Dependent Hidden-State Collapse in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference (HPEC 2026)
summary: We study Dynamical System Autoencoders (DSAE) for LiDAR point-cloud classification using spatial coordinates and Product Coefficient feature augmentations. The experiments compare separately trained DSAE architectures at encoder depths $K=1,\ldots,5$ and evaluate the resulting hidden representations with Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline. The main finding is a hidden-state collapse at $K=5$. For both xyz and xyz plus Product Coefficient inputs, the hidden-state standard deviation falls to the order of $10^{-5}$, while all three classifiers attain the same macro F1 score of $0.224688$. We prove that between-class hidden scatter is bounded by total hidden scatter, which in turn is controlled by the reported hidden-state variance. Thus a nearly constant hidden representation cannot retain substantial class-separating structure. Product Coefficients neither improve pre-collapse macro F1 nor prevent the $K=5$ collapse in the present DSAE setting. These results identify large-depth representation collapse as a concrete failure mode for DSAE LiDAR classification.

AI.tldr: DSAE for LiDAR classification exhibits a large-depth representation collapse: at K=5 hidden-state variance drops to ~1e-5, yielding identical macro F1 (0.2247) across Random Forest, kNN, and a dummy baseline for both xyz and xyz+Product Coefficients inputs; Product Coefficients do not prevent collapse and do not improve pre-collapse performance.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether increasing encoder depth in Dynamical System Autoencoders for LiDAR point-cloud classification yields richer, separable representations, or causes representation collapse that degrades discriminative power.
AI.method: Systematic depth sweep of DSAE encoders with depths K=1 to 5. Evaluate hidden representations using three classifiers (Random Forest, kNN, and a majority-class Dummy baseline) on two input variants: xyz alone and xyz with Product Coefficient augmentations.
AI.result: Hidden-state standard deviation collapses to order 1e-5 at K=5 for both input variants. All three classifiers achieve the same macro F1 score of 0.224688, indicating loss of class-discriminative information despite potential model capacity. A theoretical result bounds between-class hidden scatter by total scatter, which is governed by the very small hidden-state variance. Product Coefficients neither improve macro F1 before collapse nor prevent the K=5 collapse in this setting.
AI.conclusion: Large-depth representation collapse is a concrete failure mode for DSAE-based LiDAR classification. Product Coefficients do not remedy this collapse under the reported experimental conditions, suggesting limits to depth-based representation learning in DSAE for this task.

title: VIABench: A Comprehensive Video Benchmark Collected from Blind Individuals for Visual Impairment Assistance
summary: Visually impaired individuals (VIIs) encounter significant daily challenges due to limited access to visual information. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive results on general vision and language tasks, their practical utility in real-world blind assistance still remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce VIABench, a comprehensive video benchmark specifically designed to evaluate MLLMs in Visually Impaired Assistance scenarios using first-person videos recorded or shared by VIIs themselves. VIABench defines three core tasks, each targeting a distinct requirement in visual assistance. Proactive Reminder: Assesses the model's ability to interpret ongoing video content while proactively anticipating and verbally describing upcoming navigation-critical events; Visual Question Answering (VQA): Evaluates the model's capacity to answer user-posed questions about the environment or objects within the video; Vision-Guided Interaction: Tests context-aware reasoning to accomplish intentional interactions between user and environment. To ensure a robust and fair evaluation, we propose a rigorous benchmarking pipeline that supports both online (real-time) and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle to deliver comprehensive support for VIIs, especially in the Proactive Reminder task, which demands accurate anticipation and real-time responsiveness. We hope VIABench will drive future research toward developing customized MLLMs for real-world assistance, ultimately improving navigation and interaction experiences for visually impaired individuals. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/VIABench.

AI.tldr: VIABench: a video-focused benchmark for evaluating Multimodal LLMs in Visually Impaired Assistance, featuring three tasks—Proactive Reminder, Visual Question Answering (VQA), and Vision-Guided Interaction—with online and offline evaluation; results show current MLLMs struggle, especially on proactive, anticipatory narration.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between general vision-language models and practical, real-world assistance for visually impaired individuals by evaluating on first-person videos contributed by VIIs.
AI.method: Define three assistive tasks tailored to navigation and environment interaction, build a benchmarking pipeline supporting online (real-time) and offline evaluation, curate or utilize first-person videos from VIIs, establish evaluation protocols and metrics, and benchmark existing MLLMs; release code/data.
AI.result: Experiments reveal that current MLLMs struggle to provide comprehensive VI assistance, with Proactive Reminder being the most challenging due to the need for accurate anticipation and timely narration; the benchmark highlights substantial room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: VIABench has the potential to steer development toward specialized MLLMs for real-world visually impaired assistance, aiming to enhance navigation and interaction experiences; code and data will be released to promote community-driven progress.

title: Modeling and Validation of Quality of Control for Edge-Offloaded Collaborative Navigation
summary: Collaborative control in complex environments is severely challenged by stochastic wireless delay and reliability variations, which can degrade navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance. These network-induced uncertainties complicate the maintenance of energy efficiency during collaborative tasks, and can potentially lead to over-provisioning of resources. In this paper, for a navigation setup with dynamic collision avoidance, we address this challenge by expanding the quality of control (QoC) framework from prior works to practical robotic models. Our approach (i) models end-to-end network effects on closed-loop performance, (ii) systematically explores the impact of various control parameters dictating robotic motion on network latency-reliability (iii) validates these models through experiments on a private 5G testbed across varying delay, reliability and control configurations. Our analysis indicates the optimal control-communication co-design operating regimes for practical robots and also compares the QoC performance of standard ROS~2 quality of service (QoS) policies under real-world conditions and showing how RELIABLE QoS offers 51.5% better QoC than BEST-EFFORT under certain experimental settings.

AI.tldr: Extends the quality of control (QoC) framework to practical robotics by modeling end-to-end network effects on closed-loop performance, examining how control parameters affect latency-reliability, and validating with a private 5G testbed; finds optimal control-communication co-design regimes and that RELIABLE ROS2 QoS improves QoC by ~51.5% over BEST-EFFORT under certain conditions.
AI.motivation: Stochastic wireless delay and reliability variations disrupt navigation, tracking, and collision avoidance in collaborative robotic tasks. Energy efficiency and resource provisioning are compromised without a principled co-design. The paper aims to bridge QoC theory with practical robotic models and real-network conditions.
AI.method: (i) Develop end-to-end network-performance models for closed-loop robotic control. (ii) Systematically study how motion-control parameters influence network latency and reliability. (iii) Validate models experimentally on a private 5G testbed under varying delay, reliability, and control configurations; compare ROS2 QoS policies (RELIABLE vs BEST-EFFORT) in real-world conditions.
AI.result: Identification of optimal control-communication co-design operating regimes for practical robots. Demonstration that RELIABLE QoS offers 51.5% better QoC than BEST-EFFORT under certain experimental settings.
AI.conclusion: A practical QoC-augmented co-design framework can guide resource provisioning and parameter tuning for networked robotic systems facing stochastic network conditions; RELIABLE QoS provides tangible QoC gains over BEST-EFFORT in real-world settings.

title: SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation
summary: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

AI.tldr: SAGA introduces schema-aware grounding for text-to-SPARQL in KBQA, using a training-free, schema-constrained grounding process that maintains a persistent type state, prunes incompatible properties, and uses schema-annotated patterns to reduce empty results. It achieves state-of-the-art F1 across nine Wikidata/Freebase benchmarks and improves exact-match in most settings.
AI.motivation: KBQA systems often ground SPARQL queries through type-blind or lexical-based heuristics, causing semantically incompatible patterns and empty results. A schema-aware grounding approach can constrain exploration to semantically valid patterns without requiring expensive training.
AI.method: A training-free framework that maintains a bidirectional type state, filters incompatible property candidates before construction, presents compact schema-annotated graph patterns, and tolerates missing schema via empirical/trace-local evidence; applied within an interactive, agent-based SPARQL generation loop.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine benchmark settings across Wikidata and Freebase: SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match on eight; it also reduces empty-result queries in all Wikidata settings.
AI.conclusion: Schema-aware grounding substantially improves KB grounding quality in interactive SPARQL generation, reducing spurious patterns and empty results while delivering strong, broad performance gains without training.

title: Interleaved Noise Injection Improves Clean, Corrupted, and OOD Performance
summary: Noise injection is a well-known technique in stochastic optimization. We report its surprising effectiveness with an interleaved (on-off-on-off...) rather than the usual monotonic decay schedule. We present a theoretical analysis of noise injection, which confirms that corruption by impulse noise approximates a Jacobian regularization, whereas Gaussian noise acts as a curvature penalty. This regularization behavior has been invoked to explain why noise injection increases model robustness. But the interleaved nature of our proposed schedule produces superior results even for the optimization objective: mixing phases of noisy data permits the optimizer to escape local minima and increase exploration without the risk of catastrophically forgetting the important features from the clean data. To stabilize this training scheme against the rapid changes of the loss when switching between clean and noisy data, we introduce a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates based on clean gradient magnitudes. We compare this method with other common augmentation methods and find substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to real-world distribution shifts on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures, with the best results being achieved by stacking our method on top of other augmentations. Through saliency and attention maps we show that the effect of interleaved noise injection stems from penalizing the failure modes encouraged by the inductive bias of the models: impulse noise works against the locality bias of convolutional (ResNet) architectures, and Gaussian noise reduces the tendency of attention-based models to pick up large-scale spurious features. Interleaved noise injection is therefore an effective tool to improve the test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data at essentially zero computational cost.

AI.tldr: Interleaved on-off-on-off noise injection with gradient-norm stabilization improves robustness and generalization. Impulse noise regularizes the Jacobian, Gaussian noise regularizes curvature; the schedule enhances exploration and avoids catastrophic forgetting, achieving strong results with zero extra cost and when stacked with other augmentations.
AI.motivation: Understand and improve the regularization effects of noise injection for robustness against corruption and distribution shifts, and mitigate optimization challenges (local minima, forgetting) during training.
AI.method: Introduce an interleaved (on-off-on-off) noise injection schedule with a gradient-norm stabilization technique that scales noisy updates by the magnitude of clean gradients. Provide theoretical analysis showing impulse noise approximates Jacobian regularization while Gaussian noise imposes a curvature penalty. Evaluate on CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R for ResNet and ViT architectures; compare to other augmentations; use saliency and attention maps to interpret effects; test stacking the method with other augmentations.;
AI.result: The approach yields substantial improvements in corruption tolerance and robustness to distribution shifts across datasets and architectures. Interleaved noise outperforms monotonic schedules, with impulse noise countering locality bias in CNNs and Gaussian noise reducing reliance on large-scale spurious features in attention models. Combining the method with other augmentations provides the best performance, while maintaining essentially zero computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved noise injection, aided by gradient-norm stabilization, is an effective, low-cost tool to improve test performance on clean, noisy, and out-of-distribution data. Its regularization effects align with inductive biases of different architectures (impulse noise vs Gaussian noise), offering broad applicability to CNNs and ViTs.

title: ReBind: Multi-Reference Video Editing via Structured Instructions with Explicit Reference Relationships
summary: Recent diffusion-based video generation models have made significant progress in multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. However, existing methods still struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual sources accurately. We identify a critical deficiency in existing approaches. Existing editing instructions lack explicit reference relationships, and most multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot generate them reliably. To address this problem, we propose ReBind, a systematic framework that introduces semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens as the intermediate representation for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing. Our key insight is embedding reference tokens at semantic positions to eliminate ambiguity and establish precise bindings between visual attributes and their sources. We develop ReBind-Instruct, a specialized MLLM that learns to establish explicit bindings between visual attributes and their reference sources through a two-stage progressive scheme for precise reference relationships. We further develop ReBind-Edit, which enables lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models to coordinate multiple references by binding visual attributes to their designated sources. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReBind substantially outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image conditioned video editing. Our project webpage: https://rebind-mrv2v.github.io/.

AI.tldr: ReBind: a framework for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing using semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens; introduces ReBind-Instruct and ReBind-Edit; claims state-of-the-art results among open-source methods for reference-image conditioned video editing.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based video editors struggle to coordinate information from multiple visual sources. Editing instructions lack explicit reference relationships, and most multimodal LLMs cannot reliably generate them, leading to ambiguity in bindings between attributes and sources.
AI.method: Proposes semantic instructions with embedded reference tokens as the intermediate representation. ReBind-Instruct is a two-stage progressive MLLM-based scheme to learn explicit visual-attribute-to-source bindings. ReBind-Edit enables lightweight adaptation of text-to-video models to coordinate multiple references by binding attributes to designated sources.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show ReBind substantially outperforms general-purpose MLLMs in instruction quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source methods on reference image conditioned video editing.
AI.conclusion: ReBind provides a systematic framework for multi-reference image-conditioned video editing by embedding reference tokens at semantic positions to create precise bindings. Demonstrates strong open-source performance and offers concrete components (ReBind-Instruct and ReBind-Edit) to improve instruction quality and reference coordination.

title: OASIS-Map: Object-Level Change Detection in Multi-Session Mapping using Semantic Correspondence Matching
summary: Map representations which are consistent across repeated visits to a real-world semi-static environment are very useful for long-term robotic inspection. In such settings, the scene may evolve while the robot is absent, with objects appearing, disappearing, moving, or being replaced, quickly making a static map outdated. Existing change-detection methods reason through geometry, category-level semantics, or object persistence. However, achieving reliable object association across revisits remains a key challenge, especially under partial views, occlusion, and imperfect segmentation. In this work, we propose OASIS-Map, a multi-session mapping system that maintains a spatio-temporally consistent object-level map by establishing dense patch-level semantic correspondences between temporal observations. These correspondences detect where the scene has changed and incrementally associate objects across revisits as the robot re-observes the environment. We demonstrate OASIS-Map on three challenging real-world scenarios: object rearrangements in 3RScan, visually similar car replacements in a car park, and large-scale scene changes in an outdoor market. We achieve 0.783 F1 on change detection in a car replacement scenario in a car park and 0.667 F1 on moved object association in 3RScan. https://dynamic.robots.ox.ac.uk/projects/oasis-map/

AI.tldr: A dense patch-level, semantically-aware, multi-session map (OASIS-Map) maintains an object-level, spatio-temporally consistent representation across revisits by establishing dense correspondences between temporal observations, enabling robust change detection and object association in long-term, semi-static environments.
AI.motivation: In real-world semi-static environments, scenes evolve during absence, causing static maps to become outdated. Reliable object-level re-identification across revisits is challenging due to partial views, occlusion, and imperfect segmentation. Existing methods rely on geometry, semantics, or persistence but struggle with consistent object association.
AI.method: OASIS-Map maintains a spatio-temporally consistent object-level map by computing dense patch-level semantic correspondences between temporal observations. These correspondences reveal where the scene has changed and incrementally associate objects across revisits as the robot re-observes the environment, evaluated on three real-world scenarios.
AI.result: Quantitative results include 0.783 F1 for change detection in a car replacement scenario in a car park and 0.667 F1 for moved object association in 3RScan; the approach is demonstrated on 3RScan, car park, and an outdoor market.
AI.conclusion: Dense patch-level semantic correspondences enable robust long-term, object-level maps across revisits, improving change detection and object association under partial views and occlusions in dynamic real-world environments.

title: Contextualized Evaluation of Vision Language Models through Dynamic, Multi-turn Interactions
summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial advances on benchmarks, yet their real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. This gap stems from the fundamental misalignment between benchmarks in controlled, static settings and the dynamic, interactive, and contextualized nature of real-world applications. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDI (Contextualized Evaluations of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions), a framework that recasts evaluation as a three-party interaction between an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner conducts multi-turn, semi-structured conversation guided by a graph-based representation of the task. By navigating state-space transitions, CEDI deploys diverse strategies, from clarification requests to adversarial probes, to elicit performance evidence. We apply CEDI to visual hallucinations. Empirical results across multiple models, diverse settings, datasets, and domains show that contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal not only significantly more hallucinations than conventional static evaluation but also ones that more closely resemble those arising in practical use cases. We further show that hallucinations often accumulate over long contexts, through self-reinforcing dialogue history, and models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Together, these findings highlight CEDI as a step toward realistic, systematic, and ecologically valid assessments of MLLMs' capabilities. Code is available at github.com/williamium3000/cedi.

AI.tldr: CEDI reframes MLLM evaluation as an interactive, three-party process (evaluatee, examiner, grader) to elicit contextualized performance signals, uncovering more realistic and long-context hallucinations than static benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Static benchmarks are insufficient for real-world MLLM use where interaction, context, and dynamics matter; there is a need for ecologically valid evaluation to surface practical failure modes such as hallucinations.
AI.method: Proposes a three-agent framework: an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. The examiner uses a graph-based task representation and navigates state-space transitions via multi-turn, semi-structured conversations. The approach employs diverse strategies (clarifications, adversarial probes) and tracks effects of dialogue history across long contexts to elicit evidence of performance issues (e.g., visual hallucinations). Validation spans multiple models, settings, datasets, and domains.
AI.result: Contextualized, interactive evaluations reveal significantly more hallucinations than static benchmarks and yield ones that better resemble real-use cases. Hallucinations tend to accumulate over long contexts and are amplified by self-reinforcing dialogue histories; models are particularly vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal. Findings generalize across models and domains; code is released.
AI.conclusion: CEDI advances ecologically valid evaluation of MLLMs by framing assessment as interactive, context-aware evaluation. It provides a pathway toward more realistic benchmarking and diagnosis of failure modes, especially hallucinations, in real-world use.

title: Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), the generalizability of the resulting models remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish the first non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale. Our approach adapts PAC-Bayes compression bounds to this setting, and addresses the inherent stochasticity of token generation by applying the Gumbel-max reparameterization trick. To operationalize these bounds, we propose the Progressive RLVR framework, which integrates RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization. Progressive RLVR empirically retains 84-97% performance of standard LoRA fine-tuning while producing models that are 14,796x more compressible. We show that this framework yields non-vacuous generalization bounds in four domains: mathematical problem-solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL. Our bounds exceed the accuracy of the base model by 9-51% and lie within 6-11% of the accuracy of the fine-tuned models.

AI.tldr: Non-vacuous generalization bounds for parameter-efficient RLVR fine-tuning at billion-parameter scale using PAC-Bayes with Gumbel reparameterization; Progressive RLVR combines RLVR, on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and quantization to achieve high compression with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Understand generalization of RLVR-tuned LLMs at scale, address stochastic token generation, and enable practical compression while providing theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: Adapt PAC-Bayes compression bounds to RLVR; apply Gumbel-max reparameterization for token-generation stochasticity; propose Progressive RLVR framework integrating RLVR with on-policy distillation, TinyLoRA, and model quantization.
AI.result: Empirically preserves 84-97% of LoRA fine-tuning performance; 14,796x more compressible; non-vacuous bounds in math problem solving, programming, general-knowledge reasoning, and Text-to-SQL; bounds exceed base accuracy by 9-51% and are within 6-11% of fine-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Progressive RLVR yields non-vacuous generalization guarantees with substantial model compression and competitive accuracy across diverse tasks, demonstrating the practicality of parameter-efficient RLVR at scale.

title: GlobalForge: Towards Robust AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated image (AIGI) detectors achieve strong accuracy on clean benchmarks, but their performance drops sharply after images are propagated through real-world channels. We trace this fragility to what these detectors actually learn: they overfit to local artifacts left by generators in small spatial neighborhoods, which are easily destroyed by common propagation degradations such as JPEG compression and blur. Instead, we shift the discriminative cue from fragile local artifacts to more robust global structure. Building on this, we propose GlobalForge, a framework with two complementary modules. The Local Information Bottleneck (LIB) suppresses local components to block shortcut learning, while the Global Structural Reasoning (GSR) module forces every token to gather evidence from distant regions. Both modules are trained jointly under a contrastive structural loss based on degradation that keeps the resulting features stable under degradation. To support fine-grained robustness evaluation, we further introduce RealDeg-Bench, covering 7 common degradation operators and multi-step compound chains. GlobalForge improves average BAcc on 8 in-the-wild benchmark groups by $\mathbf{5.89\%}$ over the previous state-of-the-art, and is clearly ahead of representative baselines on RealDeg-Bench under both single and compound degradations. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GlobalForge-BE0F/.

AI.tldr: AIGI detectors overfit to local generator artifacts and fail under real-world degradations; GlobalForge combines Local Information Bottleneck and Global Structural Reasoning with a degradation-aware contrastive loss to achieve robust detection and introduces RealDeg-Bench for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current detectors' fragility stems from shortcut learning on local artifacts; need robust global cues that survive compression/blur.
AI.method: Two modules: Local Information Bottleneck suppresses local cues; Global Structural Reasoning enforces long-range evidence gathering; joint optimization with a contrastive structural loss guided by degradations; evaluation on RealDeg-Bench.
AI.result: Improves average balanced accuracy by 5.89 percentage points over prior SOTA across 8 in-the-wild benchmarks; outperforms baselines on RealDeg-Bench under single and compound degradations.
AI.conclusion: GlobalForge demonstrates that leveraging global structure and degradation-aware training yields robust AIGI detectors; RealDeg-Bench enables fine-grained degradation evaluation; code available.

title: Human-Robot Interaction in GenAI Architectures via the Agent-Client Protocol
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary:
Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are driving robotic architectures toward agent-based high-level orchestration, in which natural-language instructions can be translated into context-aware action sequences. While the integration of these agents and robotic capabilities is increasingly converging toward standardization through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the upper Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) layer remains fragmented by proprietary, ad hoc interfaces that hinder real-time human-in-the-loop collaboration.
  To address this fragmentation, this paper proposes the adoption of the Agent-Client Protocol (ACP) -- a communication standard originally introduced for coding agents in software engineering -- as a unified communication contract for the HRI layer in agent-based robotic systems. By combining ACP at the interface-agent link and MCP at the agent-execution link, we formulate a fully decoupled three-layer architecture that separates human interaction, deliberative orchestration, and physical execution. This topology removes rigid architectural dependencies, enabling heterogeneous user interfaces to connect to the same robotic system and allowing the underlying robotic platform to be replaced without requiring client-specific integration changes. Moreover, it provides native support for collaborative HRI capabilities such as real-time observability, explicit human authorization, and immediate task interruption. We experimentally evaluate the proposed architecture on a physical mobile robot, demonstrating interoperability across three heterogeneous user interfaces and validating real-time human-in-the-loop workflows with negligible latency overhead.

AI.tldr: Unifies the HRI layer with ACP and MCP to create a decoupled, three-layer, agent-based robotic architecture supporting multi-interface interoperability and real-time human-in-the-loop control; validated on a mobile robot with negligible latency.
AI.motivation: Upper-layer HRI fragmentation due to proprietary, ad hoc interfaces impedes real-time human-in-the-loop collaboration; a standard communication contract is needed to enable plug-and-play interfaces and robust orchestration.
AI.method: Introduce ACP for the interface–agent link and MCP for the agent–execution link, forming a fully decoupled three-layer architecture (interface, deliberation, execution). Implement the scheme on a physical mobile robot and verify interoperability across three heterogeneous user interfaces and real-time HRI workflows.
AI.result: Demonstrated interoperability across multiple UIs and validated real-time human-in-the-loop operation with negligible latency overhead.
AI.conclusion: ACP–MCP–based decoupled architecture decouples human interaction, deliberation, and execution, enabling heterogeneous interfaces to connect to the same robot and facilitating platform replacement without client-specific integration; supports real-time observability, explicit authorization, and task interruption.

title: VLT: A Vision-Language-Time Series Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial Intelligence
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, and 13 tables, including supplementary material. Haiteng Wang and Jingheng Yan contributed equally to this work
summary: Industrial time series serve as the foundation for Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) to ensure the reliability and safety of industrial equipment such as aero-engines. However, existing approaches are typically limited to single-modality modeling, which restricts their generalization in complex scenarios. Although recent advances in large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities for multimodal learning, bridging continuous time-series signals and discrete textual semantics remains an open challenge. To this end, we propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. A key insight is to utilize the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics. Specifically, a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) is designed to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics, while a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner enables joint modeling of spectral and semantic features within a shared representation space. Furthermore, a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism is introduced to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts via gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting. Extensive experiments on multiple industrial datasets demonstrate that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.

AI.tldr: VLT is a multimodal foundation model for industrial Prognostics and Health Management that jointly models time-series, frequency-spectrum visuals, and textual knowledge to bridge continuous signals with discrete semantics. It introduces Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) for temporal dynamics, a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner for joint spectral-semantic representation, and a time-centric gradient alignment mechanism to handle cross-modal optimization. It achieves state-of-the-art results with strong robustness in few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality settings.
AI.motivation: Industrial PHM relies on single-modality models that struggle to generalize in complex scenarios. Although LLMs enable multimodal learning, connecting continuous time-series data with discrete textual semantics remains challenging. A unified model that fuses time, spectral visual representations, and textual knowledge could improve robustness and generalization.
AI.method: Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts (Time-MoE) to capture heterogeneous temporal dynamics; Frequency-Text Augmented Learner to align spectral (frequency spectrum) and textual features in a shared representation; time-centric gradient alignment with gradient normalization and reliability-aware dynamic reweighting to mitigate cross-modal optimization conflicts.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple industrial datasets show that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, exhibiting superior robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality conditions.
AI.conclusion: VLT advances multimodal PHM by integrating time-series, spectral visuals, and textual knowledge in a unified framework, enabling stronger generalization and robustness in industrial settings such as aero-engines. The approach demonstrates the viability of using frequency-spectrum visuals as a bridge between continuous signals and discrete semantics.

title: Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code, logs, and result JSONs: https://github.com/akigogikar/RK4Optimizer
summary: Interpreting optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations has motivated applying higher-order Runge-Kutta (RK) integrators to neural networks. We build a representative Adam variant (Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair, FSAL reuse, local-error step control) and evaluate it under a strict compute-matched protocol giving every method the same gradient-evaluation budget - an accounting this literature rarely enforces. Under it the RK variant loses to plain Adam on training loss in both minibatch and full-batch (RK's best-case) training. Instrumenting it shows the "adaptivity" is illusory: normalized error stays far below tolerance, the step size pins at its growth cap from step one (98-100 percent of steps), and no rtol x hmax x h0 setting makes it act; tolerances spanning 100x give bit-identical trajectories. The method is exactly fixed-step Adam with an averaged gradient at 3-4x cost. Repairing it (true reject branch; error on the applied map) reverses the full-batch result - about 40x lower training loss than tuned Adam - and a fixed-step control isolates adaptivity (an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule) as the mechanism. But the gain is fragile to the initial step size and does not reach test accuracy. A pre-registered follow-up rules out the obvious explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob only hurts - leaving a trajectory effect, the controller selecting a minimum generalizing 1.3-3.4 points below first-order descent at equal depth. An n=10 study confirms one secondary effect: gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer, beating lr-matched Adam and AdamW on 10/10 seeds - yet RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration buys deeper deterministic minimization and a small regularization effect, but nothing a cheaper, well-tuned first-order baseline does not already provide.

AI.tldr: Higher-order Runge-Kutta variants of Adam under strict compute budgets do not outperform plain Adam; adaptivity is illusory and fixed-step behavior dominates; repairing the method can produce large gains but are fragile and do not generalize; gradient averaging provides a genuine implicit regularizer; overall, cheaper first-order baselines suffice.
AI.motivation: To assess whether viewing optimizers as gradient-flow discretizations and applying higher-order Runge-Kutta integrators yields meaningful training gains for neural networks.
AI.method: Construct a Bogacki-Shampine 3(2) RK pair variant of Adam (with FSAL reuse and local-error control) and compare under a compute-matched protocol. Diagnose adaptivity, examine fixed-step vs adaptive behavior, and perform ablations: true reject branch, full-batch vs minibatch, temperature knob, and gradient averaging across seeds. Include a follow-up with other optimizers for comparison and a n=10 study.
AI.result: Under compute-matched budget, the RK Adam variant loses to plain Adam on training loss; adaptivity is illusory—normalized error stays well below tolerance, step size sits at growth cap from step one, and tolerances spanning 100x yield bit-identical trajectories. The method effectively is fixed-step Adam with 3–4x gradient-averaged cost. Repairing it via a true reject branch reverses full-batch gains, yielding ~40x lower training loss than tuned Adam; a fixed-step controller reveals an emergent warmup-and-growth schedule but gains do not generalize to test accuracy. Follow-up rules out major explanations: deeper minimization does not overfit, and an explicit temperature knob hurts. Gradient averaging is a genuine implicit regularizer (beating lr-matched Adam/AdamW on 10/10 seeds); RMSprop and NAdam match or beat it at a third of the per-step cost. Higher-order adaptive integration yields deeper deterministic minimization and minor regularization, but nothing cheaper/better achieved by well-tuned first-order baselines.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order adaptive RK integration provides limited benefits: only marginal, fragile gains in deeper minimization and regularization, and these do not surpass well-tuned first-order methods. Gradient averaging acts as a robust implicit regularizer; in practice, cheap first-order optimizers remain preferable.

title: Team RAS in 11th ABAW Competition: Multimodal Ambivalence Recognition Approach
summary: Automatic recognition of ambivalence and hesitancy is challenging because these states may be expressed through inconsistent linguistic, acoustic, facial, and contextual patterns, while top-performing systems often rely on computationally expensive ensembles. We present a single text-centered multimodal approach for video-level ambivalence and hesitancy recognition for the 11th Affective & Behavior Analysis in-the-Wild (ABAW) Challenge. The proposed approach combines linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene features using text-centered multimodal fusion model. Text Residual Fusion treats text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments based on the other modalities. Experiments on the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) corpus confirm that text is the strongest unimodal modality. The Text Residual Fusion model achieves an average Macro F1-score (MF1) of 75.14% across the Development and Public Test subsets. On the Private Test subset, it reaches an MF1 of 78.24%, outperforming the text model by 4.03%. These results demonstrate that complementary multimodal information can improve recognition performance without requiring a large model ensemble.

AI.tldr: A text-centered multimodal fusion approach (Text Residual Fusion) for video-level ambivalence/hesitancy recognition that leverages text as anchor and achieves strong Macro F1 without large ensembles.
AI.motivation: Ambivalence and hesitancy are expressed through heterogeneous cues across text, audio, face, and scene; existing top systems rely on costly ensembles, so a single, text-centered model could reduce complexity while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Text Residual Fusion treats text as the anchor modality and applies gated residual adjustments from linguistic, acoustic, facial, and scene features to integrate multimodal information.
AI.result: On the BAH corpus, text is the strongest unimodal modality with MF1 scores of 75.14% (Development + Public Test) and 78.24% (Private Test), with the model surpassing the text-only baseline by 4.03% on Private Test.
AI.conclusion: Complementary multimodal information can improve recognition performance without requiring large ensemble models; text-centered fusion yields strong results for video-level ambivalence and hesitancy recognition.

title: Steering Robustness into World Action Models via Mechanistic Interpretability and Optimal Control
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) enable semantically- and physically-informed control but are brittle under distribution shift. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability to study how robustness-relevant perturbations are represented in WAM activation space. Comparing activations across successful and unsuccessful rollouts, we find some WAM architectures exhibit low-dimensional linear separability for robustness-critical features, while others do not. This motivates the use of contrastive activation directions for training-free WAM steering. We also show that local linearity in WAM activation dynamics enables efficient feedback steering via model-based optimal control, yielding World-Action Linear Quadratic Regulator (WA-LQR), a minimally-invasive reduced-order LQR controller. Via mechanistic evaluations, we predict strong steerability in the Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT models but weak steerability in LingBot-VA, consistent with steering intervention results. On Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT, WA-LQR generalizes contrastive directions to new tasks and improves robustness to camera, gripper, and visual-noise perturbations over unsteered and prompt steering baselines.

AI.tldr: WAM robustness is architecture-dependent; mechanistic interpretability reveals that some WAMs have low-dimensional, separable representations of robustness-relevant features, enabling training-free steering via contrastive directions; WA-LQR exploits local activation linearity for efficient model-based control, with Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT showing strong steerability and improved robustness, while LingBot-VA shows weak steerability.
AI.motivation: Understand how distribution shifts affect World Action Models and whether their activation dynamics encode robustness in a way that can be exploited for control, using mechanistic interpretability to analyze activations and steerability.
AI.method: Compare activations from successful vs. unsuccessful rollouts to assess linear separability of robustness-relevant features; propose contrastive activation directions for steering; derive WA-LQR based on local linearity for feedback control; perform mechanistic evaluations across model families (Cosmos-Policy, DiT4DiT, LingBot-VA); test WA-LQR on new tasks and perturbations (camera, gripper, visual noise).
AI.result: Some WAM architectures exhibit low-dimensional linear separability for robustness-critical features, enabling training-free contrastive steering; WA-LQR provides efficient steering via model-based control exploiting local linearity; Cosmos-Policy and DiT4DiT show strong steerability and genericization to new tasks with improved robustness to multiple perturbations; LingBot-VA shows weak steerability, consistent with steering intervention outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals architecture-dependent steerability in WAMs, and WA-LQR is a minimally-invasive, effective control approach for robust operation in steerable models, with variability across architectures (strong in Cosmos-Policy/DiT4DiT, weak in LingBot-VA).

title: RetroAgent: Harnessing LLMs to Search Over Structured Memory for Agentic Retrosynthesis Planning
summary: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning seeks to decompose a target molecule into commercially available building blocks through a sequence of feasible reactions. The vast combinatorial search space makes this task challenging even for expert chemists. Traditional methods combine tree search with offline-trained value networks that score candidates in isolation, without reasoning about complete multi-step routes. Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task, but relies on simple interfaces that limit exploration of the full search space. We introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent that bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning through a harness with structured memory. Through memory and chemistry tools, the agent observes the full search state, including explored routes, available alternatives, and properties of intermediates, enabling informed decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks demonstrate that RetroAgent delivers strong performance and generalization.

AI.tldr: RetroAgent uses an LLM-based agent with structured memory to perform multi-step retrosynthesis by combining symbolic search with neural reasoning, enabling full exploration of the search space and improved generalization.
AI.motivation: Retrosynthesis planning has a massively large search space. Traditional methods rely on offline value networks or limited LLM interfaces, which restrict exploration of complete multi-step routes and global progress.
AI.method: Introduce RetroAgent, an LLM agent equipped with a memory harness and chemistry tools that observe the full search state (explored routes, alternatives, intermediates) and make decisions grounded in both global progress and domain knowledge, thereby bridging symbolic search and neural reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical results on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks show strong performance and generalization, outperforming baselines that score candidates in isolation.
AI.conclusion: Bridging symbolic search and neural reasoning via structured memory and tool use improves multi-step retrosynthesis planning, enabling thorough exploration and better generalization.

title: A Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning Framework for Fine-Tuning Discrete Diffusion Models
summary: We formulate reinforcement learning (RL) in continuous time with discrete state spaces and possibly arbitrary action spaces via a stochastic control approach, where the state dynamics are modeled as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). We consider policy optimization problems and derive the corresponding policy gradient methods, leading to continuous-time variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). As a primary application, we develop a complete continuous-time RL framework for fine-tuning score-based discrete diffusion models. The proposed framework enables reward-driven optimization without requiring differentiability on the reward signals. In contrast to the existing GRPO-based approaches that only rely on terminal rewards, our formulation allows intermediate reward or advantage signals to be incorporated throughout the denoising trajectory. Importantly, when specialized to masked diffusion models (MDMs), our framework encompasses a rich class of policy parameterizations over the vocabulary simplex with analytically tractable probability ratios, providing a unified perspective on exploration and policy optimization in MDMs. For masked diffusion large language models (dLLMs), we further propose trajectory subsampling techniques to efficiently estimate computationally prohibitive trajectory likelihoods, reducing the computational cost of computing per-position probability ratios. We showcase the effectiveness of our methods on both low-dimensional entropy-regularized optimization problems and RL post-training of dLLMs on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

AI.tldr: Continuous-time RL via controlled CTMCs with PPO/GRPO variants; enables intermediate rewards and trajectory subsampling; applied to score-based discrete diffusion models and dLLMs for efficient, non-differentiable reward optimization.
AI.motivation: Motivated by the need to perform policy optimization in continuous-time, discrete-state environments with flexible action spaces, enabling reward-driven learning without differentiable reward signals, and to unify policy parameterizations for masked diffusion models and large language models.
AI.method: Stochastic-control formulation of policy optimization for controlled CTMCs; derivation of continuous-time policy gradient methods; development of continuous-time PPO and GRPO variants; deployment in a complete continuous-time RL framework for score-based discrete diffusion models; introduction of trajectory subsampling for dLLMs to estimate trajectory likelihoods; analytic probability ratios for vocabulary simplex in MDMs.
AI.result: The framework supports reward-driven optimization without differentiable rewards, accommodates intermediate rewards along trajectories, and demonstrates effectiveness on low-dimensional entropy-regularized tasks and on RL post-training of dLLMs for mathematical reasoning and coding tasks; trajectory subsampling reduces computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, continuous-time RL approach based on CTMCs that enables flexible reward structures (including intermediate rewards) and scalable policy optimization for diffusion-based models and dLLMs, with tractable likelihood ratios and practical subsampling techniques.

title: Pretraining Multiple Instance Learning Networks with Multi-Teacher Distillation from Pathology Slide Foundation Models
summary: Multiple instance learning (MIL) has become the main paradigm for whole-slide image (WSI) analysis in computational pathology. However, existing MIL aggregators are still typically trained from scratch for each downstream task, relying on limited slide-level labels to learn both aggregation mechanisms and downstream discriminative representations simultaneously. As a result, they often suffer from unstable optimization, overfitting, and limited transferability. Similar to pretrained ResNet and Vision Transformer models in natural image learning, MIL also requires reusable pretrained initialization. However, high-quality slide-level pretraining data remain scarce, and MIL models are usually lightweight and weakly supervised, making large-scale pretraining difficult in practice. To address this challenge, we propose a distillation-based pretraining framework for MIL, which leverages two slide-level foundation models, TITAN and CARE, as teachers to transfer their representational knowledge into a diverse set of MIL architectures. To effectively balance supervision from different teachers, we further introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss. The distilled weights are then used as initialization for downstream adaptation. We conduct systematic evaluations on 15 benchmark datasets under both linear probing and full-parameter fine-tuning, and further validate its advantages in few-shot scenarios. Experimental results show that pretraining generally improves MIL aggregators over from scratch training, especially in linear-probing and few-shot settings, while maintaining the computational efficiency of lightweight MIL models. Code is available at https://github.com/fu0201/MIL_Pretrained.

AI.tldr: A distillation-based pretraining framework for MIL in WSI analysis uses two slide-level teachers (TITAN and CARE) to initialize diverse MIL architectures via an angular dispersion distillation loss, improving transferability and performance, especially in linear probing and few-shot settings across 15 datasets.
AI.motivation: MIL in whole-slide image analysis suffers from training from scratch, unstable optimization, overfitting, and limited transferability due to scarce slide-level labels and lack of large pretraining data; there is a need for reusable pretrained initialization akin to ConvNet/ViT models in natural image tasks.
AI.method: Leverage two slide-level foundation models (TITAN and CARE) as teachers to distill their representations into various MIL architectures. Introduce an angular dispersion normalized distillation loss to balance supervision from different teachers. Distilled weights initialize downstream MIL models, with evaluations under linear probing and full fine-tuning across 15 datasets and few-shot scenarios.
AI.result: Pretraining generally improves MIL aggregators over training from scratch, especially in linear probing and few-shot settings, while maintaining the efficiency of lightweight MIL models.
AI.conclusion: A distillation-based pretraining framework provides reusable initialization for MIL, enhancing transferability and performance across architectures. The approach is validated across diverse datasets and tasks, with code available for replication.

title: AeroAct: Action-Centered World-Action Models for Language-Conditioned Quadrotor Flight
summary: Language-conditioned quadrotor flight requires a policy to ground semantic goals, anticipate the visual consequences of ego-motion, and output control references that remain smooth and dynamically executable under rapidly changing first-person views. Existing aerial vision-language navigation and vision-language-action methods commonly use discrete actions, high-level waypoints, or instantaneous velocity commands, which provide limited supervision about how flight actions change future observations. We present AeroAct, an action-centered world-action model (WAM) for quadrotor navigation. To the best of our knowledge, AeroAct is the first WAM instantiated and demonstrated for real-world aerial flight. The model adapts a pretrained video diffusion Transformer to predict local trajectory-action chunks from egocentric visual history, proprioception, and language. Future first-person frames are used during training as dense consequence supervision, while deployment directly decodes actions without generating future video. To obtain aligned visual, state, language, and dynamically feasible action data, we build a DiffAero-based pipeline with complementary Isaac Lab and 3D Gaussian splatting renderers. We further introduce a low-cost handheld collection device that couples camera observations with motion estimates to recreate flight-like egocentric trajectories, and a self-guidance procedure that improves temporal consistency across overlapping trajectory chunks. Closed-loop simulation and real-world experiments show that temporal visual context improves target tracking and object-search performance, and that WAM-based policies can be executed on a physical quadrotor.

AI.tldr: AeroAct proposes an action-centered world-action model (WAM) for real-world quadrotor navigation, predicting local trajectory-action chunks from egocentric history via a video diffusion Transformer, enabling closed-loop control with temporal visual context and language grounding.
AI.motivation: Current aerial vision-language methods rely on discrete actions or high-level waypoints, providing limited supervision on how actions affect future observations; there is a need for end-to-end grounding of semantic goals into dynamically feasible control in changing ego-visions.
AI.method: Adapt a pretrained video diffusion Transformer to forecast local trajectory-action chunks from egocentric visuals, proprioception, and language; train with future first-person frames as dense supervision; deploy by directly decoding actions; build DiffAero-based data pipeline with Isaac Lab rendering and 3D Gaussian splatting; develop a low-cost handheld data collection device; apply self-guidance for temporal consistency across trajectory chunks.
AI.result: In closed-loop simulation and real-world quadrotor experiments, temporal visual context improves target tracking and object-search; AeroAct WAM-based policies run on a physical quadrotor.
AI.conclusion: AeroAct introduces the first real-world instantiated WAM for aerial flight, enabling action-conditioned planning grounded in vision-language inputs and demonstrated viability on real hardware.

title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
summary: This study presents WrAFT, a Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool, that delivers both accurate and reliable scores and effective comprehensive feedback to argumentative essays. WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. In building the system, various Large Language Models (LLMs) have been evaluated, including LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7, through both direct prompting and supervised fine-tuning approaches. A proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores was utilized. Benchmark-based evaluation shows that WrAFT achieves state-of-the-art performance in scoring, with a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.84 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.44 against official scores on a scale of 0-5. Human evaluation of system-generated feedback also reveals high approval ratings: 96.14 percent for surface-level feedback, 93.03 percent for deep-level macro feedback, and 94.69 percent for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface has been developed for the system and is publicly available and free to use.

AI.tldr: Modular AWE system WrAFT achieves high-accuracy scoring and actionable feedback for argumentative essays; evaluated on TOEFL data with state-of-the-art scoring metrics and strong human feedback; UI available.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap for reliable, interpretable automated scoring and comprehensive feedback in argumentative writing, leveraging LLMs in a modular pipeline.
AI.method: Develop WrAFT with separate modules for scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback; compare prompting and supervised fine-tuning across LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7); train on 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official scores; evaluate with QWK and RMSE; perform human evaluation on feedback; deploy an interactive UI.
AI.result: QWK 0.84 and RMSE 0.44 on 0-5 scale for scoring; high human approval: ~96% surface feedback, ~93% macro deep feedback, ~95% micro deep feedback; public, free interface.
AI.conclusion: WrAFT shows that a modular LLM-based AWE system can deliver reliable scores and actionable feedback for argumentative writing; establishes benchmark-level scoring and strong user reception; suggests avenues for broader generalization and dataset expansion.

title: xHC: Expanded Hyper-Connections
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of Transformers into $N$ parallel streams, providing a form of memory scaling beyond model width and depth. Manifold-Constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes this formulation at scale. The large gains from $N{=}1$ to $N{=}4$ suggest residual-stream expansion as a promising scaling axis. However, existing HC-family methods typically stop at $N{=}4$. Our experiments reveal why: scaling mHC beyond this point yields diminishing performance gains and rapidly increasing training cost. We attribute this limitation to two bottlenecks: insufficient write-back information for an expanding number of streams and residual-mixing generation whose cost scales cubically with $N$. To address both bottlenecks, we propose xHC (Expanded Hyper-Connections), the first HC-family method to achieve meaningful expansion beyond $N{=}4$. xHC combines temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only $k=4$ of the $N=16$ streams while retaining dense access to the full residual state. Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC delivers strong and consistent downstream improvements. On an 18B MoE model, xHC improves the average downstream score by 4.0 points over mHC, while adding only modest training FLOPs over the vanilla baseline. Scaling-law experiments show that the vanilla and mHC require $1.50\times$ and $1.19\times$ the compute of xHC, respectively, to reach the same loss. Practical large-$N$ training also requires controlling memory traffic from the expanded residual state. We therefore introduce xHC-Flash, which reduces the per-sublayer memory traffic from $73.5C$ to $40C$, comparable to the $34C$ required by mHC at $N{=}4$, while retaining the gains of full xHC. Together, xHC and xHC-Flash make large-$N$ residual-stream expansion effective and practical for LLM pre-training.

AI.tldr: Expanded Hyper-Connections (xHC) enable large-N residual-stream expansion beyond N=4 by combining temporal feature augmentation for richer write-back with a sparse update scheme, plus xHC-Flash memory optimizations. This yields strong downstream gains with modest compute overhead, making large-N pre-training practical.
AI.motivation: HC methods boost residual-stream capacity but suffer diminishing gains and high costs as N grows beyond 4 due to insufficient write-back information and cubic residual-mixing costs. The goal is to scale residual-stream expansion to larger N while controlling compute and memory overhead.
AI.method: xHC introduces temporal feature augmentation to enrich write-back and uses a sparse residual-stream architecture that updates only k of the N streams (k=4 of N=16) while retaining dense access to the full residual state. xHC-Flash further reduces per-sublayer memory traffic from 73.5C to 40C, aligning with mHC at N=4 costs.
AI.result: Across 18B and 28B MoE models, xHC yields strong improvements, e.g., +4.0 downstream score on an 18B MoE model over mHC. Scaling laws show vanilla and mHC require 1.50x and 1.19x compute to reach the same loss as xHC. xHC-Flash reduces memory traffic substantially while preserving xHC gains.
AI.conclusion: xHC and xHC-Flash make large-N residual-stream expansion feasible and beneficial for large-scale pre-training, enabling practical deployment of high-N HC architectures.

title: Variational Inference for Bird's Eye View Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
summary: The bird's eye view (BEV) has emerged as a pivotal approach for environmental perception in autonomous driving, providing a unified spatial representation for vehicles. Nevertheless, despite BEV's significance in addressing the challenges inherent to autonomous driving, effectively fusing data from multiple camera sensors and operating in complex external driving environments remains a considerable challenge. To mitigate this issue, we recast the BEV segmentation problem within a variational inference framework. In this paper, we propose a novel transformer-based variational flow transformation network for BEV segmentation, denoted as TVB. Our architecture implicitly learns the mapping from multiple camera views to a unified canonical BEV map during training by exploiting posterior BEV supervision. TVB employs a conditional variational auto encoder (CVAE) as its backbone and produces multiple BEV map candidates. To augment the realism of the generated BEV maps, we integrate normalizing flows into the map generation process, enabling the construction of more complex and expressive probability distributions. Furthermore, we design a BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module that harnesses attention mechanisms to adaptively integrate the multiple candidate BEV maps. Experimental results, evaluated on both the nuScenes and OPV2Vdatasets, demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance in multi-camera view BEV segmentation and lane environment perception.

AI.tldr: Transformer-based variational flow network (TVB) for BEV segmentation from multi-camera inputs, combining CVAE, normalizing flows, and BEV-attention fusion to produce multiple BEV map candidates and improve fusion in challenging environments.
AI.motivation: BEV segmentation must robustly fuse data from multiple cameras in complex driving scenarios; traditional methods struggle with uncertainty across views and environment variability; a probabilistic, expressive framework can better model the mapping to a canonical BEV.
AI.method: A CVAE-based backbone generates multiple BEV map candidates. Normalizing flows are integrated to enrich the probability distributions of BEV maps. A BEV-attention fusion (BAF) module adaptively fuses the candidate BEV maps. Training uses posterior BEV supervision to implicitly learn the mapping from multi-camera views to the canonical BEV. The approach is evaluated in a transformer-based variational framework (TVB).
AI.result: The method achieves superior performance on nuScenes and OPV2V datasets for multi-camera BEV segmentation and lane environment perception.
AI.conclusion: TVB demonstrates that combining CVAE-based variational inference, normalizing flows, and attention-based fusion yields robust and expressive BEV mappings across camera views, with strong empirical results on standard benchmarks.

title: CosFly-VLA: A Spatially Aware Vision-Language-Action Model for UAV Tracking
summary: Dynamic target tracking is essential for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) operating in complex urban environments, where both the target and the camera viewpoint change continuously. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies can track visible targets effectively, but their performance often degrades when buildings, vegetation, or roadside objects block the line of sight. During sustained occlusion, a policy may lose the target state, execute actions toward an incorrect region, and amplify this error through subsequent observations until re-acquisition becomes impossible. To this end, we present CosFly-VLA, a spatially aware VLA model that jointly grounds the target, estimates its visibility, and generates continuous flight actions through a structured prediction interface. To train this policy, we use a large-scale recipe over diverse data sources. Spatially Grounded Continued Pretraining (CPT) on a 500k mixed pool injects UAV-view depth, distance, and 3-D spatial reasoning. A three-stage Curriculum-based Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) process then specializes the tracker through multi-head warm-up followed by two-stage curriculum learning over natural and hard / long-occlusion data. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training subsequently teaches recovery-oriented reasoning traces before structured answers. Finally, a closed-loop Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage optimizes tracking behavior with a multi-component reward covering stand-off tracking, grounding quality, collision avoidance, and task success. Relative to OpenVLA, CosFly-VLA-0.8B reduces open-loop Average Displacement Error (ADE) by 34.1% on seen-test and 35.3% on unseen-test. Closed-loop optimization improves Success Rate (SR) by 29.8% and 2.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate progress from visible-frame imitation toward spatially grounded action-closed-loop control, evaluated under a shared oracle state history.

AI.tldr: CosFly-VLA is a spatially grounded Vision-Language-Action model for UAV dynamic target tracking under occlusion. It jointly grounds the target, estimates visibility, and generates continuous flight actions via a structured prediction interface, trained with a multi-stage recipe (CPT, curriculum SFT, CoT, RL). It shows large improvements over OpenVLA in both open-loop and closed-loop settings.
AI.motivation: Occlusions in urban scenes (buildings, vegetation, roadside objects) disrupt line-of-sight and degrade VLA tracking; sustained occlusion can cause drift and failure to reacquire. A spatially aware, recovery-capable policy is needed.
AI.method: CosFly-VLA architecture grounds the target and estimates visibility, then outputs continuous flight actions via a structured interface. Training uses: (1) Spatially Grounded Continued Pretraining (CPT) on a 500k mixed pool injecting UAV-view depth, distance, and 3-D spatial reasoning; (2) Three-stage Curriculum-based Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with multi-head warm-up and two-stage curriculum over natural and hard/long-occlusion data; (3) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training to teach recovery-oriented reasoning traces before structured answers; (4) Closed-loop Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a multi-component reward (stand-off tracking, grounding quality, collision avoidance, task success).
AI.result: Compared with OpenVLA, CosFly-VLA-0.8B achieves a 34.1% reduction in open-loop Average Displacement Error (ADE) on seen-test and 35.3% on unseen-test. Closed-loop optimization yields a 29.8% and 2.5% improvement in Success Rate (SR) on seen/unseen tests, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates progression from visible-frame imitation toward spatially grounded, action-closed-loop UAV tracking under occlusion. The 0.8B model delivers substantial improvements, validating the efficacy of a multi-stage training recipe combining CPT, curriculum SFT, CoT, and RL for robust, occlusion-resilient tracking.

title: Are LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Production-Ready? A Trace-Driven Benchmark and Optimization Agent
comment: Both artifacts are released as open source: Atrex-Bench (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-bench) and Atrex-Kernel-Agent (https://github.com/alibaba/atrex-kernel-agent)
summary: Existing GPU kernel generation benchmarks draw problems from synthetic or curated sources that diverge from deployed workloads. We present Atrex-Bench, a benchmark whose 30 operators and 440 shapes are sampled directly from full-cluster production inference traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs. Each problem carries an importance weight derived from its share of observed GPU time, weighted by application card-hours and computed separately for the serving phases in which it runs, together with a per-problem roofline ceiling, so the aggregate score emphasizes the kernels that consume the most serving time. Evaluating six frontier coding agents on Atrex-Bench shows that even the best vanilla model reaches only ${\sim}10\%$ of the hardware roofline on production operators; and correctness alone overstates capability, since much of the apparent pass rate comes from PyTorch fallbacks rather than kernels the model wrote. To close this gap, we co-release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel-optimization agent that combines iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout for escaping stalled search contexts, and a layered GPU-optimization knowledge base (298 reference-kernel files and 244 optimization-knowledge documents, plus external upstream reference projects for API/ISA lookup). In a controlled case study, the agent converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines.

AI.tldr: Atrex-Bench is a production-derived GPU kernel benchmark with 30 operators and 440 shapes sampled from real inference traces; it weights problems by their share of serving time and roofline ceilings to highlight impactful kernels. A frontier-model evaluation shows vanilla models reach only ~10% of hardware capability, with many apparent successes due to PyTorch fallbacks. The authors release Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven optimization agent that uses iterative measure-revise search, dropout to escape stalls, and a large knowledge base to generate real kernels; in a case study, AKA converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between synthetic/curated benchmarks and real production workloads, focusing on kernels that dominate serving time to improve hardware utilization and kernel quality.
AI.method: Construct Atrex-Bench by sampling 30 operators and 440 shapes from full-cluster production traces of compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs; assign per-problem importance weights and roofline ceilings; evaluate six frontier coding agents; co-release AKA with 298 reference kernels, 244 optimization documents, and external API/ISA references; use iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout, and a layered knowledge base; conduct a controlled case study converting zero-FlyDSL fallbacks to real kernels.
