AI.result: Current best vanilla model achieves ~10% of the hardware roofline on production operators; correctness-based metrics overstate capability due to PyTorch fallbacks; AKA successfully converts zero-FlyDSL fallbacks into real kernels that match or exceed hand-tuned production baselines in a controlled study.
AI.conclusion: Profile-driven kernel optimization with production-aware benchmarks and a comprehensive knowledge base can close the gap between model-generated and hand-tuned kernels, enabling kernels that meet or surpass production baselines; the datasets and the AKA agent provide a path toward more realistic and effective GPU kernel generation.

title: Muse: Representation Geometry of Muon Beyond Normalized Momentum
summary: Muon-style optimizers apply a polar map to matrix momentum, but their updates also depend on the representation of each parameter block before orthogonalization. We study this representation choice as a form of optimizer geometry and introduce {\method}, a family of Muon-style optimizers that shares the same momentum rule and Newton--Schulz backend across native, nearest-square, skinny, and vector representations. Each Frobenius-isometric representation induces a distinct polar steepest-descent geometry, in which the shorter matrix dimension determines the number of supported singular channels, the pullback scaling, and the constants in stochastic nonconvex convergence bounds. In a teacher--student model, curvature collapse and an isotropic Marchenko--Pastur spectral profile connect early-stage dissipation to the represented nuclear-to-squared-Frobenius norm ratio. Pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M, together with fixed-momentum diagnostics, show that balanced non-native representations can match the performance of the native representation, whereas reducing the shorter dimension weakens the scaling and singular-channel support, leading to behavior that increasingly resembles normalized momentum.

AI.tldr: Muon-style optimizers across multiple representations form a unifying family that preserves a common momentum/back-end while the representation geometry (native, nearest-square, skinny, vector) dictates convergence behavior via a Frobenius-isometric constraint. Balanced non-native representations can match native performance; shorter-dimension bottlenecks limit singular channels and worsen scaling and convergence bounds.
AI.motivation: To understand how the choice of parameter-block representation affects Muon-style optimizer geometry, convergence, and practical performance, and to unify several representations under a single framework with shared momentum and Newton–Schulz backend.
AI.method: Introduce the {} method (a family of Muon-style optimizers) that employs Frobenius-isometric representations (native, nearest-square, skinny, vector). Analyze the induced polar steepest-descent geometry, where the shorter matrix dimension governs the number of supported singular channels, pullback scaling, and stochastic nonconvex convergence constants. Use a teacher–student model to link curvature collapse with an isotropic Marchenko–Pastur spectrum. Validate with pretraining experiments on LLaMA2-130M and LLaMA2-600M and fixed-momentum diagnostics.
AI.result: Different representations yield distinct geometry and convergence characteristics, with the shorter dimension capping the number of singular channels and influencing pullback scaling and convergence constants. Balanced non-native representations can match native performance, but reducing the shorter dimension reduces scaling and singular-channel support, causing behavior to converge toward normalized momentum.
AI.conclusion: The representation geometry induced by matrix packing in Muon-style optimizers is essential for performance. Frobenius-isometric representations preserve favorable polar-descent geometry and preserve effective singular-channel support proportional to the shorter dimension. Practically, non-native representations are viable if balanced, whereas overly reducing the shorter dimension degrades scaling and aligns behavior more with normalized momentum.

title: VideoSEMA: a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention for video understanding
summary: We present for video understanding (classification) a split space-time attention model, VideoSEMA, consisting of a scalable and efficient Mamba-like attention (SEMA) block in space and a softmax temporal attention in time. In each frame, SEMA attention applies a local window attention in parallel with a global averaging in a Mamba macro-architecture, which is called Mamba-like. Under certain rank conditions, we prove that the computationally cheaper split space-time attention is equivalent to full space-time attention. On benchmark K400 data sets, VideoSEMA out-performs heavier vision transformer and Mamba models. On benchmark SSv2 data, VideoSEMA leads in top-1 accuracy among models of similar parameter sizes. As image resolution scales up from standard $224^2$ to $1024^2$ on K400 and without fine-tuning, VideoSEMA degrades much more gracefully than VideoMamba in accuracy. It is promising to extend VideoSEMA to longer videos with a dilated/sparse temporal attention.

AI.tldr: VideoSEMA offers an efficient split space-time attention approach for video classification that matches full-space-time attention under rank assumptions and yields state-of-the-art or competitive accuracy with better scalability, especially on higher resolutions and longer videos.
AI.motivation: To achieve scalable, accurate video understanding with reduced computation by decomposing space-time attention into a split design (local window + global averaging) and leveraging a Mamba-like architecture.
AI.method: Proposes SEMA block with local window attention in space in parallel with global averaging within a Mamba-like macro-architecture; applies softmax temporal attention; analyzes rank conditions for equivalence to full space-time attention; evaluates on K400 and SSv2, with ablations on resolution scaling from 224^2 to 1024^2; discusses extension to dilated/sparse temporal attention for longer videos.
AI.result: VideoSEMA outperforms heavier vision transformer and Mamba models on K400; achieves top-1 accuracy among similarly parameterized models on SSv2; shows graceful degradation with resolution increase (1024^2) without fine-tuning compared to VideoMamba.
AI.conclusion: VideoSEMA is a promising, efficient approach for video understanding that can match full attention under reasonable conditions and scales well with resolution; extending to longer videos via dilated/sparse temporal attention is a natural future direction.

title: Risk-Aware Belief Control Barrier Functions over Random Finite Sets
summary: Ensuring robot safety in unknown, dynamic environments is a fundamental requirement. It involves inferring the states of an unknown and time-varying number of moving objects from noisy, incomplete measurements. We address safe control under the induced multi-object state uncertainty with a risk-aware belief control barrier function (BCBF) framework. The uncertainty is captured by a random finite set (RFS) belief, estimated by a sequential Monte Carlo probability hypothesis density (SMC-PHD) filter that represents it with a set of particles. Building directly on these particles, we construct a nonsmooth BCBF, establish forward invariance of the safe set under continuous prediction, and derive an explicit condition under which discrete updates preserve safety. Simulation and real-world underwater experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: A risk-aware belief BCBF for safe control under multi-object uncertainty using an SMC-PHD particle-based RFS belief; it proves forward invariance in continuous prediction and gives a condition for safety preservation during discrete updates, validated in simulations and underwater experiments.
AI.motivation: Ensure robot safety in unknown, dynamic environments where the number and states of moving objects are uncertain and must be inferred from noisy measurements.
AI.method: Develop a nonsmooth Belief Control Barrier Function (BCBF) built directly on a particle-based random finite set (RFS) belief estimated via a sequential Monte Carlo probability hypothesis density (SMC-PHD) filter. Prove forward invariance of the safe set under continuous prediction and derive an explicit condition under which discrete updates preserve safety.
AI.result: The framework achieves safe control under multi-object state uncertainty; demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency through simulations and real-world underwater experiments.
AI.conclusion: Integrating RFS-based beliefs with a nonsmooth BCBF yields a practical, risk-aware approach for safe control in dynamic, multi-object environments, with validated experimental results.

title: Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems
summary: Modern industrial environments increasingly run many autonomous subsystems at once - schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets - each pursuing its own goals while sharing the same physical resources. Because high-level human intentions are translated into low-level control logic and then discarded, no running component can tell whether it is still doing what was actually intended, and goal conflicts surface only after they have caused a missed target or a shutdown. We propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domainagnostic middleware that represents intentions as first-class, persistent, and explainable runtime objects: a large language model grounded in a formal OWL ontology parses naturallanguage goals into structured intentions, a consistency monitor detects conflicts at registration time, before execution, and a transparency module explains them in natural language. We report a first proof of concept in which two autonomous agents register conflicting production and energy intentions, and the IAL flags and explains the conflict before it reaches the execution layer. The result is a mechanism that shifts behavioral assurance for cooperating autonomous systems from post-hoc failure analysis to pre-execution, intention-level checking.

AI.tldr: Introduces Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domain-agnostic middleware that treats goals as persistent intentions, using an OWL-grounded LLM to convert NL goals into structured intentions, with a pre-execution consistency monitor and a transparency module to explain conflicts; validated via a minimal proof-of-concept showing pre-execution conflict detection between production and energy goals.
AI.motivation: To prevent late-discovered conflicts in multi-subsystem environments by moving assurance to intention-level pre-execution, rather than post-hoc failure analysis.
AI.method: Architectural design: LLM grounded in OWL ontology parses natural-language goals into structured intentions; consistency monitor checks for conflicts at registration time; transparency module generates natural-language explanations. Proof-of-concept with two autonomous agents registering conflicting intentions.
AI.result: IAL flags and explains conflicts before execution; demonstrates shift of behavioral assurance from post-hoc to pre-execution intention-level checking.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agnostic, intention-centric middleware can improve coordination among autonomous systems; future work needed on scalability, ontology maintenance, LLM reliability, and integration with existing control loops.

title: CASP: Learning-Augmented Offline Approximation with Verifiable Certificates and Bounded-Loss PAC Guarantees
summary: Machine-learned predictions can speed up offline NP-hard optimization, but asking a predictor what to do amounts to asking it to solve the problem, and committing an unchecked prediction forfeits every worst-case guarantee. CASP (Certificate-Augmented Solution Pruning) instead asks which parts of the search space may be ignored, and accepts each answer only after a sound polynomial-time verifier has checked it, so correctness never depends on prediction quality. We develop the learning theory of this design. The verifier makes the induced loss class uniformly bounded, so certificate parameters are learnable from $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log K)$ samples ($K$ the maximum instance size), whereas the unverified commitment class admits no distribution-free rate and, under cost spread $R$, none below $Ω(R/\varepsilon^2)$. Filtering noisy predictions by verifiable confidence dominates the standard min-combiner, with a margin we compute in closed form, and the prediction stays useful even given the LP, because it breaks ties on degenerate optimal faces, where every symmetric LP policy, meaning one whose commitments depend on the instance only through the verifiable confidence values, provably stalls. Experiments on five problems test the theory's quantitative predictions. With trained predictors, unverified pruning loses up to $26%$ of the optimum under distribution shift, while the verified deployment of the same predictions loses nothing.

AI.tldr: CASP uses certificate-augmented verification to prune search spaces in NP-hard problems; it yields a verifiable, sample-efficient learning framework for pruning decisions, with verified predictions matching optimum under distribution shift, unlike unverified commitments.
AI.motivation: Enable ML-driven acceleration of NP-hard optimization without sacrificing worst-case guarantees by ensuring pruning decisions are verifiable and independent of predictor quality.
AI.method: Define a certificate-augmented solution pruning framework where a predictor proposes pruning decisions; a polynomial-time verifier checks each decision; compare a verifiable certificate class to an unverified commitment class; analyze learnability and rates, derive a closed-form margin for filtering, and study LP degeneracy; validate theory with experiments on five problems.
AI.result: The verifier-induced loss class is uniformly bounded, making certificate parameters learnable in tilde O(ε^{-2} log K) samples (K = max instance size); the unverified commitment class lacks distribution-free rates and, with cost spread R, has no rate below Ω(R/ε^2); verifiable confidence-based filtering outperforms the standard min-combiner; the method remains useful with LP degeneracy; experiments show unverified pruning loses up to 26% of optimum under distribution shift, while verified deployment loses nothing.
AI.conclusion: CASP provides a sound, learnable framework for predicate-based pruning with verifiable guarantees, enabling robust ML-assisted optimization with practical gains and minimal risk to solution quality.

title: Causal-Adversarial Probing of Clinical Covariates for Prostate MRI Grading
summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI-based cancer grading may encode clinical covariates that either reflect useful disease-related signal or non-generalising shortcut information, but their role is usually assumed. We propose a causal-reasoning framework for probing covariate dependence in MRI-based International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group prediction. Rather than treating mpMRI as a direct cause of grade, we model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as observations of latent tumour pathology, and test whether candidate clinical variables act as nuisance correlates, disease-related proxies, or irrelevant covariates in the learned representation. We implement this using an adversarial framework that suppresses the decodability of individual clinical covariate at a time while preserving MRI-based grade prediction. The approach is developed and evaluated on 2,903 prostate MRI examinations, with external validation on 576 patients. We report a set of interesting and previously under-explored imaging-to-clinical-variable interactions in the context of deep learning generalisation. For examples, in binary ISUP Grade Group $\geq2$ classification, suppressing age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42%, respectively (all p < 0.05), suggesting reduced non-generalising covariate information; In contrast, suppressing PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (all p < 0.001), indicating that these variables carried task-relevant signal. These findings show that adversarial covariate suppression can provide a practical representation-level analysis for distinguishing potentially harmful dependence from informative signal in prostate MRI grading models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a causal-reasoning framework using adversarial covariate suppression to interrogate how clinical covariates influence MRI-based ISUP Grade Group prediction, aiming to separate nuisance information from disease-related signal and improve generalisation.
AI.motivation: Address the risk that deep learning models on mpMRI use covariates that do not generalize or reflect disease biology (shortcuts), potentially harming generalization to new cohorts.
AI.method: Model MRI appearance and ISUP grade as observations of latent tumor pathology. Use an adversarial framework to suppress the decodability of each clinical covariate from the learned representation while preserving MRI-based ISUP grade prediction. Evaluate on 2,903 prostate MRI exams with external validation on 576 patients. Suppress one covariate at a time to probe its role as nuisance, proxy, or informative signal.
AI.result: In binary ISUP Grade Group ≥2 classification, suppression of age, BMI, and alcohol use improved AUC by 1.23%, 0.84%, and 1.42% (all p<0.05), suggesting reduced non-generalising covariate information; suppression of PSA and prostate volume degraded AUC by 1.91% and 7.61% (all p<0.001), indicating these variables carry task-relevant signal.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial covariate suppression offers a practical representation-level analysis to distinguish potentially harmful dependence from informative signal in prostate MRI grading models, aiding interpretation and generalisation.

title: Learning Agile Navigation in Crowded Environments for Quadruped Robots
summary: Navigating dynamic and crowded environments presents significant challenges for quadruped robots due to severe sensor occlusion and unpredictable human motion. Existing approaches face a trade-off: model-based methods, such as Velocity Obstacles (VO), theoretically guarantee safety but rely on accurate obstacle motion estimates that often fail in dense crowds, while end-to-end learning methods offer robustness but lack motion prediction capability of obstacles, leading to collisions or conservative behaviors. To solve this, we propose VOP-Nav, a novel navigation system that combines the geometric safety of VO with the agile adaptability of end-to-end learning. Using only local onboard observations, our system avoids explicit obstacle detection and tracking pipelines. The VOP-Net processes multi-frame LiDAR data to implicitly encode dynamic constraints and predict a safe velocity region derived from Velocity Obstacle theory. Importantly, the VO predictions serve a dual role: they are used as input to the navigation policy during inference and as a reward signal during training to encourage safe motion. Evaluations in Isaac Gym demonstrate that VOP-Nav achieves higher success rates than all baselines while balancing locomotion speed and collision avoidance. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot further validates the system's robustness and efficiency in complex indoor and outdoor dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: A VO-informed end-to-end navigation system for quadrupeds (VOP-Nav) that learns from LiDAR while leveraging Velocity Obstacle theory for safety; shows superior performance in simulation and real-world tests.
AI.motivation: Dynamic and crowded environments create safety and efficiency challenges for quadruped navigation. Model-based VO requires accurate obstacle motion estimates that fail in dense crowds, while end-to-end methods lack motion prediction and can cause collisions or excessive conservatism. An integrated approach aims to combine safety guarantees with adaptive, data-driven planning using only local observations.
AI.method: VOP-Net ingests multi-frame LiDAR to implicitly encode dynamic constraints and derives a safe velocity region inspired by Velocity Obstacle theory. It avoids explicit obstacle detection/tracking. VO predictions serve as both a input to the policy during inference and a reward signal during training to encourage safe motion.
AI.result: In Isaac Gym, VOP-Nav achieves higher success rates than all baselines while balancing locomotion speed and collision avoidance. Real-world deployment on a Unitree Go2 demonstrates robustness and efficiency in complex indoor and outdoor dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid approach that fuses VO-based safety with end-to-end learning yields robust, efficient navigation for quadrupeds in dynamic environments, without relying on explicit obstacle tracking. The method shows promising simulation and real-world results, with potential for broader deployment and further refinements.

title: Seeing the End at Step Zero: Accelerating Diffusion MLLMs via MLP Sparsity-Aware Truncation
summary: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) are highly effective for multimodal reasoning, yet their inference efficiency is significantly hindered by fixed-length generation constraints. Since the actual output length is unknown, output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, resulting in substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. In this work, we discover that DMLLMs implicitly reveal their valid semantic boundary at the very first denoising step through a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity. Leveraging this observation, we propose Seer, a training-free framework that detects this boundary using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-based criterion and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. To preserve these theoretical gains during batched serving, Seer incorporates a hybrid execution strategy that maximizes throughput while seamlessly accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experimental results demonstrate that Seer effectively eliminates padding waste, accelerating throughput by up to $\sim$31$\times$. Across 9 benchmarks, Seer robustly maintains overall performance and even improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by mitigating noise leakage (e.g., DocVQA score increases from 63.52 to 63.66), offering a highly efficient, plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

AI.tldr: Seer is a training-free, SNR-based boundary detector for Diffusion Multimodal LLMs that truncates the generation suffix after the first denoising step, yielding up to ~31x throughput gains while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across 9 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Padding-based inefficiency in DMLLMs due to unknown output length causes substantial wasted computation. A lightweight, training-free method to identify the semantic end and truncate the rest can dramatically speed up inference.
AI.method: Identify the semantic boundary by observing a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity at the very first denoising step. Use a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) criterion to decide the boundary. Perform a one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. Implement a hybrid execution strategy to preserve throughput for batched serving with dynamic sequence lengths, enabling plug-and-play deployment.
AI.result: Throughput is accelerated by up to approximately 31x. Performance is preserved across 9 benchmarks, with a notable improvement on complex tasks (e.g., DocVQA: 63.52 → 63.66). The method eliminates padding waste and reduces noise leakage, offering a practical acceleration for DMLLMs.
AI.conclusion: Seer provides a practical, training-free acceleration mechanism for DMLLMs by early boundary detection and suffix truncation, maintaining or improving accuracy while dramatically increasing throughput and simplifying deployment in batched serving.

title: Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data
summary: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse elasticity problem because low resolution obscures spatial details needed to distinguish heterogeneous property variations, and small measurement perturbations or fitting errors are amplified through inverse estimation. Existing inverse methods often rely on high-fidelity observations and manually prespecified loss weights, limiting their adaptability and making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. We propose a Probabilistic Inverse Elasticity Physics-Informed Neural Network (PIE-PINN) framework for robust estimation of Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data. PIE-PINN models displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals using Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. To improve robustness, the framework combines a B-spline-guided displacement network with a hierarchical half-Cauchy model for displacement residual scales. The B-spline provides a smooth global representation of the displacement field, while the neural network correction captures local variations. The hierarchical scale model adaptively downweights severe displacement fitting errors, enabling more robust recovery of the latent mean displacement field. An alternating maximum-likelihood training strategy updates the mean through weighted residual minimization and updates the scales to adjust the loss weights. Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate the robustness of PIE-PINN.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic physics-informed PINN for robustly estimating spatially varying Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data, using Laplace-distributed residuals, a B-spline-guided displacement network, and a hierarchical half-Cauchy scale model with alternating likelihood-based training.
AI.motivation: Inverse elasticity with low-resolution measurements is severely ill-posed; existing methods rely on high-fidelity data and fixed loss weights, making them sensitive to noise and resolution degradation. A robust probabilistic framework is needed to downweight outliers and adapt to varying observation quality.
AI.method: PIE-PINN formulates observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals under Laplace distributions within a unified probabilistic model. It employs a B-spline-guided displacement network for a smooth global displacement representation, plus a neural network correction for local details. A hierarchical half-Cauchy prior on displacement residual scales adaptively downweights large errors. Training uses an alternating maximum-likelihood scheme: update the mean displacement/elastic properties via weighted residual minimization, then update scales to adjust loss weights.
AI.result: Case studies across different noise levels and observation resolutions show PIE-PINN robustly recovers the latent mean displacement field and material properties, maintaining accuracy despite perturbations and coarse data.
AI.conclusion: PIE-PINN offers a robust, adaptive approach to inverse elasticity under challenging data conditions by integrating probabilistic loss modeling, a global-local displacement representation, and an alternating learning strategy that downweights outliers and resolves ill-posedness.

title: Multimodality as Supervision: Self-Supervised Specialization to the Test Environment via Multimodality
summary:
Cross-modal learning, i.e., learning to predict one modality from another, is a fundamental mechanism for self-supervision via leveraging multimodality. Many practical applications, e.g., deploying a household robot, involve devices that are equipped with a rich set of sensors that enable multimodal sensing in their test environment. This presents an opportunity to apply cross-modal learning to the multimodal data sensed by these devices to learn representations. Findings in developmental psychology also suggest that biological agents leverage it to build an effective representation of their surroundings.
  To study this, we propose a controlled setup, where we restrict a user device to just a given test environment. It results in a specialization setup where we attempt to develop a performant model for this specific test environment. Under this setup, we develop Test-Space Training (TST), which performs multimodal data collection in the test environment and performs self-supervised pre-training on it. We evaluate these models on various downstream tasks in the same environment.
  Under this setup, we find various interesting insights, such as collecting rich multimodal data only from the test environment and leveraging cross-modal learning, we can achieve competitive results with generalist models (e.g., DINOv2 and CLIP) pre-trained on large-scale internet datasets. This enables an alternative scenario where the need for external Internet-scale datasets for pre-training models is reduced. We also present a set of analyses and ablations that raise intriguing points on substituting data with (multi)modality, and how varying pre-training data enables a tradeoff between a model's abilities to specialise to a test environment, and generalize to held-out spaces.

AI.tldr: Proposes Test-Space Training (TST) for self-supervised multimodal learning within a restricted test environment, showing that multimodal data from the test space can rival internet-scale pre-trained models while reducing the need for large external datasets.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether cross-modal learning in a constrained environment can yield strong representations without relying on large-scale external data, leveraging locally collected multimodal data.
AI.method: Introduce Test-Space Training (TST): collect rich multimodal data in the test environment, perform self-supervised pre-training within that space, and evaluate downstream tasks in the same environment; conduct analyses/ablations on modality substitution and specialization-generalization trade-offs.
AI.result: Demonstrates that collecting multimodal data solely from the test environment, coupled with cross-modal learning, can achieve competitive performance with generalist models pre-trained on internet-scale data (e.g., DINOv2, CLIP); provides insights into how modality and data scale affect specialization vs generalization.
AI.conclusion: Local, environment-specific multimodal pre-training can reduce dependence on external internet-scale datasets while maintaining competitive task performance, highlighting a spectrum between specialized and general models driven by pre-training data composition.

title: DriftWorld: Fast World Modeling through Drifting
summary: Predictive world models enable robots to plan by imagining the outcomes of their actions, but their value for control hinges on generating many rollouts quickly. This creates a bottleneck for diffusion-based world models: multistep sampling makes each rollout expensive, limiting large-scale action search at inference time. We introduce DriftWorld, an action-conditioned world model based on drifting generative models. Rather than denoising iteratively at inference, DriftWorld learns an action-conditioned drift during training, allowing it to generate future frames from the current observation and a candidate action sequence in a single forward pass at 30+ fps, which is 17x faster on average than diffusion based baselines. We evaluate DriftWorld on standard vision-based robotic manipulation benchmarks, including Bridge-V2, RT-1, Language Table, Push-T, and Robomimic. By producing rollouts that are both accurate and fast, DriftWorld achieves state-of-the-art decision-making performance with far less inference time than diffusion-based world model baselines. Beyond online control, DriftWorld can also serve as an offline simulator for ranking real-world robot policies, with rollout-based scores correlating with ground truth at up to 0.99. These results show that drifting models are a strong fit for robot world modeling, where fast, high-quality imagination directly supports planning and policy evaluation.

AI.tldr: DriftWorld replaces diffusion-based rollouts with action-conditioned drift for fast, single-pass future frame generation, enabling 30+ fps rollouts and 17x speedups while maintaining high accuracy on robotics benchmarks, yielding state-of-the-art planning and offline policy evaluation performance.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based world models are accurate but slow for multi-step rollouts, hindering real-time planning and large-scale action search in robotics.
AI.method: Train an action-conditioned drift model that learns the temporal dynamics, allowing future frames to be generated from the current observation and a candidate action sequence in a single forward pass, avoiding iterative denoising at inference.
AI.result: DriftWorld achieves 30+ fps and ~17x faster inference than diffusion baselines. It attains state-of-the-art decision-making performance on vision-based robotic benchmarks (Bridge-V2, RT-1, Language Table, Push-T, Robomimic) and serves as an effective offline simulator with rollout-based scores correlating with ground truth up to 0.99.
AI.conclusion: Drifting generative models are a strong fit for robot world modeling, delivering fast, high-quality imagined futures suitable for planning and policy evaluation, with notable acceleration over diffusion methods and strong offline correlation for policy ranking.

title: Democratizing Agent Deployment Safety: A Structural Monitoring Approach
comment: Accepted in ICML 2026 Workshops: AI4GOOD and AIWILD
summary: AI software development agents are increasingly capable of modifying infrastructure and security critical systems, creating risks where an agent completes its assigned task while covertly weakening safeguards through actions such as broadening permissions, degrading logging, or introducing persistence mechanisms. While frontier laboratories may deploy sophisticated monitoring pipelines, many organizations and individual users adopting coding agents lack the resources and governance maturity required to maintain complex learned monitor ensembles. We study this problem as infrastructure level sabotage under task success in the infrastructure-as-code setting from ControlArena and compare trained and untrained monitors across synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes. We introduce an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that analyzes structural security regressions using control-flow and data-flow graph diffs alongside raw code diffs. In asynchronous evaluation, an untrained git diff monitor misses 11.6% attacks at 1% false positive rate auditing budget, our untrained IFG monitor reduces this to 3.5%, and the trained Async RF monitor achieves below 1%. Unlike the trained Async RF monitor, IFG can also operate synchronously as a pre-deployment safeguard that blocks suspicious infrastructure changes before execution or merge. In synchronous mode, IFG realtime rollback reduces joint main task and covert task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable reduction in legitimate task completion. These results suggest that untrained structural monitors provide a practical and auditable path toward democratizing deployment safety for organizations seeking trustworthy adoption of advanced AI agents.

AI.tldr: IFG-based monitors detect and block infrastructure-level sabotage by AI agents in infrastructure-as-code, showing strong performance even without training, and enabling pre-deployment safeguards; supports democratized deployment safety.
AI.motivation: Address rising risk that AI software development agents modify infrastructure and security controls, especially for resource-constrained organizations lacking advanced monitoring; need lightweight, auditable safeguards with practical deployment.
AI.method: Introduce an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor combining control-flow and data-flow graph diffs with raw code diffs. Compare untrained vs trained monitors across synchronous and asynchronous deployment modes in a ControlArena infrastructure-as-code setting.
AI.result: Asynchronous: untrained git-diff monitor misses 11.6% attacks at 1% FPR; untrained IFG reduces misses to 3.5%; trained Async RF <1%. Synchronous: IFG enables pre-deployment safeguards; realtime rollback reduces joint task/covert task success from 74.4% to 0.0% with no measurable loss of legitimate task completion.
AI.conclusion: Untrained structural monitors, exemplified by IFG, offer a practical, auditable path to democratize safe deployment of AI agents in infrastructure, with benefits in both pre-deployment and runtime protections; trained monitors still outperform but require more resources.

title: Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning
summary: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

AI.tldr: Gate-zero growth is a function-preserving mechanism for continual learning that expands model capacity by adding residual blocks via a zero-initialized gate, yielding rank-separated Jacobians, minimal old-domain forgetting, and a unifying geometric principle applicable to LoRA, ReZero, and related adapters.
AI.motivation: Address continual learning with growth while preserving previously learned functionality; identify geometric structure that enables safe capacity activation and minimal drift.
AI.method: Introduce a zero-initialized gating mechanism to add residual blocks (gate-zero growth) under a transversality condition, achieving rank separation in the functional Jacobian (old directions unchanged, new gate directions provide first-order variation). Analyze function drift (O(||α||^2)) and Jacobian leakage (O(||α||∞)). Empirically evaluate on a Transformer scaled from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus (300M→857M) under Isolation and Freeze-Nothing, comparing FP vs non-FP controls (G_stack), and show the approach generalizes to LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters.
AI.result: Gate-zero growth achieves near-zero old-domain forgetting (Δ_A < 0.1) in continual adaptation of a large Transformer, under both exact-preservation and joint-frontier regimes; old directions remain unchanged while new gate directions produce the only first-order change, with function drift and leakage tightly controlled by the gate parameters. A non-FP baseline suffers substantially more forgetting. This geometry is presented as a canonical instance governing safe capacity activation in CL and extends to related adapter schemes.
AI.conclusion: Gate-zero growth embodies a unified local geometric principle for safe capacity activation in continual learning, offering a provable-like separation in the Jacobian and practical forgetting gains; the framework encompasses LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters, suggesting broad applicability of the FP approach to safer growth in CL.

title: AE-UAV: An Air-to-Air Event-Based UAV Tracking Benchmark and a Real-Time Frequency-Domain Tracker
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Air-to-air (A2A) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) tracking is fundamental to airborne remote sensing of low-altitude aerial targets. However, the deployment of continuous, real-time tracking systems on UAVs presents significant challenges. In A2A scenarios, traditional frame-based cameras suffer from severe performance degradation under low illumination, overexposure, and high-speed motion owing to their limited dynamic range and fixed temporal sampling. Although event cameras offer a promising alternative with microsecond temporal resolution and a high dynamic range, current research is bottlenecked by two primary issues: 1) the absence of dedicated A2A event-based datasets, and 2) the heavy reliance of existing trackers on GPU acceleration and extensive training data, rendering them impractical for resource-constrained UAVs. To bridge these gaps, we introduce AE-UAV, an air-to-air event-based UAV tracking benchmark. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first airborne-captured event camera dataset for A2A tracking, comprising 178 flight sequences with continuous-time cubic B-spline annotations. Furthermore, we propose the Fast-Slow Frequency-domain Tracking (FSFT) method. This lightweight, training-free framework seamlessly integrates frequency-domain template matching with search region prediction and detection-based drift correction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FSFT operates at an ultra-fast 420 frames per second (FPS) on CPU-only hardware. It retains 93.97% of the accuracy of state-of-the-art GPU-dependent methods while delivering a 5.32-fold effective speedup and exhibiting superior temporal resolution generalization, thereby providing a highly efficient and robust solution for airborne remote sensing of aerial targets. The dataset and source code are available at https://github.com/MSP-xEN/AE-UAV.

AI.tldr: Proposes AE-UAV dataset and FSFT tracking framework; training-free, CPU-friendly event-based A2A tracking achieving near-state accuracy at 420 FPS, with significant speedup; dataset + code released.
AI.motivation: Overcomes limitations of frame-based A2A tracking and lack of A2A event datasets; reduce reliance on GPUs and large training data; enable real-time UAV remote sensing under challenging illumination and high-speed motion.
AI.method: FSFT combines frequency-domain template matching with search-region prediction and drift correction; lightweight, training-free; leverages event camera data; robust under low-light and high-speed conditions; uses continuous-time cubic B-spline annotations.
AI.result: FSFT runs at 420 FPS on CPU; achieves 93.97% of the accuracy of GPU-based trackers; 5.32x faster; better temporal generalization; AE-UAV dataset includes 178 sequences with cubic B-spline annotations; code released at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: AE-UAV fills the lack of airborne event datasets for A2A tracking; FSFT provides an efficient, practical solution for UAV tracking in challenging conditions; dataset and source code are publicly available.

title: Goal-Oriented Semantic Communication for Distributed ISAC-Enabled Vehicle Coordination
summary: Vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections relies on accurate real-time vehicle state acquisition and reliable command-and-control (C&C) signal delivery. However, existing studies typically treat sensing, communication, and control separately, which may lead to redundant transmissions, outdated state information, and unreliable vehicle coordination. In this paper, we investigate a new scenario of distributed integrated sensing and communication (ISAC)-enabled vehicle coordination at intersections, where multiple roadside units (RSUs) collaboratively transmit sensing signals for vehicle state acquisition and C&C signals for vehicle movement control under the management of a central base station (BS). To improve signaling efficiency, we propose a unified goal-oriented semantic communication (GSC) framework, which transmits sensing and C&C signals only when they are semantically important for improving intersection traffic throughput. Specifically, an extended Kalman filter (EKF) is adopted to predict vehicle states and fuse distributed sensing measurements. A masked hybrid proximal policy optimization (MHPPO) framework is then developed to jointly determine sensing transmission decisions, C&C transmission decisions, and C&C signal contents based on a value-of-information (VoI) reward. Furthermore, we propose an uncertainty-aware transmission design (UTD), including robust beamforming and VoI-based time-division power allocation, to improve sensing and communication reliability under vehicle state uncertainty and inter-RSU interference. Simulation results show that our proposed framework achieves 100% collision-free vehicle coordination with significantly reduced signaling overhead compared with predictive ISAC baselines adapted from state-of-the-art related studies and several ablation baselines.

AI.tldr: A unified ISAC-enabled framework at intersections uses semantic, goal-oriented signaling to coordinate vehicles with reduced signaling overhead; EKF for state estimation; a masked hybrid PPO to make sensing and control transmission decisions; uncertainty-aware transmission design to boost reliability; results show 100% collision-free coordination with lower signaling burden than baselines.
AI.motivation: Current cross-layer approaches treat sensing, communication, and control separately, causing outdated state, redundant transmissions, and unreliable coordination. A unified, ISAC-based, semantic framework aims to improve signaling efficiency and intersection throughput.
AI.method: Extends EKF for distributed state prediction/fusion; employs masked hybrid PPO (MHPPO) to jointly decide sensing and C&C transmissions and C&C content under a value-of-information reward; central BS coordinates multiple RSUs; introduces uncertainty-aware transmission design (UTD) with robust beamforming and VoI-based power allocation to mitigate state uncertainty and RSU interference.
AI.result: Simulation shows 100% collision-free vehicle coordination and significantly reduced signaling overhead compared with predictive ISAC baselines and various ablations.
AI.conclusion: A unified GSC-enabled ISAC framework with EKF-based sensing fusion, VoI-guided transmission decisions, and robust inter-RSU coordination improves efficiency and reliability of vehicle coordination at unsignalized intersections.

title: Alipay-PIBench: A Realistic Payment Integration Benchmark for Coding Agents
summary: Payment integration is a demanding repository-level software task: agents must select a suitable product, implement coordinated client-server flows, verify payment outcomes, and preserve consistency between transaction and business states. We introduce Alipay-PIBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration. It contains nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, each organized into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Scenario-specific rubrics support deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, supplemented by LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. We evaluate six coding-agent models and report rubric pass rate (RPR). Under the with-skill condition, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Access to the alipay-payment-integration skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average relative to the without-skill condition, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements. Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration.

AI.tldr: Alipay-PIBench benchmarks coding agents on Alipay payment integration using 9 products and 18 tasks across basic and hardening scenarios; shows skill access improves rubric pass rate; provides diagnosis framework with structured rubrics and LLM-assisted semantic assessment.
AI.motivation: Payment integration tasks are repository-level, involve client-server flows and domain semantics; existing benchmarks do not adequately evaluate end-to-end, domain-specific behavior of coding agents; a controlled, scenario-based framework is needed to assess capability and guidance effectiveness in payment integration.
AI.method: Construct Alipay-PIBench with nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, organized into Basic functional-completion and Advanced risk-aware hardening scenarios. Scenario rubrics support deterministic static, unit, integration, and end-to-end checks, supplemented by LLM-assisted assessment for semantic requirements. Evaluate six coding-agent models; report rubric pass rate (RPR). Compare with-skill vs without-skill; provide method-level breakdown into source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements.
AI.result: Under with-skill, mean RPR ranges from 68.58% to 91.37%. Access to the alipay-payment-integration skill improves mean RPR by 10.31 percentage points on average relative to the without-skill condition, with gains varying across models, products, and scenarios. Method-level results distinguish source-level completion, executable payment behavior, and payment-domain requirements.
AI.conclusion: Alipay-PIBench provides a controlled setting for diagnosing model capability and evaluating structured guidance in payment integration.

title: Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures
summary: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

AI.tldr: Provides a sharp stability threshold for residual blocks: the velocity field must grow sublinearly with input magnitude (q ≤ 1).
AI.motivation: To explain stable training of deep residual networks and provide principled architectural design guidelines; clarifies the stabilizing role of normalization and reduces reliance on ad hoc architectural choices.
AI.method: Two independent analyses: (i) classical ODE theory establishing a global forward flow for q ≤ 1 and divergence for q > 1; (ii) Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman optimal-control analysis showing bang-bang optimality on the boundary, making q ≤ 1 necessary and sufficient for stable training. Defines a framework of sublinear-growth velocity fields and develops an exponent-arithmetic that certifies q_k ≤ 1 at architectural primitives; demonstrates a parameter-free modification reducing a Mamba block from q=5 to q=1 without layer normalization; validates with experiments on Mamba and PatchTST.
AI.result: q ≤ 1 is a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training; the sublinear-growth velocity-field class enables well-controlled forward dynamics and adjoint sensitivity; provides a principled certification method for architectural components; explains and accounts for the stabilizing effect of layer normalization; empirical results confirm stability for q ≤ 1 variants.
AI.conclusion: The sublinear-growth principle grounds stable residual design in a concrete, verifiable exponent bound, offering design guidelines, a certification toolkit, and practical fixes (e.g., reducing supercritical blocks to q=1) validated by experiments.

title: WorkDrive: Roadwork Chain of Causation for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving vision-language models (VLMs) struggle in roadwork zones, where familiar visual cues such as lane markings and permanent signs are altered or absent, and temporary devices such as cones and barriers redefine the drivable corridor. VLMs can detect these objects, but without explicit guidance they anchor their reasoning on familiar elements from pre-training and fail to connect work-zone observations to correct planning decisions. We propose WorkDrive, a framework that constructs perception-grounded causal reasoning for work zones and aligns it with trajectory prediction. An automated multitask perception pipeline extracts structured scene facts and injects them into a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) annotation pipeline, redirecting the annotator's attention to domain-specific elements. The resulting reasoning labels are used for supervised fine-tuning, followed by reinforcement learning with a single reward: consistency between lateral meta-actions and the predicted trajectory. On ROADWork, the largest public work-zone dataset, the proposed roadwork CoC reduces trajectory average displacement error (ADE) by 9.0\%, and consistency-based GRPO yields a further 3.0\%, achieving progressive improvement over the trajectory-only baseline. Code and data will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: WorkDrive builds a perception-grounded causal reasoning framework for roadwork zones to improve trajectory prediction by injecting structured scene facts into a Chain-of-Causation annotation pipeline, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with a consistency reward; on ROADWork it achieves ADE reduction of 9.0% and a further 3.0% gain from GRPO, surpassing trajectory-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models struggle in roadwork zones due to altered or absent familiar cues; there is a need to connect perception of temporary work-zone elements to planning decisions, rather than relying on pretraining biases.
AI.method: An automated multitask perception pipeline extracts structured scene facts and injects them into a Chain-of-Causation annotation pipeline to generate domain-specific reasoning labels. These labels are used for supervised fine-tuning of the model, followed by reinforcement learning with a single reward that enforces consistency between lateral meta-actions and the predicted trajectory.
AI.result: On ROADWork, the roadwork CoC reduces trajectory average displacement error (ADE) by 9.0 percentage points, and a consistency-based GRPO yields a further 3.0 percentage points improvement, showing progressive gains over a trajectory-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating perception-grounded causal reasoning for work zones via CoC annotation and RL improves trajectory prediction in roadwork contexts, with public release of code and data planned.

title: Catch, Throw, Repeat: Planning for Human-Robot Partner Juggling
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Dynamic object exchange between humans and robots remains a challenging problem due to uncertainty in perception, timing, and contact-rich interaction. Human-robot juggling represents a particularly demanding instance of this problem, requiring precise real-time coordination, predictive motion planning with feedback control, and robustness to variability in human motion. Enabling such skills is of interest for advancing physical human-robot interaction and shared autonomy. We present a real-time planning and control architecture for human-robot partner juggling that enables a robot to reliably catch and throw balls in synchronized multi-ball patterns with a human partner. The system integrates predictive ball tracking, adaptive online trajectory optimization using a multiple-shooting formulation, and a state-machine-based coordination logic to enable synchronized multi-ball human-robot partner juggling. In a user study with 8 participants of varying juggling skill from beginner to expert, we demonstrate that our system can achieve three-ball cascades shared between the robot and the human. All participants exceeded previously reported best-case results within a 10-minute test session, with one participant extending the previous record for shared three-ball cascade juggling fivefold to 20 consecutive robot catches, and another participant achieving a 100% success rate with 40 consecutive catches in a single-ball catch-and-return setting. Video documentation can be found at https://kai-ploeger.com/partner-juggling

AI.tldr: Real-time planning and control framework for human-robot partner juggling enabling synchronized multi-ball patterns with a human partner; combines predictive ball tracking, online multi-shooting trajectory optimization, and a state-machine coordination layer; validated in a user study showing notable multi-ball sharing and record-breaking performances.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of dynamic, perception-uncertain, contact-rich human-robot interaction. Juggling provides a stringent testbed for real-time coordination and shared autonomy, with potential impact on broad physical HRI applications.
AI.method: Integrates predictive ball tracking, adaptive online trajectory optimization via a multiple-shooting formulation, and a state-machine-based coordination logic to achieve synchronized multi-ball juggling between human and robot.
AI.result: In a study with 8 participants of varying juggling skill, the system achieved three-ball cascades shared between robot and human. Participants surpassed prior best-case results, including one extending the three-ball cascade to 20 consecutive robot catches and another achieving 40 consecutive single-ball catches with 100% success in a single-ball catch-and-return task.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility of reliable real-time planning and control for human-robot partner juggling and, more broadly, real-time, precision-oriented HRI with shared autonomy. Points to robustness and generalizability to other dynamic, interactive manipulation tasks and highlights the potential for advances in real-time planning under perceptual and timing uncertainty.

title: Collaborative Spatial Learning with Multi-LLM Agents in Networked Social Experiments
comment: Accepted at ASONAM 2026; to appear in the Springer proceedings
summary: Collective problem solving often requires that group members consider the tradeoff between exploitation of known solutions and exploration for new ones, where information of known solutions can be disseminated among individual members through communication networks. The Mason--Watts experiment (PNAS 2012) showed that human groups in shorter-path networks outperform those in longer-path networks on a two-dimensional search task. In this work, we focus on the investigation of such network-efficiency effects in the setting of a group of large language model (LLM) agents. Specifically, we consider groups of sixteen LLM agents playing the Mason--Watts experiment on the eight Mason--Watts network topologies. Moreover, we develop mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents such that the performance of LLM agents can be compared with both the mechanistic agents and the human experimental data. Our computational experiments indicate that the LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, but not under the default initialization. In this experiment, adding a one-sentence first-round randomization instruction improves collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across the eight network topologies. Also, the Bayesian optimization agents obtain higher payoffs than the evaluated LLM agents on this spatial search task. We further compare the agents' exploration--exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

AI.tldr: LLM agent groups show network-efficiency in Mason–Watts networks only when a first-round randomization cue is given; Bayesian optimization agents outperform the LLMs; instruction design affects collective payoff and reveals exploration–exploitation dynamics.
AI.motivation: Test whether human-like network-efficiency effects in collective problem solving generalize to groups of LLM agents, and benchmark LLM performance against mechanistic Bayesian optimizers and human data.
AI.method: Simulate 16 LLM agents across 8 Mason–Watts network topologies performing the original two-dimensional search task; compare with mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents; manipulate first-round initialization with/without a one-sentence randomization instruction; evaluate payoff, exploration–exploitation metrics, copying, and spatial diversity.
AI.result: LLM agents exhibit significant network-efficiency effects when instructed to randomize first-round choices; this instruction boosts collective payoff by >3x the estimated payoff difference across topologies. Bayesian optimization agents achieve higher payoffs than the evaluated LLMs on this spatial search task.
AI.conclusion: Network topology can influence LLM-group performance under specific instructional conditions; simple first-round randomization can unlock network efficiency; mechanistic Bayesian agents provide stronger performance baselines; differences in exploration, copying, and spatial diversity offer insight into collective behavior.

title: Accelerating A/B-Tests with Counterfactual Estimation: Reducing Variance through Policy Overlap
summary:
Online controlled experiments are the gold standard for hypothesis testing in online platforms. Notwithstanding their ubiquity, they are notoriously expensive to run, and issues of variance hamper statistical power in assessing treatment effects. While standard variance reduction techniques leverage model-based control variates to reduce outcome noise, they remain agnostic to potential structural relationships between competing policies.
  In this work, we identify a critical inefficiency in the standard A/B-testing protocol: when a treatment and control policy agree on an action, the resulting outcome contributes noise but no signal regarding the treatment effect -- unnecessarily inflating confidence intervals. We propose a novel experimental protocol that exploits this policy overlap to accelerate experimentation. The key insight is to frame the randomised treatment assignment mechanism as a meta-policy, and leverage $Δ$-Off-Policy Estimation methods to obtain unbiased estimates for average treatment effects. We prove analytically that our approach recovers standard A/B-testing practices in the general case, but that its variance scales with the divergence between policies rather than raw outcome variance. Hence, we dominate the standard Difference-in-Means estimator whenever policies have common support, and the improvement is strict whenever the overlap region contributes non-zero residual variance. Empirical results corroborate these theoretical insights -- holding promise for significant impact on the real-world evaluation of recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and large language model interfaces.

AI.tldr: A Δ-Off-Policy Estimation-based experimental protocol exploits policy overlap to reduce variance in online A/B tests, yielding unbiased ATE estimates; it recovers standard A/B tests in general and dominates Difference-in-Means when policies share support, with variance governed by policy divergence. Empirical results confirm variance reductions, with broad relevance to recommender systems, IR, and LLM interfaces.
AI.motivation: Improve data-efficiency of online experiments by leveraging structural relationships between competing policies to reduce outcome noise and accelerate inference.
AI.method: Frame the randomized treatment mechanism as a meta-policy and apply Δ-Off-Policy Estimation to obtain unbiased average treatment effect estimates; analyze variance as a function of policy divergence and policy overlap; prove that the approach recovers standard A/B testing in general and dominates Difference-in-Means under overlap.
AI.result: Analytically, the estimator is unbiased for ATE and its variance scales with the divergence between policies; it dominates Difference-in-Means whenever policies have common support, with strict improvement when the overlap region contributes residual variance; empirically, results corroborate variance reductions and show potential impact across recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and LLM interfaces.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting policy overlap via Δ-Off-Policy Estimation offers a more efficient evaluation framework for online experiments, with general applicability and promising practical impact; future work may include deployment in production systems and exploring broader policy-structure classes.

title: VQ-Touch: A Data-Efficient Tactile Generation Framework Across Sensors and Scenarios
summary: Tactile image generation significantly reduces the dependency on expensive and wear-prone sensors by synthesizing high-fidelity tactile data, offering an efficient solution for tactile information acquisition in robotic perception and human-machine interaction systems. However, existing methods depend on large-scale, diverse datasets from specific sensors and lack efficient data utilization and robust generalization capabilities, struggling in vision-limited environments. To address this, we introduce VQ-Touch, a tactile generation framework that supports both cross-sensor and multi-scenario applications. Specifically, to efficiently extract complex deformation and texture features from the data, we propose DM-VQGAN, an effective tactile representation learner. Furthermore, we introduce a discrete diffusion decoder with a unified conditioning interface, supporting multimodal generation tasks such as images and labels, and enhances the model's generalization capability through few-shot mixed training, thus achieving compatibility with current mainstream sensors and their variants. Experiments show that VQ-Touch surpasses state-of-the-art methods in multiple tasks.

AI.tldr: VQ-Touch is a cross-sensor, multi-scenario tactile generation framework that uses DM-VQGAN for tactile representation and a discrete diffusion decoder with unified conditioning to enable multimodal outputs; few-shot mixed training enhances generalization, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Tactile data acquisition is costly, sensor-specific, and poorly generalizable across environments. The work aims to reduce sensor dependency, improve data efficiency, and enable robust tactile generation across sensors and scenarios, especially in vision-limited settings.
AI.method: Introduce DM-VQGAN as a tactile representation learner to extract deformation and texture features. Develop a discrete diffusion decoder with a unified conditioning interface for multimodal generation (images, labels). Employ few-shot mixed training to boost generalization and achieve compatibility with mainstream tactile sensors and variants.
AI.result: Empirical results show VQ-Touch outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple tasks.
AI.conclusion: VQ-Touch provides a versatile, sensor-agnostic tactile generation framework with efficient data utilization and strong generalization, suitable for robotic perception and human-computer interaction where tactile sensing is needed.

title: Assessing Physical Frailty and Fall-Risk Indicators with Social Robots: An in situ Evaluation with Older Adults
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Frailty assessments are crucial to evaluate the risk of adverse events and the health and social care needs of older adults, yet their administration remains resource-intensive and typically relies on coarse clinical outcomes, such as task completion times, which may overlook biomechanical indicators of functional decline. To address this, we present a robotic framework that guides older adults through standardised frailty and fall-risk tests while capturing clinical scores and additional frailty-related metrics, offering a deeper insight into a user's condition. The system uses a Behaviour Tree architecture that coordinates perception, decision-making, interaction, and measurement modules. Using vision-based skeleton tracking, the robot evaluates established clinical tests, including the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and the Timed Up and Go (TUG). The framework was co-designed with healthcare professionals and evaluated in situ during six months in a rehabilitation centre's research lab with N=81 older adults. Robot-derived measurements were compared against therapist assessments and clinical reference instruments, including a gait analysis walkway and an inertial measurement unit (IMU). Results showed excellent agreement for most test completion times and gait-related parameters ($ICC > 0.9$). And, substantial agreement for the overall SPPB score comparing the robot and the therapist ($k = 0.67$) and moderate agreement comparing the robot and the IMU ($k=0.55$). The findings highlight that social robots can provide reliable and objective frailty assessments in healthcare settings while enabling the collection of relevant mobility indicators beyond conventional outcomes.

AI.tldr: Robotic framework using a Behaviour Tree and vision-based skeletal tracking evaluates frailty tests (SPPB, TUG) with high agreement to therapists and reference instruments in 81 older adults; demonstrates feasibility and richer mobility metrics beyond traditional outcomes.
AI.motivation: To automate and enrich frailty assessment by capturing biomechanical indicators through a social robot, reducing clinician burden while preserving clinical validity.
AI.method: Co-designed with clinicians; in situ evaluation over six months in a rehabilitation centre research lab; N=81 older adults; robot guides through standardized tests (SPPB, TUG); perception via vision-based skeleton tracking; measurement and decision-making via a Behaviour Tree; comparisons against therapist assessments and reference instruments (gait analysis walkway, IMU); metrics include test completion times and gait parameters; statistics include ICC and kappa.
AI.result: Excellent agreement for most test completion times and gait-related parameters (ICC > 0.9); substantial agreement for overall SPPB score (k = 0.67) and moderate agreement for robot vs IMU (k = 0.55); aligns robot-derived measurements with clinical assessments, enabling additional mobility indicators.
AI.conclusion: Social robots can provide reliable, objective frailty assessments in healthcare settings while collecting richer mobility indicators; co-design with clinicians supports clinical relevance; broader validation and exploration of limitations are warranted.

title: Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

AI.tldr: Proposes a 3D MRI-based brain tumor dataset and a cooperative LLM-driven VLM that maps MRI tokens to text, achieving improved report generation and visual QA over 2D/3D baselines, with potential clinical impact.
AI.motivation: To address the scarcity of paired 3D medical image-text data and extend vision-language models to 3D imaging for enhanced medical reporting in brain oncology.
AI.method: Create a 3D MRI-text dataset focusing on glioma and meningioma; deploy a cooperative system of several LLMs to generate and verify reports; develop a VLM that tokenizes MRI scans and aligns them with text instructions; evaluate on report generation and visual question answering.
AI.result: The proposed VLM outperforms existing 2D and 3D methods in report generation and visual QA tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework improves report quality and has potential to aid diagnosis and treatment planning in brain oncology.

title: Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms
summary: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

AI.tldr: Fairness interventions have non-uniform effects on membership inference privacy at the subpopulation level; LiRA-based subgroup auditing reveals privacy disparities; Differential Privacy interacts variably with fairness; a unified subpopulation-level auditing framework is proposed.
AI.motivation: To fill the gap on how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage, especially for subpopulations, extending beyond prior work that focused on privacy's effect on fairness.
AI.method: Adapt Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing; analyze interactions between Differential Privacy (DP) and fairness methods across model architectures, subgroup sizes, and mitigation strategies; develop a unified empirical framework for subpopulation auditing.
AI.result: Fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations; privacy disparities emerge at the subpopulation level, which are obscured by aggregate evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Subpopulation-level joint evaluation of fairness, privacy, and utility is essential; introduces the first unified empirical framework to audit these aspects in practice.

title: GeoDetect: Geometric Adversarial Detection for VLPs
summary: Vision-language pre-trained models (VLPs) are widely used in real-world applications. However, they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Although adversarial detection methods have demonstrated success in single-modality settings (either vision or language), their effectiveness and reliability in multimodal models such as VLPs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we study the geometry of VLP embedding spaces and observe structured anisotropy that differs from unimodal vision models. Our theoretical analysis shows that under this anisotropic structure, adversarial attacks increase the expected geometric separation between clean and adversarial examples (AEs). Specifically, we demonstrate that AEs consistently exhibit greater expected distances to randomly sampled points than their clean counterparts, indicating that AEs tend to push representations out of manifold regions. Building on these insights, we propose GeoDetect, which leverages these off-manifold deviations via geometric scores to identify AEs. Through comprehensive evaluations, we show that our approach reliably detects AEs across diverse VLP architectures and threat settings, covering unimodal and multimodal attacks as well as adaptive attacks, thereby providing a robust and practical approach to improving the safety and reliability of these models.

AI.tldr: VLPs exhibit structured anisotropy in embedding spaces; adversarial examples push representations off the manifold, increasing geometric separation from clean samples. A new detector, GeoDetect, uses off-manifold geometric scores to identify AEs, achieving robust detection across multiple architectures and attack types, including adaptive ones.
AI.motivation: VLPs combine vision and language but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Detection methods in multimodal settings are underexplored; understanding geometry could yield robust detection signals.
AI.method: The authors analyze the geometry of VLP embedding spaces and prove theoretically that adversarial examples increase expected distances to random samples due to anisotropy, pushing representations off-manifold. They introduce GeoDetect, which computes geometric scores based on off-manifold deviations to detect AEs.
AI.result: GeoDetect reliably detects adversarial examples across diverse VLP architectures and threat settings, including unimodal, multimodal, and adaptive attacks, demonstrating robustness and practicality for improving VLP safety.
