AI.conclusion: Exploiting off-manifold deviations induced by the anisotropic geometry of VLP embeddings enables effective adversarial detection. GeoDetect provides a practical, architecture-agnostic defense that enhances the reliability of VLPs in adversarial scenarios.

title: Scaling Behavior Foundation Model for Humanoid Robots
summary: Humanoid control requires natural whole-body coordination, precise real-time responses to control signals, and robust generalization across diverse environmental contexts, making it a cornerstone for generalist embodied agents. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) have recently emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges by leveraging large-scale behavioral data to achieve superior expressiveness, versatility and generalization. However, despite growing interest in scaling BFMs to further improve their capabilities, it remains unclear how key factors, including the learning paradigm, behavioral data and model architecture should be coordinated to enable effective scaling. In this work, we revisit the scaling recipe for BFMs and demonstrate that substantial performance gains can be achieved through the coordination of three core components: 1) the learning paradigm of motion tracking that reformulates diverse humanoid control problems as the reproduction of integrated whole-body behaviors in the global frame; 2) the strategic synergy between on-policy rollout quantity and reference motion diversity; and 3) the expressive and scalable model architecture termed Humanoid Transformer that facilitates the natural emergence of structured behavioral representations. Through extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world deployment, we demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in control fidelity and task generalization, reducing Mean Per-Keypoint Position Error (MPKPE) on the test set by over 10% in local mode and 82% in global mode compared with existing humanoid controllers. These results establish BFM as a principled and effective foundation for scalable and general-purpose humanoid control.

AI.tldr: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can scale humanoid control by jointly coordinating learning paradigm, data diversity, and model architecture (Humanoid Transformer), achieving substantial reductions in MPKPE (local >10%, global ~82%) and improved generalization.
AI.motivation: Address the challenges of natural whole-body coordination, real-time responsiveness, and robust generalization in humanoid control; explore how to scale BFMs by aligning learning framework, data, and architecture.
AI.method: Three-part approach: (1) motion-tracking learning paradigm reframing control as reproduction of integrated whole-body behaviors in the global frame; (2) balancing on-policy rollout quantity with reference motion diversity; (3) introducing an expressive, scalable Humanoid Transformer architecture that supports structured behavioral representations. Experiments conducted in simulation and real-world deployment.
AI.result: Demonstrates significant gains in control fidelity and task generalization; MPKPE on the test set reduced by >10% in local mode and by ~82% in global mode compared with existing humanoid controllers.
AI.conclusion: BFMs provide a principled, scalable foundation for general-purpose humanoid control; success hinges on coordinating learning paradigm, data diversity, and architecture to enable emergent structured representations of behavior.

title: MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research
summary: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

AI.tldr: Human-in-the-loop MathCoPilot unifies interactive proof planning, adaptive proving orchestration, and automated formalization into Lean, enabling researchers to guide high-level math while AI handles formal work. Evaluated on FormalMATH and PDE theorems across four LLMs; shows undergraduate-level success under favorable autoformalization but struggles with domain-specific proofs.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of autonomous LLM theorem provers by enabling continuous human guidance and a living proof blueprint to steer research while leveraging AI for detailed formalization and verification.
AI.method: Design and evaluate MathCoPilot with (1) interactive workbench and navigable proof blueprint; (2) adaptive knowledge-base search with Lean-integrated iterative verification; (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into Lean KB. Comparative evaluation of Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and others on FormalMATH subset and two real PDE theorems; scoring based on ability to produce verified Lean 4 proofs and identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs.
AI.result: Models can solve undergraduate problems with high success under favorable autoformalization; substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding; performance varies across models; demonstrated ability to detect errors in constructed proofs.
AI.conclusion: The human–AI symbiotic paradigm is promising for mathematical research, enabling direction control and formal verification, but further work is needed to close gaps in deep-domain understanding, reliability of autoformalization, and generalization across advanced theorems.

title: Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis
summary: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets. On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

AI.tldr: A new Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) method for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis, combining angular Gaussian contrastive learning, adaptive logit adjustments with bounded priors, and tail-aware augmentation. Demonstrates state-of-the-art macro performance on PTB-XL and Noc-ECG datasets, especially improving rare/morphologically unstable arrhythmias; code released on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed label distributions in ECG diagnosis reduce reliability, especially for rare but clinically important arrhythmias; existing rebalancing approaches overlook direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes.
AI.method: AG-SCL integrates: (1) an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch modeling full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings; (2) Adaptive Logit Adjustment learning bounded, label-state-specific prior corrections; (3) tail-aware augmentation that preserves morphology and protects the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band.
AI.result: On PTB-XL: balanced accuracy 0.838, sensitivity 0.709, specificity 0.968, mAP 0.495, TPR@5%FPR 0.778. On Noc-ECG: balanced accuracy 0.918, sensitivity 0.889, specificity 0.947, mAP 0.488, TPR@5%FPR 0.900. Largest gains in rare or morphologically unstable classes. Ablations confirm contributions of full-covariance modeling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation.
AI.conclusion: AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, increasing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining high specificity; code available at the provided GitHub link.

title: FoMoVLA: Bridging Visual Foresight and Motion Guidance for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://liauto-research.github.io/FoMoVLA
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in visuomotor policy learning, yet remain fundamentally reactive, mapping current observations and language to actions without explicit forward prediction of world dynamics. Existing visual foresight methods predict future visual states but lack explicit motion guidance: they show where to go but not how to get there. We argue that future feature prediction and sparse point tracking are naturally complementary: the former provides the goal state, while the latter captures the continuous motion path toward it. We propose FoMoVLA, a framework that augments VLA representations with explicit spatio-temporal supervision by jointly learning future feature foresight and sparse 2D point tracking, enhancing the continuous action policy. FoMoVLA introduces compact foresight tokens to decode future feature states, decodes sparse temporal 2D point trajectories to model compact geometric motion, and couples both through a lightweight future-conditioned cross-attention module that enables consistent reasoning between anticipated states and point dynamics. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and strong zero-shot generalization. Project page is available at https://liauto-research.github.io/FoMoVLA.

AI.tldr: FoMoVLA combines future feature foresight with sparse 2D point tracking to augment vision-language-action policies with explicit spatio-temporal dynamics, using a cross-attention module to align predicted states and point trajectories for improved visuomotor control.
AI.motivation: Current VLA models are predominantly reactive, mapping present observations and language to actions without explicit world dynamics. Visual foresight methods predict future states but lack integrated motion guidance. Jointly forecasting features and tracking sparse points provides complementary, goal-directed and motion-path information to guide continuous actions.
AI.method: Jointly train future feature foresight via compact foresight tokens to decode predicted future feature states and decode sparse temporal 2D point trajectories to model geometric motion. A lightweight future-conditioned cross-attention module couples these signals to enable consistent reasoning between anticipated states and point dynamics within a VLA framework.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on LIBERO, RoboCasa GR-1 Tabletop, and LIBERO-Plus shows state-of-the-art performance with strong zero-shot generalization across tasks and domains.
AI.conclusion: Explicit spatio-temporal supervision that fuses predicted future feature states and motion trajectories yields improved continuous visuomotor policies, suggesting a viable path toward forward dynamics-aware VLA models.

title: AHEAD: Anticipatory Hand-Driven Teleoperation via Human Intent Prediction
summary: Direct hand-driven teleoperation maps an operator's hand motion to robot end-effector commands at every frame, enabling precise control, but it requires constant monitoring and correction during approach, grasp, and placement, which can be slow and fatiguing. For repetitive pick-and-place tasks, supervisory (goal-based) teleoperation simplifies this process: the operator specifies goals/waypoints, and the robot executes the motion using planning algorithms. Yet, this introduces latency, as the robot must wait for the next command before it can plan and act. "How can we reduce robot reaction time while lowering operator workload?" To tackle this question, we present AHEAD, a real-time VR teleoperation system that anticipates operator intent to enable proactive, hand-driven control. In a digital twin, the operator performs pick-and-place naturally, using hand motion to convey high-level commands rather than a continuous robot trajectory. AHEAD processes a short window of 3D hand and head signals together with scene context through an attention-based classifier to predict the intended grasp object and placement slot. A state machine converts intent predictions into stable robot goals, enabling early motion while remaining stable under noisy predictions and corrective hand movements. AHEAD's intent prediction module achieves Top1 accuracy: 76% for grasp objects and 76% for target slots. Moreover, our user study shows AHEAD reduces robot reaction latency by 0.6 s (object) and 1.4 s (slot) relative to baselines. Participants also reported lower operator load, indicating faster robot responses while maintaining low operator effort in practice.

AI.tldr: AHEAD is a real-time VR teleoperation system that predicts operator intent to enable proactive hand-driven control, reducing robot reaction latency in pick-and-place tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce reaction latency and operator workload in teleoperation. Direct hand-driven control is precise but slow; supervisory planning helps but introduces waiting time.
AI.method: In a digital twin, 3D hand and head signals plus scene context feed an attention-based classifier to predict grasp object and placement slot. A state machine translates intents into robot goals for early but stable motion. Short temporal window and robust predictions handle noise and corrective movements.
AI.result: Intent prediction Top1 accuracy 76% for grasp objects and 76% for target slots. User study shows latency reductions: 0.6 s for object, 1.4 s for slot, with lower operator workload.
AI.conclusion: AHEAD demonstrates a viable approach to proactive teleoperation by anticipating user intent, achieving faster robot responses while maintaining stability and reduced effort; suitable for repetitive pick-and-place tasks; potential improvements could address long-horizon planning and robustness to perception noise.

title: SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize?
summary: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

AI.tldr: VLMs show limited strategic decision-making in soccer; SportD benchmark reveals suboptimal action choices and tendency to imitate familiar patterns.
AI.motivation: To determine whether vision-language models can make strategically valuable, quantitative decisions in dynamic sports tasks, beyond standard visual understanding.
AI.method: Introduce SportD, a benchmark of 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Evaluate three frontier VLMs against a possession-value model that identifies the action most increasing scoring probability. Measure optimal-action accuracy and action-value regret, and compare to professional players. Analyze biases in action variance and tendency to imitate players.
AI.result: Best VLMs choose the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, vs. 38.9% for pros. All models exhibit greater regret. VLMs favor lower-variance and lower-reward actions: shoot less often and make fewer progressive passes than optimal policy or real players. Models also imitate players’ actions even when suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation rather than full counterfactual evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SportD provides a value-grounded platform to quantify physical strategic reasoning in VLMs and highlights gaps between AI and human strategic play, enabling benchmark-driven improvement.

title: Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

AI.tldr: CPO introduces token-level contrastive disagreement for advantage shaping in RL with verifiable rewards, outperforming entropy-based methods and relating to On-policy Distillation; it improves generalization by balancing exploration and exploitation via correct/incorrect signals.
AI.motivation: Entropy-based RLVR struggles to distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its usefulness as a correctness signal. A token-level, contrastive, correctness-focused signal could improve policy optimization.
AI.method: Propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO) that quantifies token-level contrastive disagreement between a reference-guided distribution and a vanilla generation distribution to shape advantages. The theory supports its correctness signal; On-policy Distillation is shown as a special case with a teacher model; it also resolves the zero-advantage problem.
AI.result: Empirical benchmarks (in-domain and out-of-domain) show CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR while maintaining generalization. Analysis indicates correct responses aid exploration while incorrect ones promote exploitation, and balancing both yields best performance.
AI.conclusion: CPO provides a principled, effective correctness-aware policy optimization framework for RL with verifiable rewards, overcoming entropy-based limitations, unifying with On-policy Distillation, and highlighting the value of token-level contrastive signals for exploration-exploitation balance.

title: On the Disagreement in Perturbation-based xAI -- Benchmarking Perturbation Choices for Flood Detection from SAR Images
summary: Perturbation-based xAI methods are widely used to analyze the behavior and predictions of deep learning models. By altering input regions and measuring the resulting changes in class probabilities with respect to the original image, they assign relevance scores and generate heatmaps that reflect each region's contribution to the prediction. Despite their apparent simplicity, however, perturbation-based methods are sensitive to parameter choices. In this work, we focus on two key parameters of the perturbation pipeline, namely the patch geometry, including the size and shape of the perturbed regions, and the perturbation type, defined by the replacement scheme. Grounded in the use case of flood detection from Synthetic Aperture Radar imagery, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of how relevance estimation changes under different perturbation settings. Beyond visual inspection of the resulting relevance maps, we evaluate their consistency across perturbation strategies and their faithfulness to the model's reasoning. We demonstrate how different perturbation choices can steer the resulting relevance maps, yielding ambiguous and even contradictory explanations. Our findings emphasize the importance of methodological settings in perturbation-based xAI. They underscore the need to carefully inspect and evaluate perturbation choices and to treat them as an integral part when interpreting explanations, ensuring a robust understanding of both the explanations and model predictions.

AI.tldr: Perturbation-based xAI explanations are highly sensitive to patch geometry and replacement strategies, affecting relevance maps and their faithfulness; evaluation of perturbation settings is essential for robust interpretability.
AI.motivation: To determine how perturbation pipeline choices influence relevance estimation and explanations in SAR flood-detection models.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation of perturbation parameters (patch size/shape and perturbation type) across perturbation strategies, assessing consistency and faithfulness of the resulting heatmaps.
AI.result: Relevance maps vary substantially with perturbation choices; some settings produce ambiguous or contradictory explanations and reduced faithfulness, indicating that patch geometry and replacement schemes strongly shape interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Methodological settings in perturbation-based xAI must be carefully designed and reported, treating perturbation choices as integral to interpretation to ensure robust understanding of model predictions.

title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
summary: Recent robot foundation models operate with single-step or short-history visuomotor context. We introduce Test-Time-Training Robot Policies (RoboTTT), a robot model and training recipe that scale visuomotor context to 8K timesteps, three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies, without growing inference latency. At this context length, we unlock new robot capabilities: one-shot in-context imitation from human video demonstrations, on-the-fly policy improvement, robustness to perturbations, and stronger performance on multi-stage, long-horizon tasks. We also observe, for the first time, steady gains in closed-loop performance as pretraining context length scales. At its core, RoboTTT integrates Test-Time Training into robot foundation models such as Vision-Language-Action policies, yielding a sequence model whose recurrent state consists of fast weights, parameters updated by gradient descent during both training and inference, compressing histories into weight space and retrieving contextual information for long-context conditioning. To scale training context length, the recipe combines sequence action forcing with truncated backpropagation through time. On challenging real-robot manipulation tasks, RoboTTT improves overall performance by 87% over the single-step context baseline and fully completes a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task, which no baseline ever does. RoboTTT trained with 8K-timestep context outperforms the same model pretrained with 1K timesteps by 62%, suggesting context length as a new scaling axis for robot foundation models. Videos are available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/robottt/

AI.tldr: RoboTTT scales robot visuomotor context to 8K timesteps, enabling in-context imitation, online policy improvement, robustness, and long-horizon task mastery without added latency; shows context-length gains as a scaling axis and surpasses 1K baselines by substantial margins.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of short-context policies by increasing temporal context to improve performance on long-horizon tasks, enable in-context imitation from demonstrations, and allow system-wide robustness without incurring higher inference latency.
AI.method: Introduce RoboTTT: a Vision-Language-Action policy-based foundation model with a recurrent state of fast weights updated by gradient descent during both training and inference. Use test-time training, truncated backpropagation through time, and sequence action forcing to scale context to 8K timesteps. The model compresses histories into weight space and retrieves long-context information for conditioning.
AI.result: On real-robot manipulation tasks, achieves 87% improvement over single-step context baseline and completes a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task (unmatched by baselines). 8K-context yields 62% better performance than the same model pretrained with 1K timesteps. The policy shows steady gains in closed-loop performance as context length scales and exhibits robustness to perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Context length is a new scalable axis for robot foundation models. Integrating test-time training into long-context sequence models enables one-shot imitation, online improvement, and strong long-horizon performance without latency increase, suggesting broader potential for vision-language-action policies.

title: Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

AI.tldr: Action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations in VLA models; directly pushing action signals can destabilize language grounding, so the paper proposes Action QFormer, a query-based interface that reorganizes multimodal information into action-facing representations. This yields large gains in zero-shot sim-to-real navigation and action-generation accuracy while reducing out-of-distribution instruction issues.
AI.motivation: Treat action supervision as a shaping force on inherited multimodal representations rather than only a downstream objective, addressing the tension between learning action-compatible representations and preserving language grounding and object grounding.
AI.method: Introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before action generation. Evaluate in zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, analyze how action supervision reshapes representations.
AI.result: Significant quantitative gains: average closed-loop task success improves from 18.8% to 56.3%; fixed-instruction action-generation correctness rises from 22.5% to 75.5%; near-elimination of out-of-distribution instruction generations. Analyses show reduced broad upstream rewriting and preservation of targeted, constructive action-supervised adaptation, indicating more controlled shaping of representations.
AI.conclusion: Improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones but also better methods for selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information and controlling its shaping under action supervision.

title: PolyQ: Codesigning End-to-End Quantization Framework for Scalable Edge CPU LLM Inference
summary: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods offer either coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs. We present PolyQ, a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design for activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under a user-specified average-bit budget. PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from $\{2,3,4,8,16\}$, then uses a compile-time model compiler to permute and cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This turns fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment method for CPU-only inference. Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ provides stable quality scaling from 3--6\,b and improves perplexity by 2.4--32.1\% over prior methods at a 3\,b target. End-to-end measurements on three representative CPUs -- workstation, laptop, and mobile -- show that compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8\%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2\% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end. These results show that fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

AI.tldr: PolyQ enables fractional-bit, per-channel mixed-precision quantization on CPUs with a compiler-assisted workflow that groups channels into bit-homogeneous blocks and produces SIMD/LUT-friendly kernels.
AI.motivation: Existing low-bit CPU quantization methods either offer coarse points or require fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs; there is a need for practical, energy-efficient on-device inference with predictable behavior.
AI.method: Assign per-channel bit-widths from {2,3,4,8,16} under an average-bit budget; activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation; a compile-time model compiler permutes and clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks; generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels; merge compatible permutations across operators to maintain layout regularization on the runtime path; realize fractional-bit deployment on CPU-only inference.
AI.result: On Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B evaluated on WikiText-2, PolyQ achieves stable quality scaling from 3–6 bits and improves perplexity by 2.4–32.1% over prior methods at a 3-bit target. End-to-end measurements on workstation, laptop, and mobile CPUs show compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8%; prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget; energy-per-token overhead remains below 2% compared with an optimized LUT-based backend.
AI.conclusion: Fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

title: Clean-Reference Streaming Detection of Lens Occlusion and Photometric Transitions for Camera Tamper Monitoring
summary: A surveillance camera is an image sensor whose silent physical degradation invalidates every downstream consumer of its data. In-situ integrity alarms for such vision sensors require low false-alarm rates, bounded computation, and diagnosable behavior under nuisance illumination changes. This paper studies a deliberately narrow streaming integrity monitor for two low-cost sensor-fault signatures: texture-collapsing lens occlusion and abrupt photometric scene transition. The detector compares sampled luminance and local-gradient statistics with a clean-only sliding reference, applies coarse-grid structured-light rejection and mode/rapid-brightness suppression, and emits at most one notification per tamper episode. We formalize the decision predicates and derive a consistency rule for when rapid-brightness suppression makes the scene-transition path unreachable. On 320 in-scope controlled sequences, the default state machine attains 0.800 F1 and 0.822 balanced accuracy (significantly better paired correctness than the strongest baseline, though the F1 margin is not statistically resolved); on a magnitude-swept public audit it attains the highest partial AUC under a 5\% false-alarm budget, and a separate extended-stress FPR-constrained sweep reaches 0.925 recall at 0.025 false-positive rate. Public Xiph, Bremen IoT, and UHCTD diagnostics show the fixed predicates preserve low false alarms while recall concentrates inside the declared envelope (UHCTD in-scope covered recall 0.667 versus 0.016 out of scope), and a 9.09-camera-hour verified-negative public audit records zero false alarms. The method is best interpreted as an auditable sensor-health subsystem rather than a universal camera-tamper classifier.

AI.tldr: A targeted, auditable in-situ integrity monitor for low-cost surveillance cameras focusing on two tamper signatures; achieves strong detection with bounded computation and low false alarms, suitable as a sensor-health subsystem rather than a universal tamper classifier.
AI.motivation: Need for low false alarms, bounded compute, and diagnosable behavior under nuisance illumination changes to maintain trust in surveillance data.
AI.method: Streaming integrity monitor comparing sampled luminance and local-gradient statistics to a clean reference; applies coarse-grid rejection, mode/rapid-brightness suppression; one notification per tamper episode; formal predicates and a consistency rule; evaluation on multiple datasets.
AI.result: 0.800 F1, 0.822 balanced accuracy on 320 sequences; best partial AUC under 5% FPR; recall 0.925 at 0.025 FPR; zero false alarms in a verified-negative public audit; recall concentrated inside envelope; fixed predicates yield low false alarms.
AI.conclusion: Best viewed as an auditable sensor-health subsystem rather than a universal camera-tamper classifier.

title: Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination
summary: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $κ$-$τ$ apparatus: $κ$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $τ$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $κ^*$, inter-cluster $κ^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

AI.tldr: Analytic abductive reasoning framework using a κ-τ apparatus and causal clusters to manage competing latent-factor explanations under governance constraints, enabling legible, non-greedy decision support and guarding against premature convergence; demonstrated in epidemiology and cyber threat analysis.
AI.motivation: Develop the analytic mode of abductive reasoning as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment where competing latent factors coexist and interact. Provide governance conditions and a structured, shared representation to prevent premature convergence and misattribution, enhancing human–AI coordination under ambiguity.
AI.method: Formal core κ-τ apparatus: κ encodes epistemic interaction among hypotheses; τ sets a commitment threshold based on stakes. Introduces causal cluster—records participatory latent factors, weights, and interaction structure—with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster κ*, inter-cluster κ**). This structure guards against causal misattribution and supports suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object.
AI.result: Demonstrates the framework in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, highlighting legibility of suspended decomposition and its resistance to premature convergence. It offers competing explanatory scenarios weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidentiary basis to resolve among them, enabling sound action even amid unresolved ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: The framework advances human–AI reasoning by providing a structured, interpretable representation of competing explanations and their evidential support. It shifts decision-making away from single imposed answers toward governed, coexisting scenarios, improving resilience to misattribution and enabling coordinated action under uncertainty.

title: TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation
summary: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

AI.tldr: TIDE offers a trustworthy, interpretable battery degradation estimator that blends knowledge-guided priors, monotone residuals, and contextual learning, with symbolic distillation for concise interpretation, achieving ~19.7% accuracy gain over baselines.
AI.motivation: Battery health estimation in intelligent connected systems requires accurate, trustworthy decisions to avoid propagation of errors and maximize service life.
AI.method: A three-component backbone: knowledge-guided degradation prior for trust, monotone residual for interpretable aging-consistent refinement, contextual learning for battery-specific operational effects; backbone distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate for model-level interpretation.
AI.result: Across experiments, TIDE improves estimation fidelity by 19.7% over baselines, reduces aging-consistency violations via priors and monotone residuals, and provides component- and model-level interpretation.
AI.conclusion: TIDE enables practical, trustworthy, and interpretable battery health estimation for decision support in intelligent connected systems.

title: Rare Concept Generation via Counterfactual Inference in Diffusion Models
comment: Comments: 17 pages, 15 figures, to appear at ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: Rare concept generation focuses on synthesizing customized images conditioned on text prompts that describe objects with unusual attributes. Previous works failed to align the generated images with rare concepts, resulting in incorrect attribute rendering or inconsistent composition of concepts. Such failures, as we observed, stem from the inherent common knowledge bias in the training stage of diffusion models, where objects are strongly associated with their common attributes, making it difficult to break these associations when generating rare concepts. To address such challenges, in this paper, we propose a novel Counterfactual Inference-based Diffusion approach, dubbed CI-Diff. CI-Diff blocks the interference of the model's inherent common knowledge bias and utilizes the Natural Direct Effect to capture the independent influence of the text prompt of rare concepts on image generation so that decoupling the unusual attributes from the rare concepts. To this end, we reformulate the classifier-free guidance mechanism to highlight the atypical attributes. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to introduce causal inference into the rare concept generation task. Extensive experiments on the RareBench benchmark validate the superiority of CI-Diff over state-of-the-art diffusion models. Our code can be accessed from https://github.com/200204jzy/CI-Diff.

AI.tldr: Proposes CI-Diff, a causal-inference-guided diffusion model to generate rare concepts by decoupling atypical attributes from common attribute bias, achieving state-of-the-art on RareBench.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion models rely on common knowledge, causing incorrect attributes or poor composition when rendering rare concepts; need to isolate rare attributes from prevalent biases.
AI.method: Introduce counterfactual inference into diffusion; block common-knowledge bias; use Natural Direct Effect to quantify independent impact of rare concept prompts; reformulate classifier-free guidance to emphasize atypical attributes; first integration of causal inference into rare concept generation.
AI.result: Empirical results on RareBench show CI-Diff outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion models.
AI.conclusion: CI-Diff effectively mitigates bias and improves alignment with rare concepts; code available at GitHub.

title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers
summary: As Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers emerge as the core infrastructure for connecting LLMs with external tools, existing benchmarks leverage real-world MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities. However, these benchmarks overlook the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities within MCP servers, resulting in flawed assessments that fail to capture the agent's adaptability in changing tool landscapes. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{MCPEvol-Bench}, a novel benchmark for evaluating the task-solving capabilities of LLM agents under dynamic toolset evolution. Inspired by large-scale empirical study, we propose 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution within 123 MCP servers. We benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple versions of MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models struggle to adapt to evolving tools. For instance, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. These findings highlight the vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows, establishing MCPEvol-Bench as a standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

AI.tldr: MCPEvol-Bench assesses LLM-agent adaptability to evolving MCP tool interfaces using 11 mutation operators across 123 MCP servers; 12 LLMs are evaluated, showing performance drops under tool evolution and highlighting the need for adaptive agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks evaluating LLM agents typically assume static tool interfaces. Real MCP ecosystems evolve, requiring agents to adapt to changing tools and functionalities.
AI.method: Introduce 11 mutation operators to simulate tool evolution across 123 MCP servers; benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple evolved server versions to measure task-solving performance, and quantify planning/reasoning errors.
AI.result: GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 show performance declines of 13.7% and 14.4% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, with substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors, indicating vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows under tool evolution.
AI.conclusion: MCPEvol-Bench provides a standard benchmark to evaluate and improve LLM agent adaptability to dynamic tool environments in MCP contexts.

title: Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation
summary: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: Introduces Flow Matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) for conditional topology generation; trajectory-aware variant leverages physics-guided optimization history to improve stability and performance with fewer samples, extending to 3D.
AI.motivation: TO is computationally expensive due to repeated FEA and sensitivity updates; generative models risk violating structural feasibility and physical consistency. FMTO aims to enable rapid exploration by integrating physics history into a flow-based generative framework without additional inference-time optimization.
AI.method: Baseline: endpoint FMTO interpolates between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. Trajectory-aware FMTO uses volume-fraction-indexed BESO states to construct the probability path and target velocity field, thereby embedding physics-guided optimization history into the learned transport. Includes a path–velocity mismatch analysis to balance guidance strength and generation flexibility, with no inference-time optimization.
AI.result: FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO with moderate trajectory weight performs best. Extensions to trajectory-anchor density and 3D topology generation demonstrate broader applicability.
AI.conclusion: FMTO provides an efficient, physics-informed conditional topology generation framework. Proper trajectory design (moderate trajectory weight) enhances stability and performance, and the approach generalizes beyond 2D to 3D.

title: TAMF-VTON: Texture-Aware Mask-Free Virtual Try-On via High-Fidelity Image Synthesis
summary: Recent diffusion-based virtual try-on (VTON) methods remain limited by their reliance on segmentation masks, insufficient preservation of fine-grained textures, and limited support for arbitrary multi-garment compositions. Consequently, existing approaches still face significant challenges in real-world e-commerce deployment. We present TAMF-VTON, a texture-aware, mask-free framework that enables high-fidelity image synthesis under practical unconstrained conditions. Our method requires no human parsing or inpainting masks at inference time and supports diverse garment styles, categories, and quantities, enabling the simultaneous transfer of multiple items while preserving body structure and intricate texture details. This is achieved through a unified generative pipeline with three key components: (1) a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) adaptation scheme that enables efficient fine-tuning without compromising the base model's general editing capabilities; (2) a frequency-domain supervision mechanism that explicitly optimizes high-frequency spectral consistency to preserve high-fidelity textures; and (3) a robust data curation pipeline employing an adaptive inpainting strategy to simulate the inverse VTON process for high-quality training pair generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and perceptual quality. Optimized for efficiency, the model achieves inference in under 15 seconds per image on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with INT4 quantization. By combining mask-free operation, flexible multi-garment composition, faithful texture preservation, and efficient inference on consumer hardware, TAMF-VTON demonstrates a commercially viable solution for scalable deployment in real-world digital fashion scenarios. The project is available at https://www.style3d.ai/ai-photoshoot/virtual-clothing-try-on.

AI.tldr: Mask-free, texture-aware diffusion-based VTON enabling multi-item garment transfer with high fidelity and efficient inference.
AI.motivation: Overcome reliance on segmentation masks, preserve fine textures, and support arbitrary multi-garment compositions for real-world deployment.
AI.method: MoE adaptation for efficient fine-tuning; frequency-domain supervision to preserve high-frequency textures; adaptive inpainting-based data curation to generate high-quality training pairs; unified pipeline enabling simultaneous transfer of multiple garments without masks.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on quantitative metrics and perceptual quality; inference under 15 seconds per image on an RTX 4090 with INT4 quantization.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates mask-free operation, flexible multi-garment composition, faithful texture preservation, and efficient consumer-hardware deployment, offering commercial viability for scalable digital-fashion applications.

title: TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

AI.tldr: TopoAgent replaces linear planning with a self-evolving DAG-based agent that decomposes queries into atoms, isolates context, and uses adaptive atomic fission to refine bottlenecks, achieving state-of-the-art performance on math/physics/chemistry benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of monolithic, linear planning in MLLMs (visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, brittle execution) by enabling dynamic, context-isolated, topological reasoning.
AI.method: Front-end decomposer extracts visually-grounded atoms; organizes into a Directed Acyclic Graph based on dependencies; context isolation; adaptive atomic fission splits bottleneck nodes at runtime when tool capabilities are exceeded; self-evolving framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry show TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks; robust to noise and self-correcting.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic topological reasoning with DAG-based isolation and runtime refinement enhances autonomous scientific reasoning and mitigates common failures of linear agents.

title: Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization
summary: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware. However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: Introduces differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) to train deep continuous-time SNNs efficiently by mapping irregular presynaptic spikes to fixed time intervals, reducing memory and accelerating training while enabling deep CNN-like SNNs on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Overcome the prohibitive memory and computational cost of exact spike-time computation in training deep continuous-time SNNs, especially for TTFS coding with LIF neurons.
AI.method: Replace input-dependent spike-time candidates with M fixed time intervals using differentiable discretization; apply TTFS coding with LIF dynamics; introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization to organize layer-wise firing windows; demonstrate on dense LIF layers and convolutional SNNs; training on a single GPU.
AI.result: Memory complexity reduces from O(N_out N_in) to O(N_out M) for TTFS; peak memory ~100x reduction; training time ~20x faster; trains 9-layer CNN on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer CNN on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: DSTD enables scalable, memory-efficient training of deep continuous-time SNNs with substantial speedups while maintaining performance, opening the path to deeper SNNs on standard hardware.

title: An LLM-Based Automatic Sportscast Solution for Robot Soccer Matches
summary: RoboCup has always been a scenario to develop systems that solve real-world problems. Driven by the main goal of playing against the 2050 FIFA World Cup champions, the RoboCup Soccer leagues need to constantly measure how the research community is progressing. Computing visual statistics from match videos is a crucial way to track this evolution. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a fully autonomous, real-time sports commentator for RoboCup matches. By bridging the gap between raw kinematic tracking and natural language generation, our neuro-symbolic architecture extracts precise statistics from video streams and turns them into fluent, hallucination-free narration. The proposed system is capable of generating statistics and commentary both during live match streaming and in post-game analysis, easily adapting to the new dynamism of the league where different humanoid robots of different sizes share the field. Supplemental materials are available at https://lab-rococo-sapienza.github.io/MARIO/

AI.tldr: A real-time autonomous sports commentator for RoboCup that converts video-derived statistics into fluent, hallucination-free narration using a neuro-symbolic system, usable during live streams or post-game analysis and adaptable to heterogeneous humanoid robots on the field.
AI.motivation: Quantify progress in RoboCup research by extracting reliable statistics from match videos and generating natural language narration that bridges perception and reporting, enabling real-time and post-game analysis across varying robot platforms.
AI.method: Neuro-symbolic architecture that integrates precise statistics extraction from video streams with natural language generation to produce fluent, hallucination-free narration; operates in real time for live feeds and post-game analysis; designed to handle robots of different sizes sharing the field.
AI.result: Demonstrates autonomous statistics extraction and narration during live streaming and post-game review, with adaptation to dynamic RoboCup settings and heterogeneous robot teams; emphasizes fluency and accuracy without hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: The system provides a scalable bridge from kinematic tracking to language-based commentary for RoboCup, enabling real-time and retrospective analytics in a diverse, evolving competition, and offering a practical tool for evaluating and communicating match dynamics.

title: SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

AI.tldr: SmartRAG is an on-device, modular LLM system for private, low-latency QA on mobile, decomposing intelligence into Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. It uses EvoNER for continual NER expansion, stored in MRGraph, with a hybrid retrieval pipeline. Inference is kept on-device, with LLM invoked only for high-value tasks. A 1.7B-parameter backbone matches larger models on four QA benchmarks while running on commodity smartphones.
AI.motivation: To resolve edge-device constraints (privacy, latency, offline availability, budget) that compression alone cannot fix. The paper argues for decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary roles and enabling continual, cost-effective knowledge extraction without retraining large backbones.
AI.method: A four-module architecture (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking). EvoNER incrementally expands its label inventory via teacher-distilled updates, absorbing unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph. Retrieval combines graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is used only for labeling, planning, and answer synthesis.
AI.result: On TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MultiHopQA, a quantized 1.7B backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18× larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones with practical memory and latency.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that effective on-device, multi-hop QA is feasible with modular architecture and continual learning, reducing reliance on cloud or ultra-large models by distributing intelligence across specialized on-device components and selectively invoking an LLM.

title: Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

AI.tldr: GradDist quantifies bias in GNNs via gradient distribution analysis; Grad2Fair debiases using gradients without relying on demographics, enabling fairer predictions even without demographic data.
AI.motivation: To achieve group fairness in GNNs without access to demographic attributes or predictions, addressing the risk of biased constraints when using predicted demographics.
AI.method: Introduce GradDist, a gradient-based metric that measures bias by the distance between local modes of misclassification gradient distributions. Propose Grad2Fair, a gradient-guided debiasing approach that avoids demographic prediction and uses gradients to remove demographic signals during training.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world datasets shows Grad2Fair achieves superior fairness performance compared to baselines in most cases.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that stable, demographic-free group fairness in GNNs is feasible by leveraging gradient information; GradDist provides a bias quantification tool and Grad2Fair offers a practical debiasing method with open-source code.

title: Blurring Modal Boundaries: A Unified Survey from Single- to Multi-Modal Person Re-ldentification
summary: Person re-identification (ReID) serves as a critical component in intelligent surveillance systems, aiming to match identities across disjoint camera networks. While traditional methods primarily rely on single-modal RGB imagery, they are often constrained by environmental challenges such as low illumination and occlusion. To overcome these limitations, the field is rapidly evolving toward cross-modal and multi-modal paradigms. This survey presents a comprehensive overview of this transition, systematically reviewing key cross-modal tasks including visible-infrared (VI-ReID), text-image (TI-ReID), sketch-based (Sketch-ReID), and the emerging Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) ReID, which extends perception beyond direct visibility. Furthermore, we examine tri-spectral and multi-modal fusion ReID, discussing how complementary information from diverse sensors enhances robustness. Beyond summarizing datasets, challenges, and methodologies, we propose a Transformer-based baseline framework for visible-infrared ReID, designed to effectively capture modality-invariant features. Finally, based on the current landscape, we outline several promising directions for future research.

AI.tldr: Survey of cross-modal and multi-modal person re-identification (ReID), covering VI-ReID, TI-ReID, Sketch-ReID, NLOS ReID, and multi-modal fusion; introduces a Transformer-based VI-ReID baseline; discusses datasets, challenges, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Overcomes limitations of RGB ReID under poor illumination, occlusion, and non-visual sensing by leveraging cross-modal, tri-/multi-modal information; extends perception beyond direct visibility.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of cross-modal ReID tasks; aggregation of datasets and methodologies; proposes a Transformer-based baseline for visible-infrared ReID; discusses fusion strategies and tri-spectral modalities.
AI.result: Comprehensive synthesis of the field, including datasets, challenges, and methods; presents a Transformer-based baseline that captures modality-invariant features; provides guidelines and benchmarks; no empirical results reported in abstract.
AI.conclusion: Field of cross-modal and multi-modal ReID is advancing; outlines future research directions, challenges, and potential Transformer-based architectures.

title: Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications
summary: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

AI.tldr: Kaleidoscope is an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review with reliability-gated automated scoring by LLM judges; early evidence from real-world pilots across multiple use cases.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks often fail to capture the user, context, and governance requirements of real-world AI deployments; evaluations are a bottleneck for scalable, policy-compliant AI in regulated settings, especially in the public sector.
AI.method: Kaleidoscope combines persona-based test generation, contextual rubrics, and human review in an iterative workflow; LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with human-provided labels meets a configured threshold, enabling reliable automations while preserving oversight; evaluated through a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases with 108 annotated Q&A pairs, spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions, using custom rubrics for judges.
AI.result: Early pilot results show the workflow yields end-to-end features for reliable automated scoring; evidence from 3 weeks across four use cases and 108 annotated Q&A pairs across four domains and 14 dimensions demonstrates feasibility and useful inspection capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Kaleidoscope provides a practical, inspectable framework for reliable automated evaluation in policy- and governance-driven AI deployments, enabling iterative, human-in-the-loop scoring that scales with real-world applications.

title: MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits
summary:
We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

AI.tldr: MESHA is a mechanism-enforced BAI algorithm for strategic linear bandits that uses uniform sampling and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger to mitigate strategic misreporting. The authors derive an upper bound on MESHA's failure probability under a fixed budget T for any Nash equilibrium and show that OD-based sampling can fail due to strategic manipulation. Empirical results indicate MESHA outperforms both OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines.
AI.motivation: To address best-arm identification under strategic manipulation where arms can misreport features to increase their chance of being identified as the best arm; existing optimal-design based methods may be vulnerable to such reporting. The work analyzes a mechanism-enforced approach under Nash equilibria.
AI.method: Introduce MESHA, combining a naive uniform sampling rule with an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC) to detect and discard arms with large deviations in reported features. The analysis considers arbitrary Nash equilibria and derives an upper bound on failure probability under budget T. It also contrasts with OD-based (G-optimal design) sampling, arguing such methods can starve the true best arm. Empirical studies compare MESHA against OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines.
AI.result: Theoretical: upper bound on MESHA's failure probability under budget T for any Nash equilibrium; demonstration that OD-based designs fail in strategic settings due to manipulated features. Empirical: MESHA outperforms both OD-based and feature-agnostic baselines across experiments.
AI.conclusion: MESHA provides a robust BAI approach in strategic linear bandits by combining uniform sampling with an epoch-wise Grim Trigger. It mitigates manipulation, offers provable reliability under budget constraints, and exposes weaknesses of OD-based strategies in adversarial settings. Potential extensions include broader strategic environments and tighter bounds.

title: Physics-Informed Diffusion for Biomechanically Plausible 3D Sign Language Generation
summary: Sign language production, which generates continuous 3D skeletal motion from spoken language input, must simultaneously satisfy two constraints: semantic fidelity, so that a deaf viewer can recognize the intended sequence of glosses, and biomechanical plausibility, so that the generated skeleton respects anatomical constraints. Existing approaches optimize semantic reconstruction through coordinate-based objectives that treat the skeleton as an unstructured vector, thus allowing for bone length drift, joint angle violations, and temporarily locked fingers. We introduce PIDiffSign, a physics-informed diffusion model for gloss-to-pose translation that incorporates anatomical constraints into both the architecture and training objective. The model uses a Transformer encoder-decoder, where the decoder is conditioned on the diffusion time step through adaptive zero-initialized layer normalization and cross-attends to gloss representations. A differentiable geometry module enforces bone length consistency and biologically valid joint angles throughout generation. Training combines anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints with a contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance for semantically conditioned sampling. Experiments on the PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily benchmarks show consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality.
