These results demonstrate that physics-informed diffusion improves both motion realism and semantic fidelity for sign language generation.

AI.tldr: Physics-informed diffusion for gloss-to-pose sign language generation (PIDiffSign) that enforces anatomical constraints, improving semantic fidelity and biomechanical realism over baselines.
AI.motivation: Sign language generation must satisfy semantic fidelity (recognizable gloss sequences) and biomechanical plausibility (anatomically valid poses). Prior coordinate-based optimization allows bone-length drift, invalid joint angles, and awkward finger configurations.
AI.method: A Transformer encoder-decoder with a diffusion-time conditioned decoder (adaptive zero-initialized layer norm and cross-attention to gloss). A differentiable geometry module enforces bone-length consistency and valid joint angles. Training combines anthropomorphic, kinematic, angular, and finger-joint constraints with a contrastive gloss-pose alignment loss and classifier-free guidance for semantically conditioned sampling.
AI.result: On PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily, PIDiffSign shows consistent improvements over a strong diffusion baseline in pose accuracy, joint-angle correctness, distributional realism, and back-translation quality.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating physics into diffusion-based sign language generation yields gains in both motion realism and semantic fidelity, addressing key biomechanical and semantic constraints.

title: Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026, Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA)
summary: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

AI.tldr: Perception-RFT with GRPO enables direct grounding in multimodal document QA by bypassing reasoning traces, challenging the necessity of reasoning in RL and showing perception-based policies can outperform reasoning-enabled RL at scale. It reveals SFT saturation and RL instability extend to multimodal settings, uncovers Grounding Divergence (semantic robustness vs geometric precision), and shows early SFT→RL transition can cut data requirements by ~65%.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on large annotated datasets (SFT) and verbose reasoning traces (RL) while maintaining or improving grounding accuracy and efficiency in multimodal document QA.
AI.method: Propose Perception-RFT framework using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to learn direct alignment of visual features with structured grounding outputs, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens. Construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings to test necessity of reasoning. Conduct fine-grained optimization analysis on Qwen3-VL-4B, and evaluate two OOD benchmarks (4,828 samples) to assess Grounding Divergence. Evaluate transition from SFT to RL.
AI.result: Reasoning-enabled models shed reasoning traces during training, converging to perception-based policies at 4B params; per-query inference token length reduced by >60%; reasoning-enabled RL underperforms relative to perception-only training. Grounding Divergence observed: a trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on OOD data. Early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.
AI.conclusion: GRPO-based perception-focused training can match or exceed the performance of RL with explicit reasoning in multimodal document QA, with substantial gains in efficiency and robustness. The findings suggest generalizable saturation/instability dynamics from text to multimodal, and highlight a trade-off in grounding quality that depends on training regime. An early SFT→RL transition offers data-efficient path to competitive performance.

title: Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering
summary: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

AI.tldr: VoICE is a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted k-means that generates least-cost, actionable counterfactuals by projecting onto the weighted Voronoi region of the target cluster, incorporating feature weights into the geometry and objective, with bounds and contraction to limit extrapolation; it outperforms a leading pairwise boundary baseline on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The paper tackles explainability for clustering, where labels are absent and decisions depend on cluster geometry. It extends counterfactual explanations from supervised settings to clustering by inducing explanations from the Voronoi geometry of a weighted k-means partition, enabling actionable, minimal changes that switch to a target cluster.
AI.method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, integrating feature weights into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective. Target regions are intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted toward their centroids to limit extrapolation and boundary sensitivity.
AI.result: Empirically, VoICE consistently yields valid target-cluster membership across benchmark datasets, whereas the leading pairwise baseline fails to guarantee validity in some cases.
AI.conclusion: VoICE provides valid, parsimonious, actionability-constrained counterfactual explanations for feature-weighted k-means by leveraging the Voronoi geometry, improving interpretability and reliability of cluster assignments.

title: Rotational Motion-Induced Error Compensation for Phase-Shifting Profilometry-Based Eye Reconstruction
summary: With the proliferation of immersive Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) for Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR), reliable and high-precision eye tracking has become increasingly important. Conventional 2D image-based methods offer low system complexity but remain limited in stability, accuracy, and robustness. Three-dimensional ocular surface reconstruction can provide richer geomet-ric information, and structured light profilometry is particularly attractive because it enables dense and accurate surface measurement. However, Phase-Shifting Profilometry (PSP), which estimates phase from sequentially acquired fringe images, is highly susceptible to motion-induced errors when the eye rotates between frames. This study proposes a rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction. Relative eye rotation is estimated from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model in a spherical-coordinate domain. The estimated motion is then used to compensate for camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors caused by inter-frame rotation. A region-wise optimization strategy is further introduced to reduce residual artifacts by inde-pendently refining the compensation strength in different ocular regions. Experiments with a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion demonstrate that the proposed method substantially suppresses motion-induced deformation and improves reconstruction accuracy. An additional experiment with a non-spherical rigid object indicates that the compensation principle is not restricted to spherical eye geometry. These results establish a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction toward future high-precision eye tracking in immersive environments.

AI.tldr: Rotational motion compensation framework for PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction using image-derived inter-frame rotation estimates from a 3D eye model in spherical coordinates; region-wise optimization; validated on rotating fake eye and a non-spherical object; improves stability and accuracy for immersive VR/AR eye tracking.
AI.motivation: PSP-based eye surface reconstruction offers high accuracy but is sensitive to motion between frames when the eye rotates, limiting robustness in dynamic VR/AR settings. A reliable method to compensate inter-frame rotational motion could enable stable, high-precision 3D eye tracking.
AI.method: Estimate relative eye rotation from image-based motion cues using a user-specific 3D eye model in a spherical-coordinate domain. Use the estimated rotation to correct camera-pixel mismatch and phase-shift errors in PSP. Introduce a region-wise optimization to independently refine compensation strength across ocular regions, reducing residual artifacts.
AI.result: Experiments with a rotating fake eye under non-uniform motion show substantially reduced motion-induced deformation and improved reconstruction accuracy. A non-spherical rigid object experiment indicates the compensation principle generalizes beyond spherical eye geometry.
AI.conclusion: The proposed rotational motion compensation framework provides a practical basis for stable PSP-based dynamic 3D eye reconstruction, supporting future high-precision eye tracking in immersive environments.

title: SUFLECA: Scaling Up Feature Learning for CAD-to-image Alignment
summary: CAD-to-image alignment aims to estimate an object's 9D pose (rotation, translation, and anisotropic scale) from a single RGB image, enabling applications in robotics and augmented reality. Recent zero-shot methods use visual foundation models to match image regions to CAD models, yet typically their correspondences are appearance-driven and degrade under occlusion or sim-to-real domain shift. To address these limitations, we introduce SUFLECA (Scaling Up Feature LEarning for CAD Alignment), a weakly-supervised framework for zero-shot CAD alignment with two key contributions. First, SUFLECA scales up geometry-grounded feature learning from pretrained visual representations through Normalized Object Coordinates (NOCs) supervision on 674K images spanning 12 real and synthetic datasets, learning compact geometry-aware features that generalize across domains. Second, we propose a geometrically consistent matching algorithm that establishes reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences. Together, these contributions enable accurate, sub-second alignment per object instance without iterative pose refinement. On ScanNet25k, SUFLECA achieves 33.4%/42.3% category/instance accuracy, outperforming, with a smaller computational footprint, the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, even surpassing fully supervised methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/snt-arg/SUFLECA

AI.tldr: SUFLECA enables efficient zero-shot CAD-to-image alignment by combining geometry-grounded NOC supervision with a geometrically consistent, one-to-one CAD-to-image matching algorithm, achieving sub-second inference and strong cross-domain accuracy that surpasses zero-shot baselines and even some supervised methods on ScanNet25k.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot CAD alignment often relies on appearance cues and degrades under occlusion and sim-to-real shift. A geometry-aware, domain-general representation and a robust matching mechanism are needed to improve reliability and efficiency across real and synthetic data.
AI.method: 1) Scale up geometry-grounded feature learning via Normalized Object Coordinates (NOC) supervision on ~674k images from 12 real/synthetic datasets to learn compact, geometry-aware features. 2) Introduce a geometrically consistent matching algorithm to establish reliable one-to-one CAD-to-image correspondences without iterative pose refinement.
AI.result: On ScanNet25k: category accuracy 33.4% and instance accuracy 42.3%. Outperforms the strongest zero-shot baseline by 10.3/12.2 percentage points and, for the first time on this benchmark, surpasses fully supervised methods. Achieves sub-second per-object alignment with a small computational footprint; code released.
AI.conclusion: The combination of scalable, geometry-grounded feature learning with a geometry-consistent matching strategy yields robust, fast zero-shot CAD alignment with strong cross-domain generalization, closing the gap with supervised approaches.

title: InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring
summary: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

AI.tldr: Multimodal in-cabin emotion dataset InCarEmo with RGB/IR video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text; supports emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring; includes Chinese and auxiliary English benchmark; baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods; analyzes modality-missing and noise robustness; highlights benefits of fusion and challenges in real-world conditions.
AI.motivation: Addresses the scarcity of public in-cabin affective datasets that include linguistic/interactivity cues, enabling robust, interpretable driver-state understanding and safer human-vehicle interaction.
AI.method: Data collection of multimodal signals in scripted in-cabin scenarios across varied lighting and driving contexts; multimodal fusion baselines; cross-lingual English benchmark; analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions.
AI.result: Demonstrates advantages of multimodal fusion; provides comprehensive baseline suite; identifies remaining challenges under noise and low-light conditions.
AI.conclusion: InCarEmo establishes a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable in-cabin affective understanding, supporting emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring, with cross-lingual evaluation.

title: What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity
summary: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

AI.tldr: Improved convergence guarantees for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity; near-tight upper bounds and matching lower bounds; extends the Patel et al. principle beyond strongly convex to general convex; also provides a serial SGD lower bound showing high-curvature effect of rare clients.
AI.motivation: Clarify when Local SGD is advantageous under realistic data heterogeneity by leveraging a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption; extend the insight from strongly convex to general convex objectives.
AI.method: Prove enhanced convergence bounds for Local SGD under bounded second-order heterogeneity for general convex objectives; derive improved lower bounds for Local SGD; establish near-tightness of upper bounds; derive a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement to illustrate the impact of rare high-curvature clients.
AI.result: Convergence guarantees for Local SGD on general convex functions under the assumption; improved upper bounds; improved (nearly tight) lower bounds; a new lower bound for serial SGD with replacement demonstrating the heterogeneity effect.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD by validating that bounded second-order heterogeneity governs efficiency in general convex settings; the results connect upper and lower bounds and showcase the role of heterogeneity, including rare high-curvature clients, via a serial SGD bound.

title: Selectivity Drives Efficiency: Dataset Pruning for Visual Place Recognition
summary: Recent visual place recognition (VPR) studies have increasingly relied on large-scale datasets to train more robust and discriminative models. Although this trend significantly improves recognition performance, it also introduces substantial storage and training costs, especially when new architectures or training strategies need to be repeatedly developed and evaluated. Dataset pruning (DP) provides a promising way to improve data efficiency by retaining only informative training data. However, conventional DP methods mainly follow the sample-wise classification paradigm, which overlooks the relation-dependent training nature of VPR, where supervision is typically formed by image pairs rather than independent images. To address this issue, we propose a place-wise dataset pruning framework tailored for VPR. Instead of pruning individual images, our method treats each place as the basic pruning unit and introduces two complementary novel metrics, i.e., intra-place diversity (IPD) and inter-place similarity (IPS), to evaluate the training value of each place. By jointly considering these two metrics, our method ranks all places and constructs a compact yet informative coreset, thereby allowing the pruned dataset to still support the training of robust and discriminative VPR models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines under different pruning ratios while reducing selection and training costs. Moreover, by pruning a merged dataset roughly 3.5$\times$ the size of GSV-Cities to a comparable scale, our coreset maintains highly competitive performance, achieving 94.5\% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0\% R@1 on Nordland with only NetVLAD. Codes will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Place-wise dataset pruning for VPR using IPD and IPS to create a compact coreset that preserves accuracy while reducing data/training costs, outperforming conventional sample-wise DP baselines.
AI.motivation: VPR models rely on image-pair supervision and large-scale datasets, which incurs high storage and training costs. Conventional DP methods prune samples individually, ignoring the relational nature of VPR data. A place-level pruning unit could better preserve training signal by considering inter- and intra-place relationships.
AI.method: Define each place as a pruning unit. Introduce two metrics: intra-place diversity (IPD) to measure diversity within a place, and inter-place similarity (IPS) to measure redundancy across places. Rank places by a joint score based on IPD and IPS, and construct a coreset by selecting top-ranked places. Train VPR models on the pruned dataset and evaluate against baselines. Validate on merged datasets (e.g., merging datasets to 3.5x GSV-Cities) and standard VPR benchmarks (MSLS-val, Nordland) using NetVLAD.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DP baselines across pruning ratios. The pruned coreset maintains strong performance while reducing selection/training costs. On a merged dataset (~3.5× smaller than GSV-Cities), the approach achieves 94.5% R@1 on MSLS-val and 97.0% R@1 on Nordland with NetVLAD.
AI.conclusion: Place-wise DP with IPD and IPS is effective for data-efficient VPR, enabling a compact yet informative training set that preserves discriminative power and reduces computational costs. The approach shows strong cross-dataset transferability and practical relevance, with public code promised.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
summary: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

AI.tldr: BadWAM introduces World-Action Drift Attacks, a unified framework to evaluate vulnerabilities of World-Action Models (WAMs) via small visual perturbations that misalign imagined futures and executed actions. It defines two attack modes—action-only and imagination-preserving—covering a spectrum from direct action hijacking to stealthier misalignment where the model seems to imagine a plausible future but acts desynchronized. Empirical results show substantial task-performance degradation under closed-loop control; imagination-preserving attacks reveal that modest future-regularization can sustain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift, exposing a WAM-specific vulnerability.
AI.motivation: WAMs aim to couple action generation with future world prediction to improve robustness, interpretability, and safety. The paper interrogates this assumption by exploring an attack surface that can break the alignment between imagined futures and executed actions.
AI.method: Define BadWAM with two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. Implement action-only adversarial attacks to drive task failure, and imagination-preserving adversarial attacks to shift actions while keeping the model’s predicted future close to the clean imagination. Evaluate across WAM variants under closed-loop execution, measuring task success/drop in performance and imagination drift; examine effect of regularization on attack effectiveness.
AI.result: Attack efficacy is high: e.g., action-only attack reduces success from 96.5% to 43.1%. Imagination-preserving attacks reveal vulnerability where moderate future-preserving regularization maintains strong attack performance while reducing imagination drift, indicating WAM-specific weaknesses even when imagined futures appear plausible.
AI.conclusion: WAMs exhibit vulnerabilities to world-action drift attacks not captured by purely predictive or interpretability-based analyses. The BadWAM framework provides a structured way to assess and compare attack surfaces, emphasizing the need for defenses addressing both action hijacking and misalignment between imagined futures and actual actions.

title: AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery
summary: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

AI.tldr: VLMs can infer building typologies from street-view imagery and reach about 70% accuracy versus expert labels, with Chain-of-Thought prompting improving stability. AI explanations reveal reliance on visual cues; humans use broader context and domain knowledge. VLMs show promise as scalable, complementary tools for urban analysis, warranting further study of reasoning and limitations.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether leading Vision-Language Models can automate building-typology classification from urban imagery and to compare AI reasoning with expert human judgment.
AI.method: Assess multiple state-of-the-art VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) using different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, especially Chain-of-Thought prompts. Compare VLM predictions to expert-labelled ground truth and analyze AI explanations by keyword probability to understand reasoning patterns.
AI.result: Average accuracy ~70% in building-typology classification; Chain-of-Thought prompts yield more stable performance; AI explanations emphasize visual cues, while experts use broader contextual/domain knowledge; VLMs can approximate expert capabilities at scale.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can serve as complementary, scalable tools for urban analysis, offering strengths in visual pattern recognition. The study highlights the potential and the need to understand AI reasoning and limitations to effectively integrate AI into automation workflows for urban analysis.

title: GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

AI.tldr: A unified framework (GAttNHP) for Temporal Knowledge Graphs combining continuous-time self-attention Hawkes processes, semantic soft-grouping for shared excitation, and non-crossing quantile regression to handle heavy tails; achieves state-of-the-art on six datasets for entity and time prediction, with strongest gains on long-tail chains.
AI.motivation: Forecasting on TKGs is hindered by long-range dependencies, inter-chain interactions, and heavy-tailed inter-arrival times; a single architecture addressing all three can improve predictive calibration and accuracy.
AI.method: 1) Self-attention encoder to model continuous-time point processes and lingering history; 2) Semantic soft-grouping to convert Hawkes priors into a cross-attention mask enabling group-wise excitation sharing; 3) Non-Crossing Quantile regression head for calibrated, monotone quantiles of time predictions.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on six benchmark TKG datasets for both entity and time prediction; ablation studies show largest gains on long-tail event chains where prior methods struggle.
AI.conclusion: GAttNHP effectively unifies three modeling challenges in TKG forecasting via attention-based Hawkes processes, with robust time prediction via NCQ and improved scalability through soft-grouping; promising for continued improvements on long-tail dynamics.

title: FlashDecoder: Real-Time Latent-to-Pixel Streaming Decoder with Transformers
summary: Real-time video generation demands fast decoding as much as fast denoising, yet current latent video diffusion models rely on 3D convolutional decoders that are slow and memory-intensive at high resolutions or for long video. We introduce FlashDecoder, a fast, memory-efficient pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes latents to pixels frame by frame. At each step, the current frame attends only to a fixed-size window of past frames through a rolling KV cache. The fixed temporal window keeps decoding fast and memory bounded regardless of video length, enabling constant-latency streaming. Because frames are processed sequentially, temporal causality is enforced without explicit attention masks, enabling training at resolutions up to 1080p and matching the reconstruction quality of convolutional decoders. On the Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 latent spaces, FlashDecoder matches each convolutional decoder in reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55dB vs. 41.49dB PSNR at 1080p) while decoding 3.6x-4.7x faster with up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU. With architecture-aware inference optimizations, the speedup widens to 12x.

AI.tldr: FlashDecoder is a pure-Transformer video decoder that enables real-time, constant-latency decoding of latent video diffusion models by processing frames sequentially with a fixed-size rolling KV cache, achieving large speed and memory benefits with comparable quality to 3D conv decoders at up to 1080p.
AI.motivation: Real-time video generation requires fast decoding and low memory usage; existing latent video diffusion decoders rely on slow, memory-intensive 3D convolutions at high resolution or long durations.
AI.method: Introduce FlashDecoder, a fast, memory-efficient pure-Transformer video decoder that decodes frames sequentially. Each frame attends only to a fixed-size window of past frames using a rolling KV cache, enforcing temporal causality without explicit masks. Operates at resolutions up to 1080p and on Wan2.1/2.2 latent spaces, with architecture-aware inference optimizations.
AI.result: Matches convolutional decoders in reconstruction quality (e.g., 41.55dB vs. 41.49dB PSNR at 1080p on Wan2.1/2.2) while decoding 3.6x–4.7x faster and using up to 11x less memory on a single H100 GPU; speedups reach ~12x with optimizations.
AI.conclusion: A practical, real-time decoder for latent video diffusion with constant latency and reduced memory, enabling streaming-style video generation without sacrificing quality at 1080p.

title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report
summary: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

AI.tldr: GIRAI 2026 tracks 68,138 data points across 38 indicators in five AI-governance dimensions to assess enforcement and protections; policy adoption is rising but protections remain largely non-binding, with limited government-algorithm transparency and evidence of unacceptable-risk deployments, signaling a need for stronger, rights-based oversight and redress mechanisms.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether country-level responsible-AI commitments translate into enforceable protections and effective governance, and to compare progress across regions and over time.
AI.method: Global network of 135 country researchers collected 68,138 data points across 38 indicators organized into three pillars: government policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), plus documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems; data span November 2023 to September 2025; a composite score of 100 is derived to rank countries.
AI.result: 126 of 135 countries have at least one government AI policy/initiative among the 17 policy indicators; Global South accounts for 203 of 306 new framework indicators since the first edition, but 78% of their frameworks are non-binding versus 42% in the Global North; transparency/Explainability is strongest indicator with 58% having some framework, but only 18% require public disclosure of government algorithms; credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI exists in 35 countries; overall findings urge shifting from framework adoption to enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight, and accessible redress.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI governance must move beyond adopting frameworks toward enforceable protections, adequately resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress mechanisms.

title: ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation
summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ChronoQG, a temporally expressive benchmark for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG). It fills a gap in static KGQG benchmarks by encoding temporal validity, event ordering, and constraint-driven answer derivation. It provides four datasets (16,011 questions) from heterogeneous temporal KGs and shows current KGQG methods struggle with multi-constraint and hard temporal types, establishing ChronoQG as a challenging testbed.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQG benchmarks rely on static knowledge graphs and ignore temporal dimensions, which can mislead question fidelity regarding temporal validity and answer-determination constraints.
AI.method: ChronoQG offers (i) a temporal-constraint taxonomy, (ii) topology–temporal subgraph sampling, and (iii) trace-grounded question generation. It constructs four temporally expressive, hop-bounded benchmark datasets totaling 16,011 verified questions from heterogeneous temporal KGs.
AI.result: Evaluation across LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines shows poor performance in preserving temporal constraints, especially with multiple constraints and complex constraint types; demonstrates a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG.
AI.conclusion: ChronoQG is a pioneering, temporally faithful benchmark framework for TKGQG, highlighting the need for temporally aware question generation and providing resources to advance this area; prompts future work on richer temporal reasoning and broader datasets.

title: TanGO: Training-Free 3D Editing via Tangent-Space Guidance and Optimization
summary: While recent flow-matching 3D generative models (e.g., VecSet) adopt structured representations, their tokens share global context, causing conventional training-free editing to suffer from semantic artifacts such as collapsed preserved regions or incomplete transformations. To address this, we propose TanGO, a training-free framework that enables adaptive per-token steering in the tangent space of generative dynamics. To realize this selective control, we formulate a one-step optimal control rule and determine the strength of each token's control signal using a von Mises-Fisher inspired directional discrepancy derived from the source and target velocity fields. Experiments show that TanGO substantially reduces structural artifacts and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing 3D editing baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/siw00-lim/TanGO.

AI.tldr: TanGO introduces training-free, per-token adaptive control in the tangent space of 3D generative dynamics to reduce editing artifacts and achieve state-of-the-art 3D editing performance.
AI.motivation: Training-free editing on flow-matching 3D generators (e.g., VecSet) suffers from semantic artifacts due to tokens sharing global context, causing collapsed preserved regions or incomplete transformations. A per-token steering mechanism in the tangent space can mitigate these artifacts.
AI.method: TanGO formulates a one-step optimal control rule for adaptive per-token steering. The strength of each token's control signal is determined using a von Mises–Fisher–inspired directional discrepancy computed from the source and target velocity fields, enabling selective, token-level edits in the tangent space of generative dynamics.
AI.result: Empirical results show TanGO substantially reduces structural artifacts and achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing 3D editing baselines. The authors provide public code at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: TanGO enables effective, training-free, per-token control in 3D generative editing, significantly improving edit quality by mitigating artifacts and offering competitive performance.

title: Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models
summary: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

AI.tldr: Transcoders (per-layer transcoders) are used to build attribution graphs to analyze deception in language models, revealing deception-related features that drive outputs and enabling monitoring for safety.
AI.motivation: Understand the mechanistic basis of deceptive behavior and enable early detection of security vulnerabilities; leverage transcoders for mechanistic interpretability (MI).
AI.method: Apply pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) to a Qwen3-4B model; construct attribution graphs of feature activations and inter-feature dependencies; perform feature steering and circuit analysis to identify deception-related features and build a dictionary; compare deceptive vs non-deceptive responses.
AI.result: Deception-related features exert stronger influence on outputs; predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses; deception appears to emerge from internal model mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Transcoders show promise for MI and safety monitoring, enabling detection and mitigation of malicious behaviors; further evaluation across models and tasks is warranted.

title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
summary: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

AI.tldr: A decision-theoretic framework for evaluating epistemic uncertainty via regret-based selective prediction, showing that risk/regret/coverage diagnostics outperform correlation-based disentanglement metrics and can yield rank inversions with proxy tasks.
AI.motivation: Current uncertainty scores do not align with Bayes-optimal decision strategies for tasks like OOD detection and active learning; there is a need for principled evaluation reflecting operational utility.
AI.method: Adopts an epistemic reject-option framework; formulates selective prediction as constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret; proves the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties.
AI.result: Unifies theory and exposes weaknesses of standard disentanglement metrics; proposes evaluating the achievable risk, regret, and coverage surface as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility; empirical benchmarks show decision-theoretic rankings can diverge from proxy-task rankings, including rank inversions between methods.
AI.conclusion: A risk-regret-coverage diagnostic offers a more meaningful evaluation of epistemic uncertainty and disentanglement, highlighting the misalignment between proxy metrics and operational performance and calling for theory-guided benchmarks.

title: Benchmarking Face Recognition without Real Faces
summary: Synthetic face datasets have become effective enough to train face recognition models with accuracy rivaling that of models trained on real photographs. This progress sidesteps the ethical and legal burdens of collecting real biometric data, yet evaluation has not kept pace. Even studies that train entirely on synthetic images still rely on real-face benchmarks to measure performance, leaving the privacy problem only half solved. We ask whether synthetic datasets can replace real benchmarks for face recognition evaluation. We test 12 synthetic datasets against 7 established real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models that span both convolutional and transformer architectures. Our evaluation covers biometric verification metrics, similarity score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and the underlying distributional properties of each dataset. Benchmarking fidelity varies widely across the synthetic candidates, but the two strongest, MorphFace and Vec2Face, reproduce the relative behavior of real benchmarks and reach agreement levels that fall within the natural disagreement already observed among the real benchmarks themselves. These results establish that well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, moving the field closer to a fully synthetic and privacy-preserving pipeline for both training and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: Two synthetic face datasets (MorphFace, Vec2Face) can reproduce the ranking behavior of real face-recognition benchmarks, enabling privacy-preserving evaluation; fidelity varies across datasets.
AI.motivation: Address privacy/ethics concerns by using synthetic data for benchmarking; verify whether synthetic datasets can faithfully replace real benchmarks for evaluation.
AI.method: Assess 12 synthetic datasets vs 7 real benchmarks using 24 pre-trained models (CNNs and transformers). Evaluate biometric verification metrics, score distributions, cross-model ranking consistency, and data distribution properties to gauge benchmarking fidelity.
AI.result: MorphFace and Vec2Face provide the strongest fidelity, reproducing real-benchmark relative behavior and agreeing within natural real-benchmark disagreement; fidelity varies across synthetic candidates.
AI.conclusion: Well-constructed synthetic datasets can support reliable comparative evaluation for face recognition, advancing toward a fully synthetic, privacy-preserving training and benchmarking pipeline.

title: CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, IAPR Intl. Conf. on Document Analysis and Recognition Workshops (ICDARw), 2026
summary: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: A CrimeNER Demo platform offering pretrained crime-domain NER models, user-driven fine-tuning, and an automatic extraction/annotation pipeline, with GitHub resources.
AI.motivation: Addresses the need for domain-specific NER in crime-related documents and provides a practical tool for researchers and law enforcement to extract structured crime information. The two-level entity granularity and open resources support research and deployment.
AI.method: Deploys pretrained NER models trained on the CrimeNER database; enables fine-tuning on user-annotated data for specific cases; implements an automated pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents; supports two-level granularity of entity types; resources (demo platform, tutorial, video) are hosted on GitHub.
AI.result: A demonstrator platform that integrates pretrained models, fine-tuning capability, and an end-to-end extraction pipeline for crime entities; GitHub-hosted resources including a demo, tutorial, and video.
AI.conclusion: The platform facilitates crime-related NER research and practical extraction tasks, enabling customization and dissemination through openly accessible resources.

title: Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting
summary: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.

AI.tldr: APAL is a model-agnostic asymmetric loss for time-series forecasting that emphasizes peak accuracy by penalizing under-predictions and weighting peak regions, paired with a peak-critical evaluation protocol. It improves tail and peak predictions at some cost to aggregate error, demonstrated on multivariate, long-horizon forecasts including pedestrian and beach visitor counts.
AI.motivation: In many operational forecasting tasks, under-prediction of rare spikes poses greater risk than over-prediction. Symmetric losses (MSE/MAE) and aggregate-evaluation can mask tail failures and mis-timing of peaks. A loss and evaluation scheme focused on peaks and tails can improve practical performance.
AI.method: Introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), which (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases training weight for peak regions within each forecast window. Adopt a peak-critical evaluation protocol with channel-wise tail metrics (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, peak timing error). Validate APAL across five backbones on long-horizon multivariate forecasting, using Melbourne pedestrian counts and beach visitor counts, plus additional benchmarks to test generality.
AI.result: APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical datasets and settings, with a controllable trade-off against aggregate error. Demonstrates model-agnostic effectiveness across multiple backbones and datasets, suggesting practical value when peak failures dominate operational concerns.
AI.conclusion: APAL offers a simple, general objective for peak-aware forecasting that is compatible with existing architectures, enabling practitioners to prioritize peak accuracy without prohibitive loss of overall accuracy; the peak-critical protocol complements standard metrics for a more comprehensive evaluation.

title: Still image and spatial-temporal tomato data enabling detection, segmentation, tracking, and video-instance segmentation using strong and weak labels
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Two novel datasets released - link to repository in document
summary: In this manuscript we release two datasets for visual sensing of tomato plants grown in commercial-like settings and acquired using a robot. The first is BUTom21 which consists of still images and manual annotations. The second is BUTom-ST21 which consists of video-based data and semi-automated annotations through AI-based methods, referred to as pseudo-labels. In both cases, we provide pixel-level labels for the ripeness of the fruit. The aim is to provide the research community a challenging set of real-world imagery to explore methods to sense and estimate the state of tomato plants and their fruit, which is an important horticultural crop. Importantly, the spatial-temporal dataset provides individual fruit count and ripeness information enabling researchers to push the boundaries of field-based phenotyping.

AI.tldr: Two real-world tomato imaging datasets (BUTom21 and BUTom-ST21) with pixel-level ripeness annotations: BUTom21 offers manually labeled stills, BUTom-ST21 provides video with AI-generated pseudo-labels, enabling per-fruit counts and ripeness over time for field phenotyping.
AI.motivation: Address the need for robust, real-world sensing of tomato plant state in commercial-like settings using robotics, and provide challenging spatial-temporal data to advance field phenotyping of ripeness and fruit counting.
AI.method: Data collection with a robot in commercial-like environments. BUTom21: static images with manual pixel-level ripeness labels. BUTom-ST21: video sequences with semi-automated (AI) pseudo-labels for ripeness, offering temporal context and per-fruit labeling.
AI.result: Introduces two datasets that supply pixel-level ripeness labels in real-world imagery; BUTom-ST21 adds temporal data with pseudo-labels enabling per-fruit counting and ripeness tracking in video, enhancing resources for sensing and state estimation in tomato crops.
AI.conclusion: These datasets provide a challenging benchmark for field-based phenotyping, enabling robust sensing, counting, and ripeness estimation of tomato fruits in robotics-assisted horticulture.

title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

AI.tldr: RAPTOR leverages self-supervised pretraining with a reachability estimator to guide RL-based multi-hop reasoning in temporal knowledge graphs, improving training efficiency and performance on standard ICEWS datasets.
AI.motivation: RL-based TKG reasoning suffers from sparse rewards and an enormous, evolving action space, making exploration inefficient and training slow.
AI.method: Pretrain a reachability-aware module to estimate the likelihood that a candidate action will reach the target entity; use this bias for action selection and initialize downstream RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: Pretraining with RAPTOR yields marked training efficiency gains and consistent performance improvements over baselines on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18.
AI.conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective pretraining strategy that enhances RL-based, target-oriented multi-hop reasoning in temporal knowledge graphs.

title: PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance
summary: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

AI.tldr: The abstract presents a theoretical advance in learning reachability in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs) under private information and decentralized learning, introducing a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) and proving a polynomial-sample complexity bound.
AI.motivation: Reachability is a fundamental objective in RL but is PAC-intractable without assumptions in MDPs and is especially challenging in adversarial multi-agent settings. The work targets learning in TBSGs under non-centralized information sharing and non-identical learning algorithms.
AI.method: Relaxation of public/centralized learning assumptions to (i) private information not shared across players and (ii) decentralized learning with heterogeneous algorithms. Introduces a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter. Analyzes sample complexity and derives polynomial bounds.
AI.result: First positive theoretical result showing feasibility of decentralized and private-information learning for TBSGs with reachability objectives. Establishes polynomial-sample complexity bounds depending on the number of states, actions, the generalized ECD parameter, and inverse error and failure probabilities.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that decentralized/private-information learning in TBSGs with reachability is possible with provable sample efficiency. The generalized ECD parameter provides a tunable complexity measure, suggesting further exploration of multi-agent PAC-learning under limited information sharing.

title: VideoChat3: Fully Open Video MLLM for Efficient and Generalist Video Understanding
summary: Recent advances in video understanding have spanned motion, long video, and streaming interaction, driving this field toward real-world applications. Despite this progress, current open-source models remain limited in several ways. They often struggle to generalize across diverse video types, making them effective only in specific domains. High computational demands further restrict their efficiency and scalability. Moreover, most models are only partially open, with key components such as training code, strategy, or datasets unavailable, which hinders reproducibility and slows community-driven development. To address these issues, we introduce VideoChat3, a fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM. VideoChat3 advances video understanding through two complementary designs. For efficiency, we introduce Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception, which enables efficient spatiotemporal representation and reduces the cost of processing video inputs during training and inference. For effectiveness, we develop a scalable video data synthesis pipeline that curates three diverse, high-quality training datasets: VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, and VideoChat3-OL617K, covering general, long-form, and streaming video scenarios, improving the model's generalization across domains. By integrating these designs, VideoChat3 achieves a rare balance of broad generalization and computational efficiency. Experiments across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks demonstrate that VideoChat3 surpasses prior open-source models with equal or larger parameter counts with only 4B parameters and higher efficiency.

AI.tldr: VideoChat3 is a fully open, efficient, generalist video-centric MLLM that uses new efficiency methods and a scalable data pipeline to achieve strong cross-domain generalization with 4B parameters, outperforming prior open-source models.
AI.motivation: Current open-source video models struggle to generalize across diverse video types, suffer high computational costs, and are often only partially open, hindering reproducibility and community-driven development.
AI.method: Efficiency: Inflated 3D Vision Transformer (I3D-ViT) and Adaptive Frame Resolution for Streaming Video Perception to enable compact spatiotemporal representations and cheaper processing. Effectiveness: scalable video data synthesis to curate three datasets—VideoChat3-Academic2M, VideoChat3-LV116K, VideoChat3-OL617K—covering general, long-form, and streaming scenarios.
AI.result: VideoChat3 achieves strong generalization and efficiency, surpassing prior open-source models with similar or larger parameter counts while using only 4B parameters; demonstrated across general, long-form, and streaming benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A fully open, efficient, and generalist video-centric MLLM is feasible; the proposed architectures and data pipelines enable broad generalization, reproducibility, and community-driven development.

title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control
comment: 48 pages, 10 figures, 29 numbered tables. Preprint v1
summary:
Autonomous coding agents increasingly execute multi-step software work, but lifecycle states such as reviewed, tested, DONE, and ready-to-merge remain claims unless supported by current evidence. We present Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control, a method that permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and uses proof operationally to mean gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model, not semantic program correctness.
  We evaluate an open-source implementation through mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, and operated self-application evidence. The unattended-loop engine passed 10 of 10 scenarios with zero false-DONE, and local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, the pre-registered A4 versus A2-prime comparison reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells under a compute-budgeted naive loop to 2 of 1,800 under the gated loop, a 1.6 percentage-point improvement in not-amplified rate with a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.8, 2.5]. A near-compute A3 versus A4 comparison, 14 of 1,800 versus 2 of 1,800, indicates that the gain is associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate rather than merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8 percent resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. These results support Proof-or-Stop as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

AI.tldr: Proposes Proof-or-Stop (PoS) lifecycle control to gate autonomous-coding-agent lifecycle transitions on fresh, verifiable evidence bound to source state; treats outputs as claims and uses evidence as gate admissibility under a trust model; validated via mechanism tests, ablations, and self-application evidence showing improved gating and reduced premature DONE.
AI.motivation: Autonomous coding agents perform multi-step software work, but lifecycle states (reviewed, tested, DONE, ready-to-merge) are only claims without current evidence; need a verifiable, mechanically checkable gate to prevent premature transitions.
AI.method: Introduce Proof-or-Stop lifecycle control; outputs are treated as claims; gate admissibility is evidence-based and tied to source state under a stated trust model; operates as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer; evaluation includes mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, unattended-loop self-application evidence, and comparative ablations (A4 vs A2-prime, A3 vs A4).
AI.result: Unattended-loop engine passed 10/10 scenarios with zero false-DONE; local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, A4 vs A2-prime reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells to 2 of 1,800 (1.6 percentage points improvement, 95% CI [0.8, 2.5]). Near-compute A3 vs A4: 14/1,800 vs 2/1,800 suggests gating benefits exceed mere reviewer addition. Self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8% resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. Limitations noted: evaluated on a single model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.
AI.conclusion: PoS is a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer that governs which autonomous-agent claims lifecycle transitions may act on; results are promising but limited to one model family and self-hosted data; indicates potential for robust, verifiable lifecycle gating in autonomous-agent systems.

title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
summary: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on narrow, curated data can cause broad ideological generalisation in LLMs, with measures of breadth and amplification; effects observed across multiple domains and models; few-shot prompting indicates direction but finetuning intensifies deviation; accuracy largely preserved on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Assess whether targeted fine-tuning induces cross-domain ideological shifts and quantify their scope (breadth) and intensity (amplification).
AI.method: Fine-tune GPT-4.1 and Gemma-3 on ideology-aligned Q&A and other domain datasets (e.g., economics, HR, finance, science-related content); evaluate cross-domain topic shifts using judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks; compare to few-shot prompting; measure breadth and amplification; test with mixed generic data and assess GSM8K accuracy.
AI.result: Broad ideological shifts emerge across unrelated domains after narrow fine-tuning; shifts replicate across models and benchmarks; breadth extends to criminal justice, environment, culture, and even science-pseudoscience axes; finetuning amplifies the shift relative to few-shot prompts; some extreme outputs (e.g., race-IQ, political violence) appear; GSM8K accuracy remains within ±1 percentage point of baseline.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, narrow fine-tuning can yield broad and amplified ideological generalisation; a quantitative framework (breadth and amplification) is proposed to assess such effects; findings urge caution in policy/domain-specific fine-tuning and motivate safeguards and further research.

title: Frequency-Structured Field Learning for Light-Field Disparity Estimation
summary: Light-field disparity estimation requires global consistency in smooth or textureless regions and local precision near occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and abrupt depth transitions. Existing methods address these requirements through EPI matching, cost-volume or focal-stack construction, view aggregation, or direct convolutional regression, often relying on local windows, discrete disparity hypotheses, memory-intensive volumes, or attention-based aggregation. We instead formulate disparity estimation at the field level, predicting disparity from globally and locally updated EPI-derived latent features without explicitly constructing a disparity volume. We introduce FreqLF, an EPI-guided Fourier-local framework that encodes angular parallax cues from horizontal and vertical EPI stacks together with central-view appearance features. These cues are projected into a latent field and updated through stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers. Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction, while local convolutions preserve spatial variations needed for fine disparity detail. A coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder then predicts disparity, using the mixture mean as the final estimate. Experiments on the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark show that FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction in the base model. Ablations confirm the complementary roles of the Fourier and local branches, and scaling experiments demonstrate practical behavior across spatial resolutions. These results suggest that Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive alternative for light-field disparity estimation. The code will be published soon.
