AI.tldr: FreqLF introduces a Fourier-local latent-field framework for light-field disparity estimation that foregoes explicit cost-volume construction, using EPI-guided latent features updated by Fourier-local layers and a Gaussian-mixture decoder to deliver accurate disparities.
AI.motivation: To meet the need for global consistency in smooth/textureless regions and precise discontinuities (occlusions, thin structures) in light-field disparity estimation while avoiding memory-intensive cost volumes and heavy attention-based aggregation.
AI.method: Encode angular parallax cues from horizontal/vertical EPI stacks and central-view appearance into a latent field. Update the field with stacked hybrid Fourier-local layers: Fourier low-mode updates enable global feature interaction; local convolutions preserve spatial detail. Predict disparity with a coordinate-conditioned Gaussian-mixture decoder; use the mixture mean as the final estimate. No explicit disparity volume is constructed.
AI.result: On the HCI 4D Light Field Benchmark, FreqLF approaches the accuracy of strong supervised baselines while avoiding explicit cost-volume construction. Ablations show complementary roles of Fourier and local branches; scaling experiments demonstrate robust behavior across spatial resolutions.
AI.conclusion: Fourier-local latent field learning is a competitive, efficient alternative for light-field disparity estimation, balancing global consistency with local detail without requiring explicit cost-volume architectures.

title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach
summary: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

AI.tldr: An LLM-based system for detecting online firestorms using two operating modes: retrospective thread classification and sequential early warning, leveraging local chunk assessments to a thread-level judgment and estimating negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count to monitor discourse in real time.
AI.motivation: Existing detectors rely on volume, sentiment, or predefined features and miss context shifts in evolving threads; there is a need for context-aware, real-time monitoring of social media to detect and warn about firestorms.
AI.method: Proposes two modes: (1) global retrospective mode that aggregates chunk-level judgments to classify full Reddit threads; (2) sequential early-warning mode with a sliding window; the LLM estimates three indicators (negativity share, escalation level, contributor count) and thresholds are calibrated for detection; evaluated on a balanced Reddit dataset showing strong performance in the global mode and high recall in early-warning mode.
AI.result: Global mode achieves strong thread-level classification performance; early-warning mode yields high recall and detects escalation after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors, demonstrating LLMs' utility as repeated, context-aware estimators for monitoring discourse.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve beyond static judgments, functioning as iterative estimators for real-time monitoring of social media, enabling both accurate post-hoc classification and early detection of escalating firestorms.

title: Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set
summary:
This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

AI.tldr: Proposes an optimal linear ensemble of binary classifiers built on truth-table based data structuring, derives existence/uniqueness conditions for the convexified empirical risk, provides closed-form weights for ExpBoost and Logit losses, analyzes three-classifier configurations, and introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality assessment.
AI.motivation: To rigorously analyze and optimize weighted combinations of binary classifiers by structuring data into equivalence classes via truth tables, enabling non-iterative weight computation and deeper understanding of when minima exist.
AI.method: Partition data into equivalence classes using truth-table based logical structuration; formulate the convexified empirical risk via a multidimensional extension of classification-calibrated functions; derive global minimum conditions; enumerate configurations for three classifiers; obtain closed-form weight expressions for Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) losses; introduce φ-frontiers to assess stability and data quality.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of the global minimum of the convexified risk for any set of classifiers are established; with three classifiers all configurations leading to unique solutions, infima, or non-unique minima are characterized; explicit analytical formulas for optimal weights under ExpBoost and Logit losses are provided, avoiding iterative optimization; φ-frontiers offer a diagnostic tool for classifier stability and data quality.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables non-iterative, closed-form ensemble weighting for certain losses, clarifies when minima exist based on classifier count and data structuring, and introduces φ-frontiers as a practical instrument for assessing stability and data quality in classifier ensembles.

title: Introspective Attention Modulation for Safe Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. 20 pages, 7 figures. Project page: https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/
summary: State-of-the-art flow based text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit remarkable generative abilities but remain vulnerable to producing unsafe content. Prior safety efforts range from concept erasure and prompt filtering to classifier-based gating. However, simple techniques like parameter efficient adaptations of the models easily bypass such guardrails. We introduce a unique principled approach that achieves safety by regulating the model's attention dynamics through inference-time introspection, exhibiting intrinsic robustness. Our method analyzes and rebalances attention activations throughout image synthesis, steering generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment. This introspective control ensures safety of deployed models. Across standard and adversarial safety benchmarks, our approach achieves remarkable safety scores while maintaining or even improving alignment and perceptual quality. Our results reveal that attention-space regulation offers a considerably more promising path to safer diffusion transformer based image generation than the existing concept erasing mechanism.Our code can be accessed at https://basim-azam.github.io/iam/

AI.tldr: Introduces inference-time attention regulation to improve safety of diffusion-based T2I by introspection, outperforming erasure-based safeguards while preserving quality.
AI.motivation: Safety gaps in state-of-the-art text-to-image models, where prompt filtering and concept erasure can be bypassed; need intrinsic, robust safety mechanisms that persist under adversarial inputs.
AI.method: Inference-time introspection that analyzes and rebalances attention activations during image synthesis to steer generations away from unsafe concepts while preserving semantic alignment.
AI.result: High safety scores on standard and adversarial benchmarks; maintains or improves alignment and perceptual quality; attention-space regulation outperforms traditional concept erasure in safety.
AI.conclusion: Attention-space regulation via inference-time introspection is a promising, intrinsically robust path to safer diffusion transformer-based image generation; code available online.

title: Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation
summary: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

AI.tldr: Integration of IFT-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attributions and LLM-generated narratives to provide real-time, operator-centric explanations for optimization outputs in industrial control; achieves SHAP-equivalent attributions with significant speedup (40x) on an HPGR problem.
AI.motivation: Bridge the trust gap between engineers who design optimization algorithms and operators who act on their recommendations; extend explainability to optimization outputs and enable real-time natural-language explanations.
AI.method: Compute exact param sensitivities ∂p*/∂x via the Implicit Function Theorem from optimality conditions to enable GradientSHAP; combine SHAP attributions with narrative generation via LLMs; apply to an industrial HPGR control optimization problem with 22 features.
AI.result: SHAP attributions are equivalent to KernelSHAP (correlation > 0.99); over 40× speedup enabling real-time explanations; validated on industrial scenarios with domain-expert feedback.
AI.conclusion: A scalable, interpretable framework for optimization outputs that closes the trust gap between engineers and operators by providing accurate, fast, and natural-language explanations.

title: Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation
summary: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

AI.tldr: Instruction-tune RLMs on data without reasoning traces, then merge the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to reclaim domain-specific reasoning. This yields performance gains in verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks (e.g., coding, summarization) while keeping costs under USD 3 and preserving broad capabilities.
AI.motivation: Leverage abundant supervised fine-tuning data that lacks reasoning traces to improve reasoning-enabled language models, especially in domains lacking reliable verifiers where standard verification-based RL signals are scarce.
AI.method: 1) Apply classic instruction tuning on the RLM using data without reasoning traces. 2) Merge the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover and preserve the target-domain reasoning behavior.
AI.result: Demonstrates improved performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains (including coding and text summarization) and preserves model capabilities on other tasks; notably cost-effective, enabling these gains for under $3.
AI.conclusion: A cost-efficient data reuse strategy for RLMs that extends benefits to domains lacking reliable verifiers without sacrificing general capabilities.

title: DINE: Distance Is Not Enough -- Learning Global Deformation Priors for Robust Soft-Tissue Point Cloud Registration
summary: Non-rigid point cloud registration is central to soft-tissue shape analysis, but large deformations, noise, and outliers make correspondence estimation challenging. Most learning-based methods rely on local objectives such as Chamfer distance, which encourage point-wise proximity but do not constrain the global plausibility of the predicted deformation field. We address this limitation with DINE, a maximum a posteriori framework that augments distance-based registration with a learned statistical prior over displacement vector fields. DINE is applied to two registration backbones, Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet, using a two-stage strategy: a first-stage model is trained with Chamfer distance, its predicted deformation fields are used to estimate a prior, and the model is then refined with a combined distance and negative log-prior objective. We compare a full-field PCA Gaussian prior with a per-vector normalizing-flow prior. Experiments on DeformedTissue and SynBench show lower mean Chamfer distance under deformation and corruption. On DeformedTissue, DINE-PCA reduces Chamfer distance by approximately 27--69\% relative to the corresponding Stage-1 backbone across deformation levels, and improves robustness by up to 66\% for outliers and 83\% for Gaussian noise. On SynBench, improvements are modest at the smallest deformation levels and reach approximately 59--79\% from moderate to severe deformation. These results suggest that global deformation plausibility is an important constraint for reliable soft-tissue point cloud registration. (The code will be published soon.)

AI.tldr: DINE adds a learned prior over displacement fields to non-rigid point cloud registration, improving global deformation plausibility and robustness to deformation, noise, and outliers. It uses a two-stage training strategy and shows substantial gains over Chamfer-based baselines, with PCA priors performing particularly well.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of local, point-wise objectives (e.g., Chamfer distance) in non-rigid registration by enforcing a global, learned prior on displacement fields to ensure plausible deformations, especially under large deformations and corruptions in soft-tissue data.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) train a base registration model with Chamfer distance (Stage-1) on backbones Robust-DefReg and DefTransNet; (2) estimate a prior over displacement fields from Stage-1 predictions; (3) refine using a joint objective of Chamfer distance plus negative log-prior. Compare priors: a full-field PCA Gaussian prior vs a per-vector normalizing-flow prior. Evaluated on DeformedTissue and SynBench datasets.
AI.result: DINE-PCA reduces mean Chamfer distance by ~27–69% relative to Stage-1 across deformation levels on DeformedTissue; robustness to outliers improves up to 66% and to Gaussian noise up to 83%. On SynBench, improvements are modest at small deformations but reach ~59–79% for moderate to severe deformation. Overall, global deformation plausibility yields substantial gains, indicating the importance of priors in non-rigid registration.
AI.conclusion: Global plausibility constraints via learned priors significantly improve the reliability of soft-tissue non-rigid registration, especially under large deformations and data corruption. The PCA-based prior shows strong performance; code release anticipated.

title: CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models
summary: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

AI.tldr: CFM-Bench is a unified, multi-domain, multi-task benchmark for channel foundation models that enables fair cross-model comparison across diverse data, configurations, and tasks.
AI.motivation: Current CFMs are evaluated in ad hoc pipelines with varying data, configurations, and metrics, making fair ranking across models difficult; a standardized benchmark with transparent data usage and training restrictions is needed.
AI.method: Assembles six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulations, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation; official partitions isolate complete trajectories, sessions, links, realizations, or buffered regions; no external pretraining data; official training split reserved for downstream fine-tuning; six task groups across PHY, RAN, and ISAC with tasks like CSI feedback, extrapolation, localization, beam prediction; requires disclosure of all data used; prohibits training on official test units.
AI.result: Provides a common substrate to compare transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks, enabling fair benchmarking and cross-domain evaluation of CFMs.
AI.conclusion: CFM-Bench fills a benchmarking gap by providing a standardized, transparent, and transferable evaluation framework for CFMs across multiple domains and tasks.

title: Random Logit Scaling: Defending Deep Neural Networks Against Black-Box Score-Based Adversarial Example Attacks
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Machine learning models are increasingly adapted in various domains. However, adversarial examples pose a significant threat to the reliable deployment of these models. In recent years, some powerful adversarial example attacks have been proposed for the fast and query-efficient generation of adversarial examples, even in black-box scenarios, highlighting the need for scalable, low-cost, and powerful defenses. In this work, we present two contributions to the domain of black-box adversarial example attacks and defenses. First, we propose Random Logit Scaling (RLS), a randomization-based defense against black-box score-based adversarial example attacks. RLS is a plug-and-play, post-processing defense that can be implemented on top of any existing ML model with minimal effort. The idea behind RLS is to confuse an attacker by outputting falsified scores resulting from randomly scaled logits while maintaining the model accuracy. We show that RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while preserving the accuracy and minimizing confidence score distortion compared to state-of-the-art randomization-based defenses. Second, we introduce a novel adaptive attack against AAA, a SOTA non-randomized black-box defense against black-box score-based attacks that also modifies output logits to confuse attackers, demonstrating its vulnerability against adaptive attacks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Random Logit Scaling (RLS) as a plug-and-play, post-processing defense against black-box score-based attacks, and presents an adaptive attack against a non-randomized defense (AAA) to reveal its vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Adversarial examples threaten reliable ML deployment, especially under black-box, score-based attacks. A scalable, low-cost defense that preserves accuracy and reduces attack success is desirable; the work also tests the resilience of a state-of-the-art non-randomized defense (AAA) against adaptive threats.
AI.method: RLS applies random scaling to logits to generate falsified scores at inference, serving as a post-processing layer that does not require retraining. It aims to keep accuracy while confusing attackers. The study evaluates RLS against recent black-box score-based attacks and compares confidence distortion to prior randomized defenses. Additionally, the paper introduces an adaptive attack against AAA that also perturbs output logits to mislead attackers.
AI.result: RLS significantly reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art black-box score-based attacks while maintaining model accuracy and achieving lower confidence-score distortion than comparable defenses. The second contribution shows an adaptive attack on AAA, demonstrating its vulnerability to adaptive adversaries.
AI.conclusion: RLS offers a practical, low-cost defense for black-box score-based attacks with minimal impact on accuracy and confidence calibration, though its robustness to adaptive threats requires further investigation. The adaptive attack on AAA highlights the need for defenses resilient to attack strategies that explicitly adapt to defenders.

title: U-shaped Multi-granularity Learning for Vision-Language Models
summary: The prompt learning paradigm for vision-language models is effective yet faces a granularity dilemma: global prompts lack fine-grained semantic awareness, while local prompts ignore contextual associations, limiting cross-task generalization. This dilemma exists in dense prediction tasks. Inspired by U-Net, which unifies multi-level representations across granularities, we propose UPrompt, a U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework for vision-language models. Similar to how U-Net integrates fine and coarse features through symmetric encoder-decoder pathways with cross-level connections, UPrompt constructs parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities, where coarse-to-fine cascaded enhancement propagates global context to refine local details, while fine-to-coarse hierarchical supervision ensures semantic consistency across scales. Extensive experiments on 17 benchmarks validate our effectiveness. UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO, surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization, while maintaining competitive performance with minimal overhead (coarse-grained) and matching PSRC with 1/3 cost (medium-grained).

AI.tldr: A U-shaped multi-granularity prompt learning framework (UPrompt) for vision-language models to address granularity dilemmas in prompts for dense prediction tasks by unifying coarse and fine representations through encoder-decoder-like, cross-scale connections, achieving strong cross-task generalization with low overhead.
AI.motivation: Resolve the granularity dilemma in vision-language prompt learning where global prompts miss fine semantics and local prompts miss context, particularly in dense prediction tasks; inspired by U-Net to fuse multi-scale features and enforce cross-scale consistency.
AI.method: Builds parallel multi-granularity representations in both visual and textual modalities with a coarse-to-fine cascade for global-to-local context propagation and a fine-to-coarse supervisory path to maintain semantic consistency. Uses a symmetric encoder-decoder-like architecture with cross-level connections to integrate features across scales. Evaluates on 17 benchmarks, comparing to MAMET, VPKE, CoCoA-Mix, and PSRC with emphasis on efficiency (coarse- and medium-grained variants).
AI.result: UPrompt outperforms MAMET and VPKE by 4.1 and 7.3 rSum on MSCOCO; surpasses CoCoA-Mix by 5.09% in base-to-novel generalization; achieves competitive performance with minimal overhead for coarse-grained prompts and matches PSRC at 1/3 cost for medium-grained prompts.
AI.conclusion: The U-shaped multi-granularity prompt design effectively mitigates the granularity trade-off in vision-language prompts for dense tasks, enabling stronger cross-task generalization while maintaining efficiency.

title: Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers
summary: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

AI.tldr: Synthetic demographic-conditioned data can both mitigate bias during training via sequential pretraining and detect bias during evaluation, reproducing real-subgroup rankings with high fidelity and enabling reliable per-cell estimates in small test sets.
AI.motivation: Per-subgroup fairness audits in medical image classifiers suffer from small sample sizes for minority subgroups, leading to wide confidence intervals and unreliable bias detection. A demographically-conditioned synthetic generator aims to address both training bias and evaluation bias.
AI.method: Train a COVID-19 chest CT classifier using an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator to create demographically-balanced synthetic cohorts. Compare training regimes: (1) sequential pretraining on synthetic data then fine-tuning on real data versus (2) joint augmentation with synthetic data. For evaluation, assess five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, comparing the synthetic estimator to a well-powered real oracle using Spearman correlation on MCC and Recall, and examine per-cell estimates in data-sparse regions.
AI.result: Training: sequential pretraining + fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation; the classifier attains ~100× real-data efficiency and even surpasses the full-real baseline. Evaluation: across five synthetic minority cohorts and five seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the real oracle’s subgroup ranking with Spearman ρ = 1.00 for MCC and Recall, and provides more reliable per-cell estimates when the real test set has few samples.
AI.conclusion: Demographically-conditioned synthetic cohorts are most useful in the exact cells fairness audits target, serving as both a bias-mitigating training prior and a robust evaluation proxy for measuring subgroup bias with limited real data.

title: A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems
summary: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

AI.tldr: A minimal interpretive model, DynaBase, derived from DynaMix for zero-shot dynamical-system reconstruction. It uses a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor, achieving competitive performance with far fewer parameters; enables closed-form one-step MSE and reveals a 1-parameter family of maps bridging context parroting and chaotic dynamics. Training strategies shift optimization toward short-term prediction or DS reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To uncover the minimal mechanisms required for zero-shot DS reconstruction by foundation models, enabling interpretability and potential simplification of DS-reconstruction architectures.
AI.method: Iterative reduction of a state-of-the-art DS reconstruction model (DynaMix) to a two-parameter, interpretable form (DynaBase): forecast as a linear blend between the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor plus its successor; theoretical analysis yields a 1-parameter family of maps; empirical validation on chaotic and cyclic DS; exploration of training strategies.
AI.result: DynaBase achieves competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions with orders of magnitude fewer parameters. It supports closed-form one-step MSE solutions and direct optimization on DS reconstruction metrics. The analysis identifies a 1-parameter map family ranging from context parroting to chaotic behavior; training choices tune models for short-term prediction vs DS reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Minimal mechanistic components suffice for zero-shot DS reconstruction and help reconcile divergent observations in the literature; DynaBase provides an accessible mathematical framework and guides design of compact, interpretable FMs for DS tasks.

title: Stitch-Inferencer: Enhance Endoscopic Video Segmentation and Tracking via Panoramic Reconstruction
summary: Surgical video understanding is fundamental to navigation systems. Endoscopic perception is often hindered by a limited field-of-view and frequent instrument occlusions, making spatio-temporal context essential for robust inference. These challenges have motivated video models that aggregate information across frames. However, existing video models typically store past observations implicitly in learned feature representations, often requiring task-specific video training, substantial annotated data, and increased computational cost. We propose Stitch-Inferencer, a real-time, model-agnostic inference framework that replaces implicit feature memory with an explicit image-space panoramic canvas. By stitching valid observations across frames, Stitch-Inferencer preserves previously observed pixels in an online, instrument-free view, expanding the effective field-of-view and providing direct access to regions that are temporarily occluded or absent from the current frame. Downstream segmentation or tracking models are applied to a compact region of interest on the panorama, and their predictions are reprojected to the current frame, enabling existing models to exploit long-range context without retraining. Experiments on anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse baselines while preserving real-time throughput. The stitching module alone runs at over 60 FPS, providing a practical inference-time solution to enhance endoscopic perception in computationally constrained intraoperative environments. Source code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: Stitch-Inferencer replaces implicit video memory with an explicit image-space panorama to accumulate cross-frame observations, enabling real-time, model-agnostic long-range context for endoscopic perception; downstream models operate on a ROI on the panorama and results are reprojected back to the current frame.
AI.motivation: Endoscopic perception suffers from limited field-of-view and occlusions; existing video models rely on implicit memory and task-specific data, incurring training cost and latency; an explicit, online memory could expand context without retraining.
AI.method: Maintain an online panoramic canvas by stitching valid observations across frames, yielding an instrument-free view that preserves previously observed pixels. Run downstream segmentation or tracking on a compact ROI on the panorama, then reproject predictions to the current frame, enabling long-range context sharing with minimal retraining. The stitching module runs >60 FPS, aiming for real-time inference; source code to be released.
AI.result: Across anatomy segmentation and point/box tracking tasks, the approach yields consistent improvements over diverse baselines while maintaining real-time throughput.
AI.conclusion: An explicit, panorama-based memory provides a practical, model-agnostic path to leverage long-range context in endoscopic perception, suitable for computation-constrained intraoperative settings and without retraining downstream models.

title: Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development
comment: This is a pre-print i.e. the draft as submitted for review to the AGI 2026 Conference except that the figures in this preprint were not included. The paper has been accepted with some revisions requested which are included in the final copy-edited version which will be available in the AGI Springer proceedings LNC 1855 (Chapter 28) ISBN 978-3-032-33194-6
summary: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

AI.tldr: Inverts AI ethics by asking how future sentient ASI would morally assess humans; offers a preliminary post-human moral framework and argues that design, human behavior, and human nature shape humanity's future standing in a post-ASI world.
AI.motivation: To broaden AI ethics beyond human-centric alignment by considering the moral agency and judgments of future ASI, addressing long-term coexistence and governance in a post-ASI era.
AI.method: Conceptual/normative analysis. Proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles guiding predicted ASI actions, and discusses how technical design choices and human behavior influence future judgments.
AI.result: Provides a preliminary normative framework (a post-human moral principle set) and a mapping from design and behavior to possible ASI judgments, highlighting factors that could affect humanity's long-term standing.
AI.conclusion: If ASI will judge humans, ethics and design must account for those judgments now; promotes development of post-human ethics and governance to steer long-term outcomes, while recognizing speculative nature and the need for further work.

title: Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding
summary: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

AI.tldr: Proposes a computationally efficient MPLE-based method for causal inference under outcome interference in sequential Ising-like models with low-rank latent confounders; provides non-asymptotic consistency and demonstrates on synthetic data plus a vaccine-COVID case study.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable causal inference when outcomes for many units are interdependent over time, with latent confounders, using a single high-dimensional sample, and with scalable estimation.
AI.method: Model outcomes as a time-series of binary variables with Ising interactions and external fields incorporating treatments and latent confounders; impose a low-rank structure on latent effects; estimate parameters via Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation; establish non-asymptotic consistency; validate by sampling from the learned model.
AI.result: Non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation leading to accurate causal quantities after model-based sampling; demonstrated effectiveness on synthetic experiments and a real-world case study analyzing vaccine rates and COVID-19 death rates across US counties.
AI.conclusion: Offers a scalable, statistically grounded framework for causal inference under outcome interference in high-dimensional sequential data, incorporating latent confounding through a low-rank factor model, with practical applicability to epidemiological settings.

title: On Success and Simplicity: A Second Look at Transferable Vision-Language Attack Pipeline
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (TIFS)
summary: Vision-Language Pre-training Models (VLPMs) are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Recent transferable attacks on VLPMs have followed a common pipeline with complicated loss functions or multi-stage text/image attacks. However, in this paper, we demonstrate that such a sophisticated attack pipeline can be simpler yet more successful. Specifically, we identify three previously overlooked issues caused by inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations. To address them, we propose the Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline, which observably improves transferability and efficiency. Experiments on four datasets and three downstream tasks validate the superiority of our pipeline. For instance, on Flickr30k text-image retrieval dataset, our SimVLA outperforms the SOTA baseline in R@1 transferability by 8.01\%-14.71\%, while consuming only about 35.73\% of the time and 46.26\% of the max VRAM. Overall, the superiority of our SimVLA highlights the importance of leveraging domain knowledge (e.g., our proposed cross-modal word identification), while blindly pursuing intricate operations (e.g, complex loss functions and redundant multi-stage designs) may even be harmful. We hope our SimVLA can serve as a simple yet effective backbone for future extensions. Code is available at https://github.com/RYC-98/SimVLA.

AI.tldr: SimVLA presents a simple, domain-informed adversarial attack for vision-language models that outperforms complex pipelines: it identifies three cross-modal interaction issues and achieves higher transferability (8.01%-14.71% on Flickr30k R@1) with substantial efficiency gains (~36% runtime, ~46% VRAM) across four datasets and three tasks.
AI.motivation: VLPMs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and existing transferable attacks rely on intricate multi-stage designs and heavy loss functions. There is potential to improve transferability and efficiency by targeting cross-modal interactions with simpler, knowledge-driven strategies.
AI.method: Introduce the Simple Vision-Language Attack (SimVLA) pipeline that (1) identifies three overlooked issues from inappropriate cross-modal interactions and excessive operations, (2) leverages domain knowledge such as cross-modal word identification, and (3) reduces complex loss functions and multi-stage design to enhance transferability and efficiency.
AI.result: Empirical results on four datasets and three downstream tasks show SimVLA surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in R@1 transferability on Flickr30k by 8.01%-14.71%, while consuming ~35.73% of training/inference time and ~46.26% of max VRAM; code is released.
AI.conclusion: A simple, knowledge-guided attack can outperform elaborate pipelines, suggesting that careful design of cross-modal interactions is crucial. SimVLA can serve as a strong backbone for future extensions in vision-language adversarial research.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
summary: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes SMC-ES, a simulation-based method combining Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking to synthesize policies with formal guarantees (performance, safety, robustness) for autonomous CPS; demonstrates competitive results with higher computation time.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical CPS require provable guarantees; standard learning methods lack formal assurances; a method is needed to guarantee that the probability of safety/performance violations stays within epsilon with high confidence (1-δ).
AI.method: Integrate Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking. Given a set of properties, δ and ε, the method outputs a policy with a certificate that, with probability at least 1−δ, the chance of violating the properties is ≤ε. It uses simulation-based verification (SMC) and optimizes policies (via ES) while verifying candidates in a simulated environment (Gymnasium/Safety Gymnasium).
AI.result: Feasible approach: provides formal guarantees at the cost of increased computational effort and shows competitive performance compared to leading model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines on continuous control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates viability of simulation-based policy synthesis with certificates for safe and robust CPS; highlights the trade-off between computational cost and guarantee strength; suggests future work to improve efficiency and scalability of verification.

title: LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget
summary: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

AI.tldr: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack enabling million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It demonstrates scalable execution on Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2, achieving 2.1M positions per group (groups of 2 or 8) with minimal additional memory, a 4.46M position stress test, and end-to-end validation on GLM-5.2 across 78 layers with 32 GPUs. The work establishes execution capacity rather than full training correctness due to a detached prompt state and incomplete distributed forward/gradient paths.
AI.motivation: Address the widening gap between long inference-context lengths (million-token scales) and RL post-training contexts (typically 256K or less) in AI agents. This gap impedes scalable long-horizon RL while constrained by fixed hardware budgets.
AI.method: Propose LongStraw, an architecture-aware execution stack for long-horizon RL post-training. It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time to shrink the live training graph. It is instantiated with GRPO and implemented for hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention Mixture-of-Experts GLM-5.2. Experiments run on eight H20 GPUs (grouped Qwen scoring and backward pass at 2.1M positions for group sizes 2 and 8; memory overhead grows by ~0.21 GB when increasing group size) and a separate stress test up to 4.46M positions; additional validation on 32 H20 GPUs evaluates an end-to-end path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2.
AI.result: Empirical evidence of execution capacity: up to 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8 with only modest memory overhead; stress test reaches 4.46M positions; end-to-end GLM-5.2 validation at 2.1M tokens across 78 layers; however, results are limited to execution capacity because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward/gradient composition paths remain incomplete.
AI.conclusion: LongStraw demonstrates the feasibility of million-token RL post-training under fixed hardware budgets by reducing live graph size via replay and selective state retention. It establishes execution capacity but does not prove training correctness due to intrinsic detachment of prompt state and incomplete distributed gradient mechanics; future work should address full training-path integration.

title: From Draft to Draft-Free: One-Step Video Object Removal via Privileged Distillation and Fast Planting
summary: Video object removal is a fundamental yet challenging task in video editing. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically fall into two categories. Traditional approaches based on optical flow or attention mechanisms often introduce noticeable artifacts and yield unnatural results. In contrast, diffusion-based methods improve visual realism but demand multiple denoising steps, limiting their practicality. To address these issues, we propose From-Draft-to-Draft-Free (D2DF), a framework that distills the ability of transforming coarse drafts into refined videos into a one-step video generation model. Within D2DF, a teacher model is trained to refine low-quality removal results ("drafts") into high-fidelity videos by multiple steps. Then, through Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD), we distill this capability into a student model that performs one-step removal conditioned on the draft. To eliminate draft dependency, we introduce a Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) module based on our Temporal Masked Transformer that autonomously generates scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free one-step model. Extensive experiments show that both draft-conditioned and draft-free versions achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics, surpassing traditional and multi-step generative methods in both quality and efficiency. The denoising process for a single video takes only about 1 second.

AI.tldr: One-step video object removal via distillation from a draft-refinement teacher (D2DF), enabling draft-conditioned and draft-free models with fast inference.
AI.motivation: Two main drawbacks in existing methods: artifacts from traditional optical-flow/attention methods and inefficiency of multi-step diffusion. A one-step, reliable, efficient method is desirable.
AI.method: Train a teacher to refine low-quality removal drafts to high-quality videos; apply Prior-Privileged Consistency Distillation (PPCD) to distill to a student model for one-step removal conditioned on drafts; introduce Self-Guided Fast Planting (SGFP) with a Temporal Masked Transformer to generate scene-consistent pseudo-drafts in latent space, enabling a fully draft-free model.
AI.result: Draft-conditioned and draft-free variants achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple metrics; surpass traditional and multi-step methods in quality and efficiency; denoising a single video in about 1 second.
AI.conclusion: D2DF successfully converts multi-step refinement into a practical one-step video object removal framework with draft-conditioned and draft-free options, combining distillation and autonomous pseudo-draft generation for real-time performance.

title: Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era
summary: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

AI.tldr: ArtSplit provotype quantifies human vs AI contributions to provoke reflection on ownership rather than resolve it; highlights that measurement may misalign with artistic intent and potentially dilute artistic agency.
AI.motivation: Address the contested notion of ownership in AI-assisted creation; lack of consensus on how to define/attribute ownership when humans and AI contribute intertwined work; explore implications of measurement approaches.
AI.method: Design of ArtSplit provotype that quantifies contributions across stages of the creative workflow; used as a provotype to elicit artists' responses to ownership via measurable actions, not to adjudicate ownership.
AI.result: The provotype elicited critiques from artists; findings indicate quantification does not align with creative intent/agency and that measuring ownership risks altering or diluting established social understandings of creative work.
AI.conclusion: Challenges the impulse to turn a socially situated, creative practice into a purely technical problem, preserving the importance of intent and agency over measurable actions.

title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a group-based reinforcement learning objective (multi-axis max@K) to improve target-mode coverage in diffusion-based text-to-image models, aiming to reduce demographic skew and increase appearance fairness while maintaining image quality and alignment.
AI.motivation: Samples from the same prompt often cover a limited subset of visually distinct modes, leading to reduced diversity and potential demographic skew in person-centric prompts. The work formalizes target-mode coverage and seeks to enhance it via a credit-assignment mechanism.
AI.method: Introduce multi-axis max@K: for a group of samples and per-category scores, take the maximum score per category across samples, then sum these maxima. Credits are assigned to a sample only if it raises a category's group-wise maximum, enabling different samples to contribute to different categories. Validate on synthetic mixture and SD3.5-M with deterministic color rewards; extend to perceived-appearance fairness; evaluate with three automatic evaluators across held-out prompts.
AI.result: The method improves the Fairness Score by 0.23–0.36 across three automatic evaluators relative to the base model, while preserving image quality and text alignment.
AI.conclusion: Multi-axis max@K provides a structured credit assignment that promotes broader target-mode coverage in T2I generation and yields fairness improvements without sacrificing fidelity or prompt adherence.

title: JADE-GS: Joint Alternating Deblurring Guided by Events in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: When a camera moves fast during exposure, blur destroys the intra-exposure motion a 3D model needs to recover the sharp scene, while event cameras capture exactly this signal at microsecond resolution. Turning them into reliable 3D supervision faces two obstacles. First, the two restoration priors fail in opposite ways: physics-based event-integration priors preserve edges but accumulate drift; learned networks recover texture but distort boundaries. Second, existing pipelines run in one direction only, so raw event noise or the biases of fixed 2D pseudo-labels pass uncorrected into the geometry. JADE-GS addresses both: a pixel-adaptive routing gate fuses the complementary priors, and the resulting 2D restorer is coupled to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop, where detached, multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor. Across synthetic and real benchmarks, JADE-GS attains the best perceptual quality, leading LPIPS and CLIP-IQA on both benchmarks with competitive PSNR and SSIM, and trainsin about one hour under 5 GB on a single consumer GPU while preserving real-time rendering.

AI.tldr: JADE-GS presents a pixel-adaptive gating mechanism that fuses physics-based event-integration priors with learned restoration, coupling a 2D restorer to a 3D Gaussian Splatting student in a bidirectional loop to produce geometry-aware, real-time capable 3D reconstruction from fast-exposure blur captured by event cameras.
AI.motivation: Two restoration priors (physics-based event integration and learned networks) fail in opposite ways: one preserves edges but drifts over time, the other recovers texture but distorts boundaries. Additionally, unidirectional pipelines let raw event noise and fixed pseudo-label biases propagate into geometry. A joint, bidirectional, geometry-aware framework is needed to leverage complementary priors and produce reliable 3D supervision.
AI.method: JADE-GS introduces a pixel-adaptive routing gate to fuse priors. A 2D restorer is coupled with a 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) student in a bidirectional loop. Detached, multi-view-consistent renders and a physics-based reblurring constraint regularize the restorer, turning a fixed preprocessor into a geometry-aware predictor.
AI.result: On synthetic and real benchmarks, JADE-GS achieves the best perceptual quality, surpassing baselines in LPIPS and CLIP-IQA metrics on both benchmarks, with competitive PSNR and SSIM. Training time is about 1 hour on a single consumer GPU with under 5 GB memory, while preserving real-time rendering capability.
AI.conclusion: JADE-GS delivers state-of-the-art perceptual quality for joint 2D-3D restoration from event-camera data, balancing accuracy with efficiency and enabling geometry-aware, real-time rendering through a bidirectional, tightly coupled 2D-3D framework.

title: BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research
summary: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

AI.tldr: BrainPilot is an open-source, multi-agent framework for brain science that uses a PI agent to coordinate domain-specialist agents, with a traceable Graph of Trace and an Auditor to ensure integrity. It relies on a large knowledge base and a library of reusable methodologies, evaluated on standard tasks and a new BrainPilotBench-v0 benchmark, achieving competitive performance at lower cost.
AI.motivation: To address the need for cross-scale, cross-modality brain science reasoning with auditable, domain-informed AI assistance. Current agents often lack domain expertise, risk fabricating claims, and drift in multi-step reasoning, which is costly in brain science where results influence downstream research and require expert intervention.
AI.method: A PI agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in a curated brain science knowledge base (7,233 items) and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven domains. All major steps are recorded in the Graph of Trace, linking subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims. An Auditor agent integrates fabrication checking. Evaluation includes three brain science tasks from Agents’ Last Exam, a new BrainPilotBench-v0 benchmark, and end-to-end case studies, using an open-source backbone model.
AI.result: BrainPilot achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks while reducing costs, leveraging traceability and domain-aware components to enhance reliability and reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: BrainPilot demonstrates that an open-source, auditable, domain-informed multi-agent system can accelerate brain science research by providing structured workflows, verifiable results, and accessible intervention points for researchers.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging
summary: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

AI.tldr: Semantic-aware multimodal contrastive learning (MseaCL) mitigates semantically similar false negatives in medical data by leveraging radiology report similarity, improving downstream pediatric brain MRI tasks; pretraining yields notable AUC gains (≥22.6%).
AI.motivation: Address false negatives in instance-based CL when cross-modal samples share high-level semantic attributes in healthcare.
AI.method: Train on pediatric 3D brain MRI and radiology reports; incorporate radiology report semantic similarity as guiding signals during contrastive learning; apply as a pretraining stage.
AI.result: Demonstrates improvements in downstream tasks; specifically at least a 22.6% AUC increase for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aware CL can produce more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical contexts; further validation across modalities and cohorts is warranted.

title: Video = World + Event Stream
summary: We present Wan-Streamer v0.3, which reframes our native-streaming interaction model under a single organizing view: a video is a world plus an event stream. The world is the persistent context in which a video unfolds, including the environment, scene, subjects, ambient acoustic conditions, voice characteristics, and other relatively stable conditions. The event stream is everything that changes over time within that world, including scene or environmental changes, subject behavior, speech, and other sounds. This yields a general-purpose pretraining task over large amounts of real video: given a world and incoming input, predict how the world moves, changes, and responds in real time. The resulting competence can be specialized to a broad family of real-time downstream tasks. We instantiate it on real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction, where the event stream is the agent's speech together with free-form behavior. Functionally, the model's multimodal understanding process is vision-language-action-like: it maps multimodal user input to language-form speech and behavior actions. Wan-Streamer v0.3 preserves the v0.2 operating point: 640x368 video at 25 FPS, a 160 ms streaming unit, approximately 200 ms model-side response latency, and approximately 550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.

AI.tldr: Wan-Streamer v0.3 reframes real-time video understanding as a world plus event-stream model to enable general-purpose pretraining for real-time multimodal interaction, achieving real-time latency targets on a fixed-resolution video feed.
AI.motivation: Create a unified, scalable pretraining objective that captures both persistent world context and dynamic events to support real-time audio-visual interaction tasks.
AI.method: Define a world (stable context) and an event stream (time-varying aspects). Train on large real video so that, given world and incoming input, the model predicts world evolution in real time. Instantiate for real-time full-duplex audio-visual interaction with a 640x368, 25 FPS video, 160 ms streaming unit, ~200 ms model-side latency, and ~550 ms total interaction latency under a 350 ms bidirectional network budget.
AI.result: Demonstrates a general-purpose pretraining framework and its specialization to real-time audio-visual interaction, maintaining specified latency characteristics and operating point.
AI.conclusion: The world+event-stream framing enables a broad family of real-time downstream tasks via a unified pretraining objective, with practical latency guarantees for interactive applications.

title: Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) enables long-context training under memory constraints by segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage, achieving far longer effective sequence lengths with modest VRAM and competitive accuracy compared to dense attention; HGA's throughput improves as context grows.
AI.motivation: Dense attention makes long training sequences expensive in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The goal is to push context length far beyond standard attention limits while keeping memory and compute in check for adapters (e.g., 4-bit QLoRA) and production-scale models.
AI.method: Introduce Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Active segments remain differentiable; older KV are detached to RAM or NVMe. HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens per query block. Evaluations run on Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, comparing against dense attention.
AI.result: On a 16 GB GPU, dense training fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096; HGA scales to 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Training runs up to 131,072 tokens with memory growing gently as resident chunk summaries accumulate; RAM/NVMe capacity becomes the practical limit. At 2K length, HGA-trained adapters achieve 2.7405 nat vs 2.7383 nat for dense-trained adapters (dense readout), while the stock model achieves 2.9541 nat. HGA is marginally faster at 2K (217.75 vs 207.02 tokens/s). The HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K as context grows. Dense attention is used for main quality comparisons to remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA also supports retrieval/generation, with production-grade serving under development.
AI.conclusion: HGA enables scalable, memory-efficient long-context training for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. It maintains comparable quality to dense attention at short contexts while dramatically extending feasible context lengths and offering better throughput growth as context expands. Practical limits are set by RAM/NVMe capacity, and a production-grade serving solution is in progress.

title: Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits
summary: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

AI.tldr: Introduces Kernel-WIS, a kernel-based off-policy evaluation estimator for offline contextual bandits. It is asymptotically consistent and empirically surpasses strong baselines (including vanilla WIS), especially under behavior-policy misspecification.
AI.motivation: Address the high-variance, potentially biased issues of existing off-policy evaluation methods when using offline data in contextual bandits, and to provide robustness to misspecified behavior policies.
AI.method: Kernel-WIS uses kernel smoothing to bound importance weights (combining the boundedness of vanilla WIS) while exploiting the linearity of importance sampling. This yields a biased- but asymptotically consistent- estimator with improved finite-sample performance under misspecification.
AI.result: The estimator is shown to be asymptotically consistent and empirically outperforms strong baselines, including vanilla weighted importance sampling, across scenarios with complex misspecification and other challenging conditions.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-WIS offers a robust, scalable approach for offline OPE in contextual bandits, mitigating variance from extreme weights and improving performance relative to standard IS methods, particularly when the behaviour policy is misspecified.

title: Weakly-Supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection via SAM-driven Pseudo Annotation and State Space Interaction-based Diffusion
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, accepted by IEEE TMM
summary: Weakly-supervised RGB-D Salient Object Detection (SOD) is explored to reduce the heavy burden of pixel-level annotations. But scribble annotations lack the structure and details of objects, resulting in inaccurate saliency maps. In this paper, we propose a novel scribble-supervised RGB-D SOD method, consisting of a Segment Anything Model (SAM)-driven pseudo annotation generation method (\emph{SAM-PAG}) and a state space interaction-based conditional diffusion model (\emph{$S^2$Diff}). Specifically, SAM-PAG is tailored to address the issue of sparse supervision information. In SAM-PAG, we adopt the advanced SAM to expand sparse scribbles to dense pixel-level pseudo annotations through the dual-branch structure and the consistency of segmentation masks. In $S^2$Diff, we adopt the diffusion model to iteratively refine the noisy saliency maps with the guidance of conditional information, generating accurate saliency maps. Naturally, the core of our $S^2$Diff lies in the acquisition of conditional features and the denoising of saliency maps.
